161 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.27.3 The Committee takes note of the Department of Health and Family Welfare’s 
detailed clarification and the subsequent improvement in fund uti lization under several 
national programmes, particularly the National Programme for Prevention and 
Management of Trauma and Burns , the National Programme for Prevention and 
Control of Non -Communicable Diseases (NP -NCD), and the National Programme for 
Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE) , where utilization has significantly increased 
following administrative approvals. The Committee, nevertheless, is worried over the 
persistently low utilization under the National Mental Health Programme (NMHP) , 
which reflects  systemic bottlenecks such as delays in meeting financial compliance 
conditions, weak state -level implementation capacity, and inadequate coordination 
mechanisms. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to institute a 
robust monitoring and acco untability framework with quarterly financial and physical 
progress tracking to ensure that fund release is linked to performance indicators  rather 
than mere administrative compliance. Further, dedicated capacity -building and 
technical support units should  be strengthened further at the state level to assist with 
financial management and reporting. The Committee also recommends that the 
Department of Expenditure and Department of Health and Family Welfare must  
streamline procedural requirements for fund rel ease under centrally sponsored 
schemes, particularly for mental health interventions, so that programme delivery is not 
hampered by administrative delays. A mid-year utilization review  mechanism may also 
be instituted to identify underperforming components  and allow timely reallocation of 
unspent funds to more efficient programmes. 
 
 
3.28 Human Resource for Health and Medical Education 
Recommendations/Observations 
3.28.1 The Committee observes with concern that in the FY 2023 -24, the BE allocation 
amounting to Rs. 6500 crore was significantly reduced to Rs. 1519.87 crore at RE stage 
reflecting into huge decline by 76.62%. The Committee wishes to express further concern that 
even this reduced amount at RE stage could not be utilized fully (Actual expenditure 2023-24 
is Rs. 1321.78 crore). Adding to the woes, in the FY 2024-25 also, the budgetary allocation of 
Rs. 1274.79 crore at BE stage was decreased to Rs. 579.12 crore at RE stage.  The reduction 
in budgetary allocation under the Scheme become more alarming  and attention seeking of 
budget planner particularly when the Scheme contains components of establishment of new 
medical colleges attached with district/referral hospitals, up -gradation of State Government 
Medical Colleges for increasing the MBBS seats an d PG seats.  On the one hand, the 
Government aims at increasing patient -doctor ratio as per WHO norm for ensuring better 
health care and on the other hand, Government is significantly reducing the budgetary 
allocation.  The Government must adopt the prudent budgetary process. 
 
(Para 4.6.2 of the report) 

162 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.28.2 The recommendations of the Committee have been noted. At present, the committed 
liabilities under the schemes amount to Rs. 6,312.37 crores. The funds under the scheme are 
sanctioned based on the demands raised by the States/UTs and submission of Utilization 
Certificates in a given financial year. However, many States/UTs have struggled to raise 
demand due to non-release of matching state share. Some of the other possible reasons for t he 
same are litigations, land issues and other clearances issues. 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.28.3 The Committee takes note of the explanation submitted by the Department of 
Health and Family Welfare regarding the underutilization of funds and the reduction in 
budgetary allocation under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for the establishment of 
new medical colleges and upgradation of existing government medical colleges. While 
the Committee acknowledges that factors such as delays in the release of matching Stat e 
share, land -related issues, and pending clearances have contributed to slower 
implementation, the Committee is deeply concerned that these recurring administrative 
and procedural bottlenecks continue to impede the expansion of critical medical 
education infrastructure. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to 
establish a dedicated monitoring and coordination cell  to track project -wise progress, 
expedite resolution of State -level bottlenecks, and ensure timely submission of 
Utilization Certif icates. The Committee further urges the Department to engage 
proactively with State Governments through periodic high -level review meetings  to 
address issues related to land acquisition, statutory clearances, and financial 
compliance. The Committee also em phasizes the need for advance planning and phased 
fund release mechanisms  to prevent large -scale budget cuts at the RE stage and ensure 
steady progress in achieving the national goal of improving the doctor –population ratio 
in line with WHO norms. 
 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
3.28.4 The Committee recommends that the Department of Health and Family Welfare 
implement a proactive, multi-pronged strategy to ensure consistent and efficient utilization of 
allocated funds for the Human Resource for Health & Medi cal Education schemes by 
enhancing the absorption capacity. Specifically, given the recurring issues of underutilization 
due to lack of state demand, delayed state share release, and Real -time System of Integrated 
Quick Transfers (SNA SPARSH) compliance de lays, the Department should establish a 
dedicated task force to provide intensive, institutionalised support to each state and union 
territory. This task force will conduct pre -emptive assessments of state needs, offer hands -on 
assistance with SNA SPARSH c ompliance, and facilitate timely release of state matching 
funds through regular communication and problem -solving workshops. Furthermore, the 
Department should implement a quarterly review system that incorporates direct feedback 
from states, allowing for  real-time adjustments to funding allocations and program 

163 
 
implementation. This approach will not only address the immediate issue of underutilization 
but also build stronger collaborative relationships with states, ensuring the long -term success 
of expandi ng medical education infrastructure and increasing the availability of medical 
professionals. 
(Para 4.6.6 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.28.5 The recommendations of the committee have been noted. The Government is closely 
monitoring the utilization of fund s and implementation of the SNA SPARSH guidelines by 
the States/UTs through regular review meetings at various levels of the government.  At 
present, out of 21 States/UTs notified to be implemented on SNA SPARSH model, 14 States 
have been successfully on-boarded. Further, assistance and hand -holding of the States/UTs in 
implementation of the SNA SPARSH model for release of funds under the scheme is being 
provided. 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.28.6 The Committee notes the submission of the Department in regard to 
implementation of the SNA SPARSH under Human Resource for Health and Medical 
Education system and the progress made in onboarding 14 out of 21 States/UTs under 
the SNA SPARSH model and the ongoing efforts to provide assistance to remaining 
States. The Committee, however, expresses deep concern about the continued delays and 
uneven implementation of fund utilization mechanisms, which hinder the optimal 
execution of Human Resource for Health & Medical Education schemes. The 
Committee, therefore, reiterates  its earlier recommendation that a dedicated task force 
or coordination cell be formally constituted within the Department to provide targeted, 
state-specific technical and administrative support  for SNA SPARSH compliance and 
timely fund release. This cell should maintain a real-time digital dashboard  to monitor 
the status of each State/UT, identify bottlenecks early, and escalate unresolved issues to 
higher administrative levels for prompt resolu tion. The Committee also recommends 
that capacity-building workshops  be institutionalized for State officials to strengthen 
their financial and procedural readiness. A system of quarterly performance grading of 
States based on fund utilization and compliance efficiency may further incentivize better 
performance and ensure sustained improvement in the absorption capacity and timely 
implementation of medical education and health workforce initiatives. 
 
3.29 Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM) 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
3.29.1 The Committee expresses concern over the declining trend of fund utilisation under 
PM-ABHIM during the last two financial years 2023-24 and 2024-25 i.e. 42.99% and 62.74% 
respectively, of the BE allocation that casts aspersion on absorption capacity of Sch eme and 

164 
 
the professional proficiency of implementing agency of the Scheme. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends a more streamlined and front -loaded disbursement process 
for the PM -ABHIM scheme as the scheme contain visionary aim and objective of 
Government to fill critical gaps in health infrastructure, surveillance and health research – 
spanning both the urban and rural areas so that the communities are Atmanirbhar in managing 
such pandemic/ health crises. The data clearly shows consistent underut ilization of allocated 
funds, particularly in the initial phases of each fiscal year, despite the capital intensive 
infrastructure project under the scheme. While the Department attributes this to the lead time 
of capital expenditure projects, the signific ant reductions from Budget Estimates to Revised 
Estimates indicate a predictable pattern of slow pace of expenditure. To address this, the 
Committee suggests that the Department implement a system where a larger portion of the 
annual budget is released dur ing the first quarter, contingent on states submitting detailed 
project implementation plans and timelines. This would allow for early initiation of 
infrastructure projects, reducing the lag time and ensuring more consistent expenditure 
throughout the fisc al year. Moreover, the Department should focus on providing technical 
assistance and capacity building to states to expedite project approvals and implementation, 
thereby mitigating delays and ensuring the timely achievement of the scheme's objectives. 
(Para 4.7.4 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.29.2 PM-ABHIM, an infrastructure initiative aimed at strengthening healthcare 
infrastructure down to the block level, operates as a capital grant. Consequently, the initial 
expenditure tends to be gradual due to the inherent lead time in infrastructure development. 
However, as the scheme approaches its final year, expenditure is anticipated to accelerate with 
the completion of ongoing projects.  To ensure appropriate expenditure progression, 
States/UTs were requested t o submit Quarterly Expenditure Plans (QEP), as outlined in the 
Ministry's D.O. letter dated April 7, 2025. Furthermore, in accordance with the Department of 
Expenditure (DoE) guidelines issued on July 13, 2023, August 4, 2023, October 4, 2024, and 
December 17, 2024, 31 States have been notified under the SNA SPARSH Platform for PM -
ABHIM, with 28 States already on boarded. This platform operates by providing States with 
expenditure limits rather than direct cash releases, enabling them to incur expenses by 
submitting daily payment files to the Ministry through their respective State Treasuries. In the 
new mechanism SNA SPARSH, up to 50% of the Allocated Budget can be given as Mother 
Sanction to the States, on request of the States, which the States can utiliz e till exhaustion of 
75% of the limit given and can apply for Mother Sanction for the remaining Budget.  
3.29.3 The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) actively monitors and 
evaluates the progress of all States/UTs through regular review meetings , video conferences, 
and field visits by senior officials. Additionally, regional and state -level workshops have been 
conducted to bolster the capacities of State Program Management Units (PMUs). These 
PMUs have been established within the States to offer essential technical and administrative 
support, thereby facilitating timely construction. Regional workshops were undertaken for 
providing technical assistance & capacity building. Moreover, Common Review Missions

(CRMs) are conducted periodically to asses s and monitor the scheme's progress and 
implementation status.

3.29.4 The Committee takes note of the detailed response of the Department and

Recommendations/Observations

families under AB-PMJAY Vay Vandana scheme, irrespective of their socio-economic status.

The Committee observes that an amount to the tune of Rs. 1443.00 c rore has been earmarked 
for treatment of senior citizens of the age of 70 years and above holding 
AyushmanVayVandna Cards.  The Committee is of the view that age criteria of 70 years and 
above for AyushmanVayVandna Cards should be rationalized to 60 years and above 
irrespective of their socio -economic status for widening the coverage of the scheme in the 
better interest of common masses. 
(Para 4.8.9 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.30.2 The recent expansion of AB-PMJAY to cover senior citizens aged 70 years and above 
under the AyushmanVay Vandana card initiative aims to provide equitable healthcare access 
to India‘s elderly population, regardless of their socio -economic status. Under this initiative, 
launched in October 2024, all senior citizens aged 70 years  and above, from approximately 
4.5 crore families (estimated 6 crore individuals), are eligible for free annual treatment 
benefits of up to Rs. 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization.  
As of 23rd April 2025, over 58 lakh senior citizens have already been enrolled under this 
scheme and a total of Rs. 1,443 crore has been earmarked in budget estimate 2025 -26 
specifically for the treatment of beneficiaries under the AyushmanVay Vandana Card 
expansion. The Department remains c ommitted to enhancing the inclusiveness and 
effectiveness of AB-PMJAY and will continue to explore ways to extend healthcare coverage 
to vulnerable sections of the population in a financially sustainable manner. 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.30.3 The Committee  appreciates the steps taken by the Department of Health and 
Family Welfare in implementing the Ayushman Vay Vandana initiative under AB -
PMJAY and acknowledges the impressive enrolment of over 58 lakh senior citizens and 
the dedicated budgetary provision o f ₹1,443 crore for their treatment. The Committee, 
however, observes that while the current coverage for citizens aged 70 years and above 
is a commendable beginning, it still excludes a large segment of the elderly population 
between 60 to 69 years who are  equally vulnerable to chronic and age -related diseases 
and may not have adequate financial means for quality healthcare. The Committee is 
pleased to observe that the Department is positive enough to continue and explore to 
extend healthcare coverage to vu lnerable section of the population. The Committee, 
therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation to revisit and rationalize the age criteria 
to include citizens aged 60 years and above , ensuring equitable healthcare protection for 
all senior citizens ir respective of socio -economic status. Further, the Committee 
recommends the Department to undertake a feasibility study  assessing the financial, 
infrastructural, and operational implications of such expansion. The Committee also 
suggests periodic evaluation of the scheme’s utilization patterns and health outcomes  to 
ensure that the benefits reach the intended beneficiaries and to support data -driven 
decisions for future expansions of universal health coverage under AB-PMJAY. 
 
 

167 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
3.30.4 The Committee, keeping in view huge expenditure on the critical healthcare, should 
revise healthcare coverage from existing Rs. 5 lakh per family per year to Rs. 10 lakh per 
family per year. 
(Para 4.8.11 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.30.5 The Committee‘s recommendation to increase the healthcare coverage under the 
Ayushman Bharat-Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB -PMJAY) from Rs. 5 lakh to Rs. 
10 lakh per family per year, considering the high costs of critical healthcare, is noted. As per 
current utilization trends, 99.4% of cases involve wallet utilization of less than Rs. 2,00,000 
per family, demonstrating that the existing Rs. 5 lakh cover adequately addresses the 
hospitalization needs of the vast majority of beneficiaries. For rare cases i nvolving prolonged 
illnesses or high -end procedures requiring additional financial support, the Rashtriya Arogya 
Nidhi (RAN) scheme provides assistance of up to Rs. 15 lakh to patients from poor families, 
including those eligible under SECC criteria for AB -PMJAY, for treatments not covered by 
the scheme. This complementary mechanism ensures that critical healthcare needs are met 
without imposing financial burdens on beneficiaries. Therefore, it can be understood that AB 
PM-JAY along with other schemes of Go vt of India are able to cater to the hospitalization 
requirement of the majority of the eligible beneficiaries. 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.30.6 The Committee takes into consideration  the plea of the Department that the 
existing coverage of ₹5 lakh per famil y under AB -PMJAY meets the hospitalization 
needs of most beneficiaries, and that additional financial protection is available under 
the Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi (RAN) for critical cases. The Committee is , however, of the 
considered view that the rising cost of advanced medical procedures, specialized  
treatments, and long -term care  necessitates a progressive enhancement of financial 
coverage under AB-PMJAY. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry 
undertake a comprehensive actuarial and utilizati on study  to assess the financial and 
operational feasibility of increasing the insurance ceiling to ₹10 lakh per family, keeping 
in view high cost of treatment of patients with chronic, life -threatening disease. 
Alternatively, as an interim measure the Department may consider for strengthening the 
integration between AB -PMJAY and RAN  to ensure seamless support for beneficiaries 
requiring extended or repeated treatments, and to develop an automatic top -up 
mechanism for families exhausting their coverage limi t under AB -PMJAY. This 
calibrated approach would ensure enhanced financial protection and accessible 
treatment of patients under PMJAY while maintaining fiscal sustainability and 
equitable access to critical healthcare.

3.31 Coverage of OPD Services and Cost of Medicine under the Ayushman Bharat 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
3.31.1 The Committee recommends the phased inclusion of essential OPD services and a 
broader range of post -hospitalization medication coverage within the Ayushman Bharat 
PMJAY scheme. While acknowledging the scheme's focus on secondary and tertiary inpatient 
care, the current exclusion of routine OPD services and limited post -hospitalization 
medication coverage creates a significant gap in accessible healthcare. To ensure continuity 
and build upon the existing framework, the recommendation should propose a phased 
approach, starting with the inclusion of essential OPD services for chronic diseases and 
commonly reported ailments. Furthermore, extending post -hospitalization medication 
coverage beyond the current 15 -day limit, particularly for conditions requiring prolonged 
treatment, would significantly reduce the financial burden on beneficiaries while addressing a 
need for comprehensive healthcare access. 
(Para 5.11.2 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.31.2 The Committee's recommendations regarding the phased inclusion of essential OPD 
services and extended post -hospitalization medication coverage under the Ayushman Bharat 
PMJAY scheme are duly noted.  It is to be noted that in the current  framework, medication 
costs are covered during hospitalization and for 15 days‘ post -discharge under AB PM -JAY. 
Additionally, free OPD services are available through the Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM) 
network as part of the broader Ayushman Bharat initiativ e. AB PM-JAY presently focuses on 
secondary and tertiary inpatient care. 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.31.3 The Committee notes the response of the Department that outpatient services are 
currently provided through the Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM) network and that 
AB-PMJAY focuses primarily on secondary and tertiary inpatient care. While 
acknowledging the complementary role of AAM in providing OPD services, the 
Committee is of the view that the absence of integrated OPD and extended post -
hospitalization medicat ion coverage within AB -PMJAY limits continuity of care  and 
increases the out -of-pocket burden, especially for patients with chronic and long -term 
conditions. The Committee, therefore, urges the Department to initiate a pilot project in 
select districts to assess the feasibility of including essential OPD consultations, 
diagnostic services, and post-hospitalization medication coverage beyond the current 15-
day limit, viz.up to 30 or 45 days,  under AB -PMJAY for continuity of treatment of 
disease under single umbrella. This pilot should focus particularly on non-
communicable diseases and geriatric care , where follow -up treatment and medication 
adherence are critical. Based on the outcomes of this pilot, a phased national roll -out 
scheme may be undertaken to ens ure a seamless continuum of care between AAM and 

169 
 
AB-PMJAY, thereby enhancing accessibility, affordability, and overall health outcomes 
for beneficiaries. 
 
3.32 Misuse of Fund under AB-PMJAY Scheme 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
3.32.1 The Committee recommends the National Health Authority (NHA) implement a 
proactive, data -driven, and transparent monitoring system focusing on early detection of 
potential misuse patterns in AB -PMJAY. This system should go beyond reacting to reported 
fraud by continuously analysing claim data, hospital activity, and patient feedback to identify 
statistical anomalies and emerging trends indicating potential abuse. Specifically, the NHA 
should develop and publicly report on key performance indicators related to fraud detec tion, 
including the frequency of pre -authorization requests for specific procedures, the ratio of 
medical camp referrals to hospital admissions, and the rates of hospital de -empanelment and 
penalties by state. In the collection and analysis of statistical data and feedback, the extensive 
use of AI and digital tools should be considered upon by the Department. This transparent, 
data-driven approach will not only allow for quicker intervention but also serve as a deterrent, 
ensuring the scheme's resources are  used for their intended purpose and maintaining public 
trust.  
(Para 5.12.4 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.32.2 A proactive, data -driven, and technology -enabled monitoring framework has been 
established under the Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) to 
enable early detection and deterrence of misuse and fraudulent activities. NHA has developed 
a multi -layered surveillance ecosystem that goes beyond reactive investigation and ensures 
continuous monitoring of claim patterns, hospital b ehaviours, and beneficiary interactions.  
Key Measures and Systems Implemented: - 
(i) National and State Anti -Fraud Units (NAFU and SAFUs):  
Dedicated anti-fraud teams have been established to investigate irregularities, coordinate 
with State Health Agencies (SH As), and enforce penal actions such as de -empanelment, 
blacklisting, and financial recovery. 
(ii) FACTS and RADAR Dashboards:The Fraud Control Tracking System (FACTS) and Risk 
Assessment Detection and Analytical Reporting (RADAR) dashboards support real -time 
tracking, reporting, and resolution of suspicious activities. These tools identify anomalies 
in hospitalization trends, claim volume surges, and procedural patterns. 
 
(iii) Advanced Fraud Detection Triggers: The fraud detection framework has evolved from 
basic rule-based filters to a sophisticated system of AI -enabled triggers, including:  
 
 Image Deduplication: Detects use of duplicate or manipulated images to prevent multiple 
enrolments and fraudulent claims. 

170 
 
 Forged Document Sampling: Applies image processing al gorithms to identify tampering 
techniques like copy-move or external element insertions in medical documentation. 
 Document Similarity Analysis (OCR): Extracts text from scanned documents and 
performs word-level comparisons to identify manipulated or recycled documents based on 
similarity percentages. 
 Social Network Analysis: Uses Graph Theory to detect interconnected fraud networks, or 
cartels, through linkages among beneficiaries, hospitals, and service providers. 
 Image Segmentation: Segregates and validat es clinical elements within medical 
documents to ensure authenticity of diagnostic and treatment-related data. 
 Facial Comparison Technology: Matches reference photos with claim -related images to 
detect impersonation and identity fraud during admissions and card creation. 
 These automated triggers enable real -time detection and intervention, ensuring that 
fraudulent entities are swiftly identified and deterred. 
(iv) Public Reporting and Transparency:Periodic reporting on fraud detection outcomes, de -
empanelment, penalties imposed, and recoveries made are encouraged to promote 
accountability. As of date, over 1,100 hospitals have been de -empanelled and significant 
financial recoveries and penalties have been imposed across various States. 
 
3.32.3 The Department con tinues to strengthen its anti -fraud capabilities through emerging 
technologies and advanced analytics to ensure optimal utilization of public resources and to 
safeguard the integrity of the scheme. 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.32.4 The Committee appreciates t he comprehensive and technology -driven measures 
adopted by the Department and the NHA for fraud detection and prevention under AB -
PMJAY, including the establishment of National and State Anti -Fraud Units (NAFU 
and SAFUs), deployment of AI -enabled analytical tools, and creation of the FACTS and 
RADAR dashboards. These efforts mark a commendable shift toward proactive 
surveillance and deterrence of misuse and fraudulent activities. The Committee observes 
that while significant progress has been made in intern al monitoring , however, there 
remains a need to institutionalize periodic public disclosure of performance indicators  
related to fraud detection, de -empanelment, and recovery actions to enhance 
transparency and public confidence. The Committee, therefore, recommends that NHA 
should publish a biannual ―Fraud and Integrity Report‖  detailing fraud detection 
trends, actions taken, and improvements in monitoring mechanisms at both national 
and state levels. Further, capacity-building programmes for State Anti -Fraud Units  
should be strengthened to ensure uniform standards of investigation and enforcement 
across all States. The Committee also suggests the integration of beneficiary feedback 
analytics and hospital audit outcomes  into the AI -driven monitoring framewo rk to 
create a more holistic, responsive, and publicly accountable system for safeguarding the 
integrity and trustworthiness of AB -PMJAY so as to make AB -PMJAY a popular 
scheme amongst common masses especially, rural, semi-urban and tribal areas.

3.33 Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme (PMNDP) 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
3.33.1 The Committee is of the view that the Dialysis facility under PMNDP should be given 
to the needy persons. The facility is being availed by persons who can afford treatment from 
their own pocket in private hospitals. The scheme provisions need to be reviewed. The 
Committee finds that the dialysis centres are at the district level at present, however, the 
Committee desires the Department should make strategy for sett ing up of Dialysis facility at 
the Taluka level also as kidney patients are increasing. 
(Para 5.13.3 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.33.2 The database for the Below Poverty Level (BPL) population is based on the 
Population Census held by Government of India  in 2011. The current assessment report for 
the number of BPL population is not available. The exact prevalence and incidence rate of 
chronic kidney disease is not known due to the absence of renal registry in the country.   The 
provision available under Pr adhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme (PMNDP) mandates 
free dialysis to the BPL category patients and the other patients (Non -BPL) who can afford 
dialysis in the private at subsidized cost. Currently, under NHM 100 % of the service 
procedure fees for patients from BPL economic group is covered. The PMNDP portal has the 
facility to register the BPL and Above Poverty Level (APL) financial status based on the 
entitlement card issued by the States/UTs at the time of new patient registration. A total of 
60,489 BPL patients and 16976 APL patients have been registered on the PMNDP portal 
since 1st January 2024 to 31st  December 2024. PMNDP was launched in FY 2016 -17 by 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare with the objective to have a dialysis centre in all the 
district hospitals across the States/UTs in the country. The programme has the provision for 
scaling up the dialysis services down below the District Hospital level till Taluka 
(Community Health Centres) based on demand gap assessment by the States/UTs. Few  States 
have already established dialysis care units at the Taluka level as implemented in the states of 
Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Goa, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Odisha, 
Tamil Nadu, Telangana, West Bengal & Kerala. 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.33.3 The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Department under the Pradhan 
Mantri National Dialysis Programme (PMNDP) in ensuring free dialysis services to BPL 
patients and the initiative taken by several States to extend dialysis facilities to the 
Taluka level. The Committee, however, notes with concern that the reliance on the 
outdated 2011 Census data for determining BPL status may lead to the exclusion of 
genuinely needy patients and the inclusion of non -eligible beneficiaries. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department, in coordination with the States/UTs, 
should develop an updated, verifiable, and dynamic beneficiary database  leveraging 
digital health platforms such as ABHA ID and SECC data to ensure accurate 

172 
 
identification of economically weaker patients. Further, to address the growing burden 
of chronic kidney disease, the Committee urges the Department to expedite the scaling 
up of dialysis centres to all Taluka -level Community Health Centres (CHCs)  through a 
time-bound natio nal expansion plan, ensuring equitable geographic access. The 
Committee also emphasizes the need for the creation of a National Renal Registry  to 
generate reliable epidemiological data for effective planning, monitoring, and resource 
allocation under PMNDP  and take into stock actual number of renal patients so that 
fresh policy initiative can be undertaken.

3.36 Accessible and Affordable Treatment of Rare Diseases 
Recommendations/Observations 
3.36.1 The Committee notes that 63 rare diseases are covered under National Policy for Rare 
Diseases (NPRD) which of course needs to be reviewed and expanded from time to time. In 
order to make the treatment of rare diseases accessible and affordable, the Department may 
make provision for cheaper diagnosis, prevention and treatment. The Committee also desires 
that the Department should launch national campaign/awareness programme for seeking 
treatment of the rare diseases. 
(Para 5.19.3 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.36.2 Under the National policy of Rare Dise ases (NPRD) 2021, there is a mechanism for 
review and expansion of Rare Disease. The Central Technical Committee for Rare Diseases 
(CTCRD) under the Chairmanship of DGHS is mandated to periodically review the list of 
diseases under Group 1, Group 2 and Gro up 3 based on updated scientific data by the 
Technical Committee which includes experts from the field. The Committee after discussion 
within Institutional Rare Disease Committee at CoE, Nodal Officer submit a detailed write -up 
about the disease, for discu ssion and consideration for inclusion of the disease under NPRD 
2021 to Central Technical Committee for Rare Diseases (CTCRD). Since the inception of the 
NPRD 2021, 14 rare diseases in addition to existing mentioned in the policy, have been 
included under NPRD 2021, following a robust and scientific process.  To promote Research in 
the field of rare diseases, DHR -ICMR has launched two major initiatives for the prevention and 
control of rare diseases: - 
 
 DHR-ICMR Program for Indigenous Therapeutics for Rare D iseases: This program 
promotes industry -academia partnerships. Academia and R&D organizations receive 
funding through ICMR‘s extramural program, while industry partners focus on drug 
development, with ICMR supporting preclinical, clinical research, and reg ulatory 
approvals. The goal is to develop indigenous therapies for clinical use, with intellectual 
property remaining with the inventor and drugs being marketed at affordable prices. 
 
 DHR-ICMR-National Registry for Rare and Other Inherited Disorders: Estab lished in 
2019, this ongoing, multi -centre hospital-based registry collects comprehensive data on 
individuals diagnosed with rare diseases. Currently, it holds information on over 15,400 
patients. The registry includes data on various disorders like Storag e Disorders, Inborn 
Errors of Metabolism, Skeletal Dysplasia, and more. Contributing centres from 14 states 
and union territories ensure nationwide representation. The registry aligns with the 
National Policy on Rare Diseases (NPRD) and informs government efforts, with plans to 
integrate the registry with a National Rare Disease Information Portal, which will be 
completed in three months. 
 
3.36.3 The MoHFW identified 8 Centres of Excellence (CoE) for Rare Diseases under NPRD 
2021, which have now been extend ed to 13 in 12 States/UTs across the country. These are 
premier Government tertiary hospitals with facilities for diagnosis, prevention and treatment 

176 
 
of rare diseases.  The responsibilities and activities of the Centres of Excellence (COEs) 
identified under the policy are as follows: - 
 Education & Training at all levels  
 Screening – Antenatal, neonatal (specified disorders), High risk screening (Both antenatal 
& in new-borns and children)  
 Diagnostics- Cytogenetic, molecular, Metabolic  
 Prevention by prenatal screening &diagnosis  
 Research in the area of low-cost diagnostics & therapeutics.  
 Treatment of rare diseases.  
 
3.36.4 As per NPRD 2021, based on the recommendations of the technical committee, more 
CoEs can be added for regional o utreach if they are found to be suitable in terms of 
infrastructure and human resources. To strengthen the infrastructure of the CoEs identified 
under the policy and to facilitate early diagnosis to enable further course of treatment the 
COEs are given one -time financial support up to a ceiling of Rs 5 crore for procurement of 
equipment as per individual centers need for screening, diagnosis and prevention (prenatal 
diagnosis) of rare diseases based on a gap analysis. In addition, financial support for purc hase 
of consumables for diagnosis is also supported under ‗Materials and Supplies‘ budget head to 
CoEs. The Central Government has given full exemption from Basic Custom Duty (BCD) and 
Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) on most of the drugs and Food for Special 
Medical Purposes (FSMP) imported for personal use or through CoEs for rare diseases for 
treatment of all rare diseases listed under the NPRD 2021 through a general exemption 
notification. To increase the awareness about Rare Diseases, the MoHFW  observe Rare 
Disease Day on the last day of February. This year in 2025, sensitization workshops for 
raising awareness of medical professionals were organized in 11 States/UTs by CoEs from the 
month of Jan – Feb 2025 with support from MoHFW.  
Further Recommendation 
 
3.36.5 The Committee acknowledges the significant progress in expanding the scope of 
the National Policy for Rare Diseases (NPRD) 2021, viz. the inclusion of additional 
diseases, establishment of 13 Centres of Excellence (CoEs), and the launch of initiatives 
such as the National Registry and the Indigenous Therapeutics Programme. The 
Committee observes that awareness, early diagnosis, and affo rdability of treatment 
remain key challenges , particularly in rural and underserved areas. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry intensify its national awareness and outreach 
campaign through collaboration with State Governments, medical i nstitutions, and civil 
society organizations to ensure greater public and professional understanding of rare 
diseases. Further, the Committee urges the Department to expedite the 
operationalization of the National Rare Disease Information Portal  and integrate it with 
the CoEs and the National Registry for real -time data sharing, patient tracking, and 
referral facilitation. The Committee also recommends increasing the number of CoEs 
across all regions , particularly in the North -East and smaller States, to im prove 
accessibility. In addition, affordable diagnostic and therapeutic solutions should be 

177 
 
prioritized under the DHR -ICMR Indigenous Therapeutics Programme  with defined 
timelines for clinical translation. The Committee emphasizes that a dedicated National 
Awareness and Prevention Mission on Rare Diseases  may be launched and promote 
early detection, genetic counseling, and social support mechanisms for affected families.

Recommendations/Observations

3.37.13 Continuous Glucose Monitors (CGMs) and diabetic medicines are essential for 
effective diabetes management which is a chronic disease condition. However, the high cost 
of CGMs, their limited lifespan and the lack of long -term insurance coverage for these 
devices and medicines create significant challenges for patients. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends increasing the lifespan of CGM sensors, implementing pri ce controls and price 
caps on CGM sensors, cardiac stents, etc., mandating insurance coverage for CGMs and 
diabetic medicines on a long term basis to ensure affordability and accessibility. The 
Committee further desires that ‗Make in India‘ initiative shou ld be promoted to reduce prices 
and achieve self-sufficiency in CGM production. 
(Para 5.20(xii) of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.37.14 Continuous Glucose Monitoring devices (CGM) device provides real -time 
glucose readings, helping individuals and healthcare providers better manage blood sugar 
levels and prevent complications. CGM devices are primarily used by individuals with 
diabetes, particularly those who use insulin to manage their condition, to help them monitor 
and manage their blood sugar levels in rea l-time.CGMs are especially beneficial for people 
with type 1 diabetes who rely on insulin to manage their condition. The lifespan of a CGMS 
(Continuous Glucose Monitoring System) sensor, like most CGM sensors, is designed to 
function optimally for 7 to 14 days. However, the implantable sensors life span can last for a 
longer period, such as 90 days.  The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has 
focused on regulating prices of essential medicines and medical devices. Specific information 
available about a rate ceiling for CGM devices in not available, however, the proposal can be 
sent to NPPA for their consideration.  The "Make in India" initiative aims to reduce import 
costs and make CGM technology more accessible by promoting local manufacturing. Make in 
India initiatives are driving the development and manufacturing of CGM devices, with 
companies like Beurer India and Abbott launching products like the GL 22 and Free Style 
Libre, respectively, to cater to the Indian market.  
Further Recommendation 
 
3.37.15 The Committee acknowledges the response of the Department 
highlighting the current operational lifespan of CGM sensors especially beneficial in 
type-I diabetes, the potential for longer -lasting implantable sensors, the role of NPPA in 
price regul ation, and the efforts under the ―Make in India‖ initiative to encourage 
indigenous production of CGMs. The Committee observes with deep concern over the 
absence of concrete regulatory intervention on pricing and insurance coverage that 
continue to make CG Ms and essential diabetic medicines unaffordable for a large 

183 
 
segment of patients especially who rely on insulin to manage , particularly those 
requiring lifelong monitoring and medication. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Department, in coordin ation with NPPA and IRDAI, formulate a 
comprehensive framework for price regulation, insurance inclusion, and procurement of 
CGMs and diabetic medicines under national health schemes, ensuring affordability and 
equitable access. The Committee further recom mends that the Department should 
support domestic research and development, and large -scale production of CGMs 
through targeted incentives, public –private partnerships, and expedited approval 
processes under the ―Make in India‖ initiative , to reduce import  dependency and 
achieve long -term self -reliance in diabetes management technologies. The Committee 
also desires that the Department must explore mechanisms to extend the lifespan and 
cost-effectiveness of CGM sensors through innovation and standardization , in 
consultation with industry and scientific experts.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS  - AT   A  GLANCE 
 
Staff Strength in the Department 
 
1. The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry in pursuing the 
matter of vacancies with the Cadre Controlling Authorities concerned, thereby resulting 
into reduction of 123 vacant posts  due to posting of 63Assistant Statistical Officers and 
60 Multi Tasking Staff. The Committee,  however, observes that despite the  efforts so 
made, a substantial number of 305 posts still remains  vacant, which may yet continue to 
hamper the administrative efficienc y and timely execution of the Ministry’s 
programmes and schemes. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry 
adopt a time-bound action plan, in coordination with the Cadre Controlling Authorities 
and recruiting agencies, to fill up the remaining  305 vacant posts at the earliest so that 
the functional proficiency of the Ministry is optimised and set objectives of various plans 
are achieved without any stumbling block. 
(Para 3.1.3 of the ATR) 
 
Budgetary Projection vis-a-vis Allocation and Expenditure 
 
2. The Committee is of the opinion that health is a multiplier sector of the economy, 
determining productive capital formation and capacity building.  Therefore, the 
Government needs to invest maximally to build other significan t superstructures of the 
economy. The Committee is not appreciative of the plea of the Department of 
highlighting budgetary allocation of too wide base years that is BE 2013 -14 and BE 
2025-26.The Committee observes that despite the increase in the absolute  budgetary 
figures i.e., from Rs. 35,063 crore in BE 2013 -14  to Rs. 95,957. 87 crore  in BE 2025-26, 
the health expenditure continues to remain low as a proportion of GDP i.e. 0.3% at 
current price. The Committee, therefore,  emphasizes that sustained under -projection of 
demand may constrain the human capacity building of the nation to address emerging 
challenges and achieve national health targets. The Committee,  in this regard, 
recommends that the Ministry adopt need-driven approach while projecting its financial 
requirement, ensuring realistic estimation of financial requirement under continuing 
health plans and Schemes/ programmes/ projects as well as futuristic plans and projects. 
The Committee further urges the Ministry to engage with the Ministry of Fi nance to 
progressively enhance the projected demand of health sector with a view to achieving 
the national goal of increasing public health expenditure to at least 2.5% of GDP in line 
with the National Health Policy,2017. 
(Para 3.2.3 of the ATR) 
 
3. The Committee applauds the initiatives taken by the Ministry, including its 
engagement with States to enhance their health budgets to 8% of total State budget, the 
provision of health grants through the 15th Finance Commission, and the 
implementation of th e Pradhan Mantri –Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure 

189 
 
Mission (PM-ABHIM) to strengthen healthcare infrastructure and preparedness. While 
these steps are commendable, the Committee observes that the overall public health 
expenditure continues to remain bel ow the National Health Policy, 2017 target of 2.5% 
of GDP. The Committee, therefore, reiterates the need for the Ministry to pursue the 
matter vigorously with the Ministry of Finance to secure higher allocations in 
forthcoming budget cycles, particularly i n light of rising inflation, population growth, 
and post -pandemic healthcare needs.  The Committee believes that the Department 
would work upon further to eliminate gaps by addressing lacuna in the healthcare 
system and seek requisite fund from the 16 th Finance Commission. The Committee 
further recommends the Ministry to establish measurable outcome indicators to monitor 
the effective utilization of funds under PM -ABHIM and ensure that both Central and 
State governments align their health budget priorities with the broader goal of achieving 
equitable, accessible, and resilient healthcare infrastructure across the country. 
(Para 3.2.6 of the ATR) 
 
4. The Committee understands that  capital expenditure inherently fluctuates based 
on the pace and stage of project s, and that the social service nature of the Department 
limits its scope, however, the Committee emphasizes the importance of forward-looking 
planning for raising healthcare infrastructure in far flung rural, semi rural and tribal 
areas and strengthening the primary, Secondary and tertiary healthcare hospitals where 
centrally sponsored schemes are required to be launched and implemented with due  
impetus. The Committee, therefore, feels that the Ministry should develop a 'pipeline' 
document that, while accounting for the fluctuating nature of capital demands, maps out 
the planned trajectory of major infrastructure and capital creation projects  (including 
GIA-Capital) over a three to five -year period. This strategic document should clearly 
articulate the projected annual requirement and justification  for capital funds, thereby 
enabling more predictable and sustained year -on-year growth  in capital allocations 
(even if actual expenditure fluctuates) and  thereby ensuring that the budget process i s 
driven by pre-determined development goals  besides considering the recurring annual 
demands and project status. 
(Para 3.2.9 of the ATR) 
 
Government Health Expenditure in India 
 
5. The Committee appreciates the sustained effortsof the Department of Health  and 
Family to expand healthcare access and affordability through flagship initiatives such as 
NHM, PMJAY, PM -ABHIM, ABDM, and PMBJP, which have collectively contributed 
to the reduction in Out -of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE) and enhancement of healthcare 
infrastructure. The Committee also acknowledges the steady rise in Government Health 
Expenditure as a share of GDP and Total Health Expenditure. However, the Committee 
observes that OOPE at 39.4%in 2021 -22 still remains considerably high, particularly 
given I ndia’s large population living in poverty and vulnerable socio -economic 
conditions. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry intensify its focus 
on strengthening primary healthcare delivery through Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, 

190 
 
ensuring wider coverage of free drugs and diagnostics, and improving the efficiency and 
reach of Jan AushadhiKendras in rural and remote areas. Further, the Committee urges 
the Ministry to establish a clear roadmap with measurable milestones for reducing 
OOPE below 20%within the next two years by deepening financial protection under 
PMJAY, enhancing State -level health spending, and improving public awareness of 
available government health schemes and services. 
(Para 3.3.4 of the ATR) 
 
6. The Committee commends the steady increase in Government Health 
Expenditure (GHE) both as a share of GDP and of Total Health Expenditure (THE), as 
well as the corresponding decline in Out -of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE), reflecting the 
Government’s commitment to strengthening public health fi nancing.  The 
Committee,however,observes that despite this progress, India’s GHE remains 
significantly below global benchmarks, particularly those of high -income countries 
where the higher volumeof health expenditure is fundedby Governments of the 
countries. The Committee, therefore, reiterates that the Government should continue to 
enhance GHE in a phased and sustained manner to achieve the National Health Policy 
target of 2.5% of GDP from existing 1.84% as share of GDPwithin projected time 
frame. The Comm ittee further recommends that the Departmentmustundertake a 
comparative study of successful international health financing models to identify 
adaptable best practices for India’sinvestment on healthcare sector. The Committee 
alsourges the Department to ens ure effective convergence and coordination among key 
national health missions and schemes so that increased expenditure directly translates 
into improved service delivery, equitable access, and further reduction of OOPE for the 
wholepopulation, especially among vulnerable and low-income groups. 
(Para 3.3.7 of the ATR) 
 
7. The Committee takes into account the response of the Department which 
attributes that the data lag to the inherent process of compiling actual expenditure from 
Central and State Governments. The Committee notes with concern that the NHA 
Estimates are available at an 18-month lag , while currently preparing the NHA for 
2022-23, confirms the systematic nature of the delay but the Department fails to outline 
any measure to mitigate its impact. The Committee does not agree with plea of the 
Department for the operational necessity for an 18 -month lag in utilizing confirmed 
actual expenditure data, the Committee, however, recommends that the Department

comprehensive, continuous, and transparent q uality control mechanism is essential to

due to high domestic demand and lack of a structured framework. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, in coordination 
with the Ministries of Tourism and External Affairs, develop a comprehensive National 
Medical and Wellness Tourism Strategy  with a clear roadmap for leveraging both 
public and private healthcare infrastructure. Such strategy should include identification 
of select public hospitals with spare capacity to serve international patients , 
establishment of Medical Tourism Facilitation Cells , and formulation of standardized 
service and pricing protocols  to ensure quality and transparency. The Committee 
further recommends creating a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model for capacity 
building, accreditation, and international promotion , supported by targeted training for 
healthcare workers and seamless vi sa facilitation for medical travelers. Such a 
coordinated and institutionalized approach will not only enhance India’s global 
reputation in medical and wellness tourism but also generate additional revenue for 
reinvestment in the public healthcare system. 
 
(Para 3.35.4 of the ATR) 
Accessible and Affordable Treatment of Rare Diseases 
61. The Committee acknowledges the significant progress in expanding the scope of 
the National Policy for Rare Diseases (NPRD) 2021, viz. the inclusion of additional 
diseases, establishment of 13 Centres of Excellence (CoEs), and the launch of initiatives 
such as the National Registry and the Indigenous Therapeutics Programme. The 

215 
 
Committee observes that awareness, early diagnosis, and affo rdability of treatment 
remain key challenges , particularly in rural and underserved areas. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry intensify its national awareness and outreach 
campaign through collaboration with State Governments, medical i nstitutions, and civil 
society organizations to ensure greater public and professional understanding of rare 
diseases. Further, the Committee urges the Department to expedite the 
operationalization of the National Rare Disease Information Portal  and integrate it with 
the CoEs and the National Registry for real -time data sharing, patient tracking, and 
referral facilitation. The Committee also recommends increasing the number of CoEs 
across all regions , particularly in the North -East and smaller States, to im prove 
accessibility. In addition, affordable diagnostic and therapeutic solutions should be 
prioritized under the DHR -ICMR Indigenous Therapeutics Programme  with defined 
timelines for clinical translation. The Committee emphasizes that a dedicated National 
Awareness and Prevention Mission on Rare Diseases  may be launched and promote 
early detection, genetic counseling, and social support mechanisms for affected families. 
 
(Para 3.36.5 of the ATR) 
 
Other Recommendations of the Committee 
 
62. The Committee ta kes note of the measures taken by the Department and the 
regulatory bodies such as National Medical Commission (NMC) and Indian Nursing 
Council (INC) to improve the quality and standards of medical and nursing education in 
alignment with global benchmarks,  including accreditation of NMC by WFME for a 
period of 10 years indicating quality of the Indian Medical Colleges and implementation 
of NQAS-based frameworks providing excellence in nursing education sector leading to 
Quality Assurance and Quality Sustena nce in nursing education sector. The Committee 
observes with deep concern that the population-based approach for sanctioning medical 
colleges, as mandated under the UG -MSR 2023, has been deferred for successive 
academic years 2024 -25 and 2025 -26, thereby delaying the correction of regional 
imbalances in medical education and healthcare accessibility. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department should expedite the implementation of the population-
based criterion  for establishing medical colleges to ensure equitable distribution of 
healthcare infrastructure across States and regions, especially in underserved and 
densely populated are as. Further, the Committee recommends that periodic quality 
audits and independent assessments  be institutionalized for both medical and nursing 
colleges to ensure adherence to NQAS and global best practices. The Committee also 
urges the Ministry to fast-track the nationwide rollout of the Quality Council of India 
(QCI)-led accreditation of nursing institutions  and develop a centralized digital 
dashboard for monitoring institutional ratings, faculty adequacy, and training 
outcomes. In addition, the Committe e emphasizes the need for continuous professional 
development programmes, faculty exchange, and integration of simulation -based and 
digital learning tools  to further enhance the competency and global competitiveness of 
India’s healthcare education system. 
(Para 3.37.5 of the ATR) 

216 
 
 
63. The Committee appreciates the progress achieved in operationalizing a large 
network of Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs) and ensuring availability of staff, 
essential diagnostics, and generic medicines under the Free Drugs and Di agnostics 
Services Initiative. The Committee notes that despite the commendable coverage 
achieved, a considerable proportion of AAMs are yet to attain full compliance in the 
availability of essential medicines and diagnostic services, which are vital for e ffective 
primary healthcare delivery. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Department intensify its efforts to achieve 100% availability of essential drugs and 
diagnostics across all AAMs  through improved supply chain management, real -time 
monitoring, and periodic stock audits using digital dashboards. The Committee also 
recommends strengthening human resource deployment  by filling the remaining 
vacancies of Community Health Officers (CHOs) and allied health staff through 
targeted recruitment drive s and skill enhancement programmes. The Committee 
suggests that the Department institutionalize a performance-linked incentive mechanism 
for States/UTs based on availability of essential supplies and service delivery standards 
at AAMs. The Committee also e mphasizes the need for integration of telemedicine, e -
diagnostics, and central procurement systems  to ensure timely and equitable access to 
quality healthcare and medicines, particularly in remote and rural areas. 
 
(Para 3.37.8 of the ATR) 
 
64. The Committee takes note of the various benefits and  payment made to ASHA 
workers intended towards enhancing the incentives and social security benefits 
including the recent upward revision of their routine and recurring activity incentive 
from ₹2,000 to ₹3,500, ben efits under the ASHA Benefit Package, and their inclusion 
under schemes such as PMJJBY, PMSBY, PM -SYM, and AB -PMJAY. The Committee 
is of the view that despite these revision in remuneration and benefits, the total 
remuneration received by ASHAs continues t o remain inadequate considering the 
critical and multifaceted role ASHAs play in delivering primary healthcare services at 
the grassroots level and their increasing workload with the expansion of government 
health programmes. The Committee, therefore, reco mmends the Department to 
formulate a comprehensive policy framework to ensure fair, uniform, and sustainable 
remuneration for ASHAs across all States/UTs , taking into account regional cost -of-
living variations and inflation. The Committee further recommend s that the 
Department should consider transitioning ASHAs from a purely incentive -based model 
to a mixed model with a fixed monthly honorarium supplemented by performance -
linked incentives , thereby ensuring income stability and recognition of their essenti al 
public health contribution. The Committee also urges the Department to institutionalize 
mechanisms for periodic review of incentives , strengthen health insurance and pension 
coverage, and ensure timely disbursement of dues to maintain ASHAs’ motivation and 
retention in the community health workforce. 
 
(Para 3.37.12 of the ATR) 
 

217 
 
65. The Committee acknowledges the response of the Department highlighting the 
current operational lifespan of CGM sensors especially beneficial in type -I diabetes, the 
potential for longer -lasting implantable sensors, the role of NPPA in price regulation, 
and the efforts under the ―Make in India‖ initiative to encourage indigenous production 
of CGMs. The Committee observes with deep concern over the absence of concrete 
regulatory intervention on pricing and insurance coverage that continue to make CGMs 
and essential diabetic medicines unaffordable for a large segment of patients especially 
who rely on insulin to manage , particularly those requiring lifelong monitoring and 
medication. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department, in 
coordination with NPPA and IRDAI, formulate a comprehensive framework for price 
regulation, insurance inclusion, and procurement of CGMs and diabetic medicines 
under national health schemes , e nsuring affordability and equitable access. The 
Committee further recommends that the Department should support domestic research 
and development, and large -scale production of CGMs through targeted incentives, 
public–private partnerships, and expedited ap proval processes under the ―Make in 
India‖ initiative , to reduce import dependency and achieve long -term self -reliance in 
diabetes management technologies. The Committee also desires that the Department 
must explore mechanisms to extend the lifespan and co st-effectiveness of CGM sensors 
through innovation and standardization , in consultation with industry and scientific 
experts. 
(Para 3.37.15 of the ATR)

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health 
and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its

Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi and Problems Faced by Patients in availing 
healthcare and treatment”. 
 
2. In exercise of its constitutional mandate, the Committee, in its meeting held on 18th 
November, 2024 identified the subject "Working of All India Institute of Medical Sciences 
(AIIMS), New Delhi and Problems faced by patients in availing healthcare and treatment" and 
decided to undertake a detailed study on the Subject. The primary objective behind identifying 
the subject Committee is to examine the organizational structure of the Institute alongwith its 
governing structure, foundational mandate for delivery of top tier medical education, ground 
breaking research, patient care besides ongoing infrastructure projects, faculty, staff position vis

REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
1.0 AIIMS, New Delhi, created in 1956 as an autonomous Institute through an Act of 
Parliament is an Institute of National Importance (INI) and globally known to deliver top-tier 
medical education, ground breaking research, exceptional patient care and good governance 
for innovative implementation of healthcare national policies and programmes besides 
serving as a nucleus for nurturing excellence in all aspects of healthcare. 
 
1.1 Over the decades, AIIMS, New Delhi has expanded in scale, capacity, complexity and 
has attained reputation and status, however, despite its outstanding contributions in academic 
and clinical domains, there remain persistent challenges in service delivery that directly affect 
patient comforts and access to care. Long waiting times, overcrowded outpatient departments, 
pressure on emergency services, shortage of beds and limited infrastructure for attendants and 
patients continue to impede the full realization of the institution’s potential. There is also an 
evident need to assess systemic issues related to patient grievance redressal, appointment 
scheduling, interdepartmental referrals, diagnostics bottlenecks and cost barriers. 
 
1.1.1 The Parliamentary Committee, through its mandate, plays a critical role in ensuring 
institutional accountability, transparency in public service delivery and aligning the 
performance of institutions like AIIMS with national health priorities and citizen 
expectations.  The Committee through detailed study of “Working of All India Institute of 
Medical Sciences (AIIMS)” intends to understand the following issues pertaining to the 
institutes:– 
(i) Problems faced by patients in availing healthcare and treatment; 
(ii) Problems being faced in the routine functioning of the AIIMS, Delhi; 
(iii) Medical services and other facilities available in the institutes; 
(iv) Availability of opportunity for medical education at both under-graduate and post-
graduate levels; 
(v) Status of skilled development of Allied Professionals; 
(vi) Standard and clinical exposure to Nursing personnel; 
(vii) Progress of ongoing infrastructural projects; 
(viii) Implementation status of Master Plan; 
(ix) Availability of faculty and non-faculty against the sanctioned strength; 
(x) Key Areas of Concerns including SWOT analysis of the institute; 
(xi) Comparative study of the institute with leading hospitals of the world; 
(xii) Strategy required to overcome the overload of patients and consideration of 
overall suggestions for improvement in the working of the Institute; 
(xiii) Problems faced by patients while availing healthcare and treatment at AIIMS, 
Delhi; 
(xiv) The steps, policy interventions, design and organizational changes that being 
carried out to address the complex issues; 
(xv) Exploring the possibility of the setting up of another AIIMS like institution in 
NCR to overcome the problems of work overload in AIIMS, New Delhi. 
 

 
2 
 
1.1.2 The Committee believes that a close scrutiny of AIIMS, New Delhi, thus, is crucial to 
strengthen governance, equity and outcomes not only within the institution but across the 
national tertiary healthcare system.  
 
1.1.3 The erstwhile Committee on Health and Family Welfare had earlier presented/laid its 
87th Report on “The Functioning of All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS)” to both 
Houses of Parliament on 11th August, 2015 and the same was forwarded to the Ministry for 
furnishing Action Taken Notes on the recommendations contained in that Report. The 
Ministry, in response to that furnished the Action Taken Notes, thereon, however the 
Committee could not present Action Taken Report on the 87th Report due to paucity of time.  
 
1.1.4 The previous Committee in its meeting held on 13th May, 2025 heard the 
representative of Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and top management of AIIMS, 
New Delhi. The Committee undertook a study visit to AIIMS, New Delhi on 13th June, 2025 
to take stock of ground realities on the actual working of the AIIMS, New Delhi and 
problems faced by patients in availing healthcare and treatment. During the course of the 
visit, the Committee interacted with the representatives of various associations that inter-alia 
included Faculty Association, Nurses Association, SC/ST Association, Karamchari Union, 
Officers Association and Resident Doctors Association and gathered detailed information 
pertaining to Master Plan, Basic Infrastructure & On-going and future projects, Various 
departments imparting UG and PG Courses alongwith faculty and non-faculty Staff in-
position against the sanctioned position, Beds occupancy rate, Functional OTs, Governing 
Structures, Health Research Ecosystem, undertaken Research Projects alongwith its key 
areas, Human Resource Management, Strategic steps taken to extend Patient Care and 
Comforts, including Grievance Redressal Mechanism, global standing of AIIMS, New Delhi 
vis-a-vis leading healthcare institutes of developed countries. The Committee also interacted 
with the representative of AIIMS Administration & Management and sought details of steps 
taken to combat the challenges being faced by the Administration as well as the patients 
seeking treatment in the Institute.   
 
1.2 HISTORICAL BACKGROUND  
 
1.2.1 The All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) was originally conceived by the 
Advisory Committee on Professional Education, established to implement the 
recommendations of the Bhore Committee (1943), which laid the groundwork for modern 
India's health policy and infrastructure. Chaired by Dr. A. L. Mudaliar and including eminent 
members such as Dr. B. C. Roy, the Committee proposed the creation of a premier medical 
institute that would serve as a hub for training medical educators, provide state-of-the-art 
hospital facilities for medical education and promote comprehensive research essential for 
effective teaching and training. 
 
1.2.2 The vision of the Advisory Committee was translated to reality through the dedication 
and leadership of Ms. Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the first Health Minister of the country, who 
introduced the AIIMS Bill in Parliament on 18th February 1956, which was eventually passed 
as the AIIMS Act, 1956. She not only secured the necessary funding and selected the 

 
3 
 
founding faculty but also became the first President of the Institute in 1957. Her aim was to 
establish an institution that would allow Indian students to pursue world-class postgraduate 
medical education within the country.  
 
1.3 VISION AND SPECIAL CHARACTERS  
 
1.3.1 The All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi is an Institute of 
National Importance (INI) which functions under a trinity of mission - medical education, 
research and patient care and later on added the fourth vision of Good Governance- each 
reinforcing and strengthening the other. The vision of AIIMS, New Delhi is rooted in its 
foundational mandate to function not merely as a medical college or hospital, but as an 
Institution of National Importance empowered with the status and responsibilities of a 
University. 
 
1.3.2 During the course of the interaction the Committee was apprised of the four pillars of 
vision of AIIMS, New Delhi as enumerated below:- 
 
Medical Education Research Patient Care Good Governance

1.4 Aims and Objectives of AIIMS 
1.4.1 As informed by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the following are the aims 
and objectives of AIIMS:- 
 
(i) To develop pattern of teaching in under-graduate and post-graduate medical 
education in all its branches so as to demonstrate a high standard of medical 
education to all medical colleges and other allied institutions in India. 
(ii) To bring together in one place educational facilities of the highest order for the 
training of personnel in all branches of health activities. 
(iii) To attain self-sufficiency in post-graduate medical education.

the Institute’s medical services, supported by highly specialized centres catering to specific 
needs. The Burns and Plastic Surgery Block and the Surgical Block are equipped to handle

3.3.3 Upon enquiring about the reason for non-functionality of beds, the Committee was 
informed that 520 posts for the Mother and Child Block and 720 posts for the National 
Cancer Institute (NCI), Jhajjar, have recently been sanctioned by the Department of 
Expenditure. The process of recruitment for these sanctioned posts is presently underway and 
it is expected that upon joining of the new faculty and staff, all the currently non-functional 
beds will be made operational. Additionally, 328 beds in the Main Hospital remain non-
functional owing to the ongoing renovation of a dilapidated building—one of the oldest 
structures in the Institute, constructed over half a century ago—which had to be vacated in the 
interest of patient safety. 
 
3.3.4 The Committee was further informed that the operationalization of beds in the newly 
commissioned blocks and centres would be significantly enhanced upon completion of the 
ongoing recruitment drive and approval of additional manpower proposals. Renovation work 
is actively underway in various areas of the Main Hospital, including AB1, AB5, C3 and D7 
blocks. The Institute has taken steps to rationally redistribute patients to functional wards to 

 
10 
 
ensure continuity of care and frequent coordination meetings are held between clinical 
departments, engineering divisions and manpower units to expedite restoration of full 
functionality. 
 
3.3.5 With regard to the non-functional status of operation theatres, the Committee was 
apprised that the primary cause is the shortage of faculty in the Department of Anesthesiology 
and associated support staff. Similarly, the shortfall in functional ICU beds has been 
attributed to inadequate availability of qualified faculty and support personnel. However, the 
Committee was assured that with the recent sanctioning of approximately 1,400 posts across 
various cadres, the Institute is actively engaged in recruitment efforts to operationalize all 
non-functional ICU beds and OTs at the earliest possible time. 
 
3.3.6 The Committee expresses concern that despite having 112 Major OTs, 44 Minor 
OTs and 433 ICU beds, a significant portion of infrastructure remains underutilized, 
with 26 Major OTs and 81 ICU beds non-functional and 843 hospital beds lying 
unutilized. This is an alarming situation and sheer apathy in view of the fact that 
thousands of patients look up to AIIMS for healthcare needs. The AIIMS management 
should overcome its lethargy and address the contradiction wherein on one hand 
patients are made to wait for long periods for surgical interventions whereas on the 
other hand the OTs are lying non-functional. Such non-functionality not only 
undermines patient care but also reflects gaps in maintenance, resource utilization and 
management failure to ensure timely operationalization of critical facilities. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Institute to take immediate corrective measures 
to operationalize the non-functional OTs and hospital beds.  The Committee is of the 
considered view that there is urgent need to enhance the number of beds in cardiology, 
neurology and trauma departments as cardiac disorders and brain strokes account for 
large number of death (almost 30%) in India, therefore, time is a crucial factor in the 
treatment of heart attacks, brain strokes and road accidents, therefore, optimal 
treatment in time within the golden hour is required to save the life. The Committee is 
of the view that department of cardiology must fulfil the sanctioned strength vis-à-vis in-
position strength (teaching and non-teaching) so as to capacitate the department to 
handle current patient load keeping in view the rising cases of heart diseases across the 
country. The Committee is of the considered view that the department of cardiology 
must strengthen in terms of manpower, research and infrastructure to be fully equipped 
to tackle the increasing incidence of heart attack. The Committee strongly recommends 
for an indepth analysis as to why experienced cardiologists leave AIIMS or are not 
allowed to function independently. 
 
3.3.7 The Committee also recommends for a time-bound action plan for repair, up-
gradation and staffing, along with periodic monitoring mechanisms to ensure 
sustainability of operations. The Committee further recommends that AIIMS should 
strengthen its maintenance and infrastructure planning mechanisms to minimize service 
disruption and ensure that all sanctioned beds and operation theatres are made fully 
functional at the earliest.

3.3.8 The Committee notes that a significant number of ICU beds and operation 
theatres at AIIMS, New Delhi, remain non-functional primarily due to shortage of 
faculty and support staff, as well as ongoing renovation of old hospital blocks. The 
Committee, in this regard, recommends that AIIMS, New Delhi, should accord the 
highest priority to expediting the recruitment process to fill up the sanctioned faculty 
and technical positions within a defined timeframe. The Committee also recommends 
that the Institute, in consultation with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 
prepare a comprehensive manpower deployment plan to ensure optimal utilization of 
available infrastructure and prevent recurrence of such functional shortfalls. The 
Committee recommends that wherever feasible the manpower gaps be filled by 
appointing Resident Doctors on a large scale.  
 
3.4 Status of ongoing and proposed expansion plans, present and proposed 
infrastructure for patients and faculty/officials of the hospital. 
  
3.4.1 AIIMS New Delhi currently has over 3300 operational beds and provides advanced 
medical care to over 12000 patients daily. To overcome the shortage of beds for 
emergency/in-patients and those waiting for procedures and surgeries, continuous expansion 
of various facilities is underway. The ongoing and proposed expansion plans for AIIMS-
Delhi are as under:- 
  
(A) AIIMS MASTER PLAN 
3.4.2 The Union Cabinet in its meeting held on 28th February, 2019 accorded in-principle 
approval for the implementation of a Master Plan to transform AIIMS, New Delhi into a 
world-class Medical University. The integrated Master Plan, covering nearly 190 acres across 
five land parcels with phased development over seven years at an estimated cost of 
₹15,558.37 crore.  The Committee was informed that AIIMS had submitted the Expenditure 
Finance Committee (EFC) memorandum with the Detailed Project Report (DPR) to the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) on 23rd March, 2022 and subsequently 
provided responses to queries from the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Environment, 
Forest and Climate Change and NITI Aayog on 27th February 2023. On 23rd October 2024, 
the MoHFW advised AIIMS to submit a revised EFC/PIB memorandum, de-linking the two 
projects, viz. construction of the new OPD Block at Masjid Moth (₹484.51 crore) and hostel 
accommodation at the Trauma Centre Extension (₹876 crore) as independent proposals. 
Given the time elapsed since the original costing, the DPR is being updated based on current 
Plinth Area Rates and the revised EFC memorandum for the Master Plan was to be submitted 
to MoHFW. 
 
3.4.3 The Officers Association of AIIMS, in its submission to the Committee, highlighted 
that although the Institute has invested considerable effort and resources in preparing this 
comprehensive Master Plan, funding constraints have prevented timely execution. The 
Association emphasized that full implementation would substantially enhance infrastructure, 
expand institutional capacity and strengthen AIIMS’s academic, research and clinical outputs, 
ultimately improving patient care. 
 

 
12 
 
3.4.4 The Committee, while appreciating the vision of transforming AIIMS Delhi into 
a world-class Medical University through its integrated Master Plan, expresses concern 
over the slow pace of implementation despite the Cabinet’s in-principle approval being 
granted as early as 2019. The Committee is of the view that further delays are 
unwarranted and risk enshrined thereto, thus undermining the objectives of this 
ambitious initiative. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Health 
and Family Welfare, in coordination with all concerned agencies, to expedite the 
implementation of the Master Plan through strict adherence to timelines, robust 
monitoring mechanisms and prioritization of critical infrastructure. The Committee 
also recommends the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to extend adequate 
financial and administrative support and also provide financial and administrative 
flexibility to AIIMS to address evolving functional requirements during the seven-year 
implementation period, thereby ensuring that the vision of establishing AIIMS as a 
world-class Medical University is realized as per stipulated time-frame. 
 
3.4.5 The Committee also recommends that the Master Plan should adopt a holistic 
approach by ensuring the comprehensive development of hospital, research, academic 
and residential zones. In addition, the Plan should provide for the establishment of 
integrated 24×7 operational zones that will facilitate uninterrupted patient care, foster 
advanced research and enable continuous academic collaboration.

kitchen, IT and other services for the new blocks in the campus, is a critical backbone project. 
Despite significant progress of nearly 70 percent completion, the project has been marred by 
repeated delays due to prolonged approval processes with civic bodies, environmental
