7.15.6 The Committee appreciates the patient-centric initiatives undertaken by AIIMS, 
New Delhi through the introduction of the Santusht Portal and QR code–based 
grievance reporting, which empower patients to raise complaints and monitor their 
resolution in real time. The Committee recommends that patient centric initiative 
should be scaled up beyond the pilot phase and extended to all blocks and centres of 
AIIMS, New Delhi and eventually replicated across other AIIMS institutions 
nationwide. 
 
7.15.7 The Committee is also of the view that while institutional mechanisms are 
necessary, feedback collection must also be supplemented by an independent system to 
ensure credibility and transparency. The Committee, therefore, recommends AIIMS to 
explore the feasibility of engaging a reputed third-party agency to conduct regular 
patient satisfaction surveys and capture unbiased feedback on key parameters such as 
cleanliness, quality of food, waiting times, communication with doctors, nursing care 
and overall patient comfort. Such approach/initiative would ensure that patients feel 
free to share their honest experiences without fear of reprisal, thereby providing the 
administration with actionable insights for service improvement. 
 
7.15.8 The Committee observes that AIIMS, New Delhi has redefined the benchmarks 
of public healthcare delivery in India, functioning under extraordinary pressure while 
sustaining high-quality care. The unparalleled volume and complexity of work handled 
by the Institute underscores its role as the foremost national centre of excellence in 
patient care, education and research and demonstrates its indispensable place in India’s 
healthcare ecosystem. The Committee, however, observes that the current 
infrastructure and manpower is under stress due to the ever increasing volume of 
patients. The Committee, therefore, recommends that urgent steps be taken to 
strengthen infrastructure, enhance manpower and expand capacity across clinical, 
diagnostic and research domains in view of the extraordinary patient load and the 
critical role of AIIMS. The measures so undertaken would ensure that the Institute 
continues to deliver high-quality, specialized care while also advancing its mandate in 
education and medical research. 
 
8.0 HUMAN RESOURCE 
 
8.1 Human Resource Policy and Management 
8.1.1 The Recruitment and Staffing policy mandates AIIMS to follow a merit bases recruit 
based system govern by the AIIMS Act, 1956. Faculty are appointed through transparent 
selection processes, involving the Standing Selection Committee. For non-Faculty position at 
AIIMS, Delhi, the recruitment and promotion processes are governed by the rules and 
guidelines laid down by the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), Government of 
India that inter alia include provisions related to reservation, pay scale, promotion criteria and 
service condition ensuring uniformity and transparency across Central Government 
Institutions. Under Training and Development, a regular in-service training, CME 
programmes and skilled enhancement were conducting for clinical and non- clinical staff. 

 
63 
 
AIIMS promotes academic growth through fellowships, sabbaticals (up to 2 years at a stretch 
in India or abroad), and international collaborations. For Performance Evaluation, Staff 
performance is monitored through Annual Performance and Appraisal Reports (APARs) and 
Assessment Promotion Scheme (APS). Promotions and career Progression are linked to 
academic output, clinical service, and research contributions. 
 
8.1.2 As Retention and Welfare Measures, AIIMS provides housing, healthcare, pension 
benefits, and access to institutional facilities. However, residential accommodation for faculty 
and students needs to be increased. However, attrition remains a concern, especially due to 
increased workload and attractive proposition in the private Sector. Under Digital HR system, 
implementation of Bio-metric attendance, e-office modules, SAHAS, and HR dashboard has 
improved transparency and administrative efficiency.  
 
8.1.3 The Committee takes into account Human Resource Policy and Management of 
AIIMS and opines that the AIIMS Management would undertake concerted efforts and 
measures in appointment of Faculty through a transparent Selection Process as per the 
provisions of AIIMS Act, 1956. The Committee also desires that the Recruitment and 
promotion process of non-faculty must be clearly govern by rules and Regulations as 
laid down by the DoPT keeping in view the Reservation policy, Pay Scales and service 
conditions. 
 
8.1.4 The Committee came across high rate of attrition of doctors and personnel from 
other allied services in AIIMS, New Delhi due to low salary and necessary facilities vis-
a-vis renowned hospitals thereby increasing workload on the remaining workforce. The 
Committee was impressed that the Government has imposed a cap that the salary of 
DM, Cardiologist, Nephrologist or Endocrinologist etc. would not be higher than the 
Chief Secretary, therefore, these doctors do not stay in higher institutions and leave it 
immediately after doing their super specialization to join the private sector where a new 
Cardiologist are paid to the tune of Rs. 4 to 5 lakhs whereas the Government pays 
around one lakh as per the pay structure available in the country, if so, is the fact, the 
Committee wills to point out that if the salary of the Member of Parliament is lower 
than the Chief Secretary, therefore, why not the salary of doctor can be higher than the 
Chief Secretary. The Committee is of the opinion that lot of money and time is spent to 
become a DM so for their retention in AIIMS, New Delhi it is necessary to pay them 
higher salary and better facilities available to lead a satisfied and actualised life. The 
Committee, in this regard, is of the considered view that if the Government wills to run 
super-speciality centres in AIIMS, New Delhi or all over the Country the Government 
should remove the pay barrier cap and raise the pay scale of doctors for their assured 
retention, on the one hand and to develop and standardized tertiary healthcare centres. 
The Committee strongly believes that tertiary level healthcare institutions can do more 
quality work, more research work and would be more contributory from the futuristic 
point of view once the salary of doctors in super-specialised centres is enhanced and 
made comparable to healthcare institutions in the private sector. 
 
8.1.5 The Committee is of the view that since AIIMS, Delhi envisage itself as a centre 
of excellence in Medical Education in Research and in Patient care. Its HR Policy must 

 
64 
 
be aligned with its mission and vision i.e. in consonance with meritocratic recruitment 
supported academic integrity, training programme fostering clinical and Research 
Excellence and digital HR systems aiming at enhancing the governance and 
accountability. AIIMS management should chalk out specific course of action to fill up 
gaps in such alignment viz Low Faculty to Student ratio impacts the teaching and 
research mission, Limited career progression impacts motivation and innovation, 
Overburdened staff due to high patient load affects quality of care and academic output 
and More protected time needed for research or academics.  
 
8.2 VACANCIES IN FACULTY POSITION 
 
8.2.1 The Committee enquired about the sanctioned vis-à-vis in-position strength of all 
posts under the teaching and non-teaching faculty at the institute, the recruitment process as 
well as the measures taken to expedite the filling up of the existing vacancies. The All India 
Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, informed the Committee that there has 
been a considerable shortage of both teaching and non-teaching staff. 
 
8.2.2 The Committee was informed that the sanctioned strength of faculty is 1,306, out of 
which only 798 positions are filled up, leaving 508 vacant. Of these, 117 posts of Professor 
under direct recruitment have remained vacant since 2012 due to a court case concerning 
inter-se-seniority between direct recruits and Assessment Promotion Scheme (APS) 
appointees. The Institute further informed that the Governing Body, in its meeting held on 
13th December 2023, approved filling up of these posts through direct recruitment and the 
decision was ratified by the Institute Body (IB) on 11th March 2024. It further conveyed that 
recruitment to these posts is expected to commence shortly. 
 
8.2.3 The Institute also reported that the shortage is most pronounced at the level of 
Assistant Professor, with 383 vacancies. It added that 73 of these vacancies arose recently, 71 
due to the creation of new posts on 16th April 2025 and two, following resignations in the 
same month. The Institute informed that recruitment for Assistant Professors was delayed due 
to reforms introduced to ensure greater transparency. These reforms include conducting the 
recruitment process entirely online, introducing objective evaluation criteria and 
incorporating block chain methodology. It further informed that the Governing Body 
approved the final objective criteria in March 2024, which were formally notified on 8th July 
2024. In addition, four vacancies each for Associate Professor and Tutor in the College of 
Nursing have also been reported. 
 
8.2.4 During the interaction with Officers Association of AIIMS, the Association 
highlighted that the acute shortage of sanctioned posts across various levels in AIIMS, 
particularly at senior and middle management, has resulted in work overload, stagnation in 
career progression and a decline in service quality. The Association stressed that the 
sanctioning and timely filling up of these posts is critical for ensuring smooth operations and 
supporting the scalability of the institution. It was further noted that several departments have 
already submitted proposals for the approval of DM and Non-Academic Senior Resident 

 
65 
 
posts, but these are still pending approval, thereby exacerbating the shortage of skilled 
manpower. 
 
8.2.5 AIIMS, New Delhi informed the Committee that to address the vacancies at the level 
of Assistant Professor and in the College of Nursing, 265 posts were advertised on 7th April 
2025 and the recruitment process is underway. The Institute further informed that 53 
additional posts will be advertised after the revision of recruitment rules and nomenclature, 
while the 73 newly created post of Assistant Professor will be advertised within one month. 
 
8.2.6 In order to meet immediate requirements, the Institute informed that eight Assistant 
Professors have been engaged on a contractual basis. It also informed that, out of 167 recently 
advertised post of Assistant Professor across various disciplines, 74 candidates have already 
joined, while the remaining are in the process of joining. The Institute reiterated that 
recruitment of Professors under direct recruitment mode, delayed for long due to the court 
case, will also be undertaken soon. 
 
8.3 VACANCIES IN NON-FACULTY POSITIONS 
 
8.3.1 With regard to non-faculty staffs, AIIMS, New Delhi stated that out of 13,911 
sanctioned posts, 10,855 are currently filled, leaving 3,056 vacant. Among these, 967 posts 
were newly created for the Mother and Child Block on 15th March 2025 and for the National 
Cancer Institute, Jhajjar on 8th April 2025. Of the total vacancies, 2,008 are to be filled 
through direct recruitment and 1,048 through promotion. 
 
8.3.2 The Institute informed that in the direct recruitment category, 1,033 posts across 
Group A, B and C, including those in the nursing cadre have already been advertised. It added 
that the advertisement process for another 51 Group A posts is in an advanced stage. A 
further 441 vacancies, which arose after the last recruitment cycle, will be included in the 
upcoming Nursing Officer Recruitment Common Eligibility Test (NORCET) and Common 
Recruitment Examination (CRE) examinations. AIIMS reported that 300 posts have not been 
advertised as their services are outsourced, while 183 could not be advertised due to 
administrative reasons such as revision of recruitment rules and post conversion. 
 
8.3.3 For the 1,048 promotion posts, AIIMS stated that 122 were newly created for Mother 
and Child Block (MCH) and National Cancer Institute (NCI). While Departmental Promotion 
Committees (DPCs) and Limited Departmental Competitive Examinations (LDCEs) are being 
conducted, many posts remain vacant due to a lack of eligible candidates in feeder grades. 
 
8.3.4 The Institute highlighted that attrition is highest in the nursing cadre. To address this, 
it informed that recruitment of nursing officers is now being conducted twice a year through 
NORCET. Recruitment of paramedical and support staff, it added, has been streamlined 
through an annual cycle under the Common Recruitment Examination (CRE). 
 
8.3.5 AIIMS also informed that 625 posts of nursing officers were advertised under 
NORCET-8, with final results declared on 6th May 2025. It also stated that 379 non-faculty 
posts under Group B and C were advertised through CRE 2024, with the computer-based test 

 
66 
 
conducted from 26th to 28th February 2025; results have already been declared and 
recruitment is in progress. Additionally, 29 Group A non-faculty posts were advertised, with 
applications closed on 10th April 2025. 
 
8.3.6 The Committee is constrained to observe that the All India Institute of Medical 
Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, is presently functioning under severe shortage of both 
teaching and non-teaching staff. Out of a sanctioned strength of 1,306 faculty posts, as 
many as 508 remain vacant, while in the case of non-faculty staff, 3,056 out of 13,911 
sanctioned posts are unfilled. The Committee notes with concern that such manpower 
deficit might adversely affect the Institute’s capacity to discharge its dual mandate of 
providing quality medical education and delivering world-class healthcare services. 
 
8.3.7 The Committee is alarmed to note that the highest number of vacancies exists at 
the level of Assistant Professor, which directly impacts the student–teacher ratio, 
academic mentorship and research productivity. The Committee further observes that 
vacancies in the cadre of Professors have been long pending due to protracted litigation 
and administrative delays, which might adversely impact leadership in several key 
departments.  
 
8.3.8 The Committee desires that AIIMS, New Delhi must have rationalized the 
pyramidal structure in appropriate ratio of Assistant Professors, Associate Professors 
and above as the future of Institution depends on the base of pyramid and the Assistant 
Professors are the future of the Institution, therefore, concerted efforts must be made to 
fill up the post of Assistant Professors, of course, keeping it to consideration the need to 
follow the roster system as per the constitution norms.  
 
8.3.9 In respect of non-faculty staff, the Committee is deeply concerned that shortages, 
particularly in the nursing cadre will not only increase the workload of the existing 
personnel but also pose a serious risk to patient safety, service delivery and the overall 
efficiency of healthcare operations. 
 
8.3.10 The Committee is of the firm view that such prolonged vacancies have the 
potential to dilute the academic standards of AIIMS Delhi and undermine its reputation 
as a centre of excellence in medical education, research and patient care. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that AIIMS Delhi should fast-track the ongoing 
recruitment processes and ensure that appointments to both faculty and non-faculty 
positions are completed within strict timelines. The Committee is of the opinion that 
while the reforms to introduce transparency, objective evaluation criteria and 
technology-driven recruitment are commendable, these measures, however, should not 
cause undue delay in filling up urgent vacancies. The Committee further recommends 
that contractual appointments be expanded as an interim measure to bridge immediate 
gaps, especially in the high-demand specialties and in the nursing cadre. 
 
8.3.11 The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare extend all necessary support to AIIMS, New Delhi by way of expediting 
necessary approvals, removing administrative bottlenecks and providing adequate 

 
67 
 
budgetary backing to conduct timely recruitment. The Committee further recommends 
that a system of biannual recruitment for nursing officers and an annual recruitment 
cycle for faculty and paramedical staff be institutionalised across all AIIMS institutions 
so as to prevent the recurrence of such large-scale vacancies in the future. The 
Committee also recommends the Ministry to explore conducting NORCET more 
frequently than twice a year to increase the strength of nurse staff.   
 
8.3.12 The Committee strongly recommends that a joint monitoring mechanism 
between AIIMS Delhi and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare be established to 
periodically review recruitment progress, ensure accountability and project manpower 
requirements in consonance with the expansion plans of the Institute. The Committee 
emphasizes that addressing these shortages on an urgent basis is imperative to 
safeguard the academic excellence and healthcare standards of AIIMS Delhi. Any 
further delay in filling up these vacancies would, in the considered view of the 
Committee, severely compromise the ability of the Institute to retain its premier status 
and to meet the ever-growing demand for specialized medical services in the country. 
 
8.4 CADRE REVIEW & RESERVATION IN PROMOTIONS 
8.4.1 The Committee received representations from various associations of AIIMS, New 
Delhi all of which underscored pressing human resource challenges that have remained 
unaddressed for years. The Nurses Union stressed the urgent requirement of a cadre review to 
create adequate promotion posts, particularly for Senior Nursing Officers and other higher 
positions, as the lack of opportunities has resulted in stagnation and hampered career 
progression.  
 
8.4.2 Echoing similar concerns, the SC/ST Employees Association highlighted that a large 
number of Group D posts have remained vacant for prolonged periods. They further 
emphasized the need for a cadre review along with strict implementation of reservation in 
promotions as per DoPT guidelines and National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) 
directives, pointing out that eligible candidates continue to face delays in career advancement. 
They also called for the establishment of a full-fledged reservation cell, regular updating of 
department and cadre-wise rosters, external experts from SC/ST Commission to point out any 
oversight and the inclusion of SC/ST representatives in policy-making and advisory 
committees to ensure fairness and transparency in implementation.  
 
8.4.3 In parallel, the Karamchari Union and Officers Association drew attention to the fact 
that the last cadre review at AIIMS, New Delhi was conducted in 1992 and, despite 
subsequent approval of a new review by the Standing Finance Committee and Governing 
Body, the proposal continues to remain stalled at the Ministry. This prolonged inaction, they 
noted, has resulted in widespread stagnation, outdated recruitment norms and the absence of 
clear promotion pathways, which in turn undermines staff morale, weakens retention and 
adversely affects the overall efficiency of the Institute. 
 
8.4.4 The Committee, after careful consideration of the submissions by representatives 
of various associations on pressing human resource challenges, is deeply concerned 

 
68 
 
about the prolonged neglect of cadre review, last being conducted in 1992 leading to the 
acute shortage of promotion opportunities across different cadres in AIIMS. The 
Committee observes that the absence of cadre reviews at rational period of interval has 
led to stagnation, weakened staff morale and diminished efficiency, while the delay in 
filling up vacant posts, especially in Group D, continues to affect service delivery. 
Despite approval of fresh cadre review by the Standing Finance Committee and 
Governing Body, the proposal remain stalled at the Ministry level. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry take immediate steps to approve and 
implement the long-pending cadre review, ensuring the creation of adequate promotion 
posts for nurses, sanctioning of long-vacant positions and the establishment of clear and 
updated recruitment and promotion pathways for all categories of staff.  
 
8.4.5 The Committee further recommends the immediate implementation of provision 
of reservation in promotions in strict conformity with DoPT guidelines and National 
Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) directives, alongside the creation of a fully 
functional reservation cell with regular monitoring of rosters and active participation of 
SC/ST representatives in advisory and policy-making committees. By addressing these 
issues in a comprehensive and time-bound manner, the Ministry will not only enhance 
staff motivation and retention but also strengthen institutional efficiency and ensure 
that AIIMS continues to function with the highest standards of excellence. 
 
8.5 IMPLEMENTATION OF ROTATORY HEADSHIP POLICY 
 
8.5.1 AIIMS, New Delhi informed that a Committee chaired by Dr. V. K. Paul, Member of 
NITI Aayog, was constituted by the President of AIIMS, New Delhi, to examine the proposal 
for introducing a system of rotation of headship in AIIMS, New Delhi, PGIMER, Chandigarh 
and other newly established AIIMS institutions. After careful examination of the report of the 
Committee, it was decided that a collegium system would be implemented as an interim 
measure, with the proposal for rotatory headship to be reconsidered after a period of one year. 
In accordance with this decision, the Institute has since adopted and operationalized the 
collegium system for the selection and functioning of departmental heads. 
 
8.5.2 The Committee was informed by the Faculty Association of AIIMS (FAIMS) about 
the urgent need for the immediate implementation of the Rotatory Headship policy at AIIMS, 
New Delhi. They informed that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare had 
communicated in 2023 its commitment to operationalize the long-standing policy by June 
2024. However, despite broad-based faculty support, the policy remains pending for 
implementation. 
 
8.5.3 The Association emphasized that the intended reform is not a mere procedural change 
but a vital step toward strengthening democratic governance within the Institute. The 
introduction of Rotatory Headship would ensure equitable distribution of leadership 
responsibilities, prevent the centralization of power and promote departmental excellence 
through diverse leadership perspectives. The Association further underlined that timely 
implementation of this policy would not only enhance faculty morale but also reinforce long-

 
69 
 
term institutional trust and integrity. They, therefore, requested that the policy be 
implemented without further delay, in alignment with the directives of the Ministry and in the 
larger interest of transparency, fairness and institutional growth of the Institute. 
 
8.5.4 The Committee concurs with the submission of the Faculty Association of AIIMS 
(FAIMS) regarding the urgent need to implement the Rotatory Headship policy at 
AIIMS, New Delhi. Recognizing the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare’s earlier 
commitment to operationalize the said policy by June 2024, the Committee observes 
with a caution that further delay would undermine both faculty morale and institutional 
trust. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Institute take immediate steps to 
implement the Rotatory Headship policy and ensure democratic governance, equitable 
distribution of leadership roles and prevention of power centralization. The proposed 
reform, long overdue, is essential to foster departmental excellence, transparency and 
fairness and to uphold the reputation of the Institution as a model of academic and 
professional integrity. 
 
8.6 ABSORPTION/REGULARISATION OF PROJECT RESEARCH STAFF 
 
8.6.1 The Project Research Staff of AIIMS, New Delhi submitted a representation before 
the Committee seeking reconsideration of the Institute’s recent order (Ref No. 14/2022-Estt 
(RCT)), which rejected their request for absorption and regularization despite over 15 years 
of continuous service in various research projects. Having dedicated some of the most crucial 
and productive years of their professional lives to AIIMS, the staff emphasized that the 
decision contradicts both the Institute’s established policy and past practices. 
 
8.6.2 The project research staff submitted that since 1992, AIIMS has had a clear policy of 
absorbing research staff with 15 years of service into regular posts, subject to their 
qualifications, experience and availability of vacancies. Historically, over 164 project staff 
has been absorbed between 1992 and 2021 under this policy, in compliance with Supreme 
Court directives, High Court judgments and decisions of the AIIMS Governing Body. 
However, despite multiple committee recommendations since 2021, the current eligible batch 
of staff continues to await absorption. 
 
8.6.3 The rejection also contradicts the recommendations of various screening and 
recruitment committees, as well as the deliberations of the Governing Body. The 160th 
Governing Body meeting held on 13th December, 2023 specifically directed the constitution 
of a committee to examine the representations for absorption of project staff completing 15 
years of service. Following this, a committee was constituted in March 2024, which after due 
examination strongly recommended absorption of eligible project research staff.  
 
8.6.4 The representation also draws attention to the legal precedents that support their case. 
In V.L. Chandra vs. AIIMS (1990), the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed the absorption of 
project employees completing 15 years of service and emphasized the creation of a core 
research cadre to strengthen the Institute’s research output. Similar directions were reiterated 
by the Supreme Court in 2003 (SLP No. 19225/02) and by the Delhi High Court in AIIMS vs. 

 
70 
 
Om Prakash (2002). These judicial pronouncements, along with AIIMS’s own precedents and 
committee recommendations, clearly establish a binding framework for absorption. 
 
8.6.5 In light of these facts, the staffs have appealed for urgent reconsideration of their 
request for absorption and regularization, arguing that their long-standing service, proven 
expertise and judicially backed rights merit regularization. They are of the contention that 
denial of absorption not only undermines institutional policy but also risks demoralizing a 
trained and experienced workforce that has significantly contributed to AIIMS’s research 
legacy over decades. 
 
8.6.6 The Committee observes with concern that the Institute’s Order (Ref. No. 14/20-
Estt.(RCT) rejecting the absorption and regularisation of the eligible research staff 
despite 15 years of continuous service in various research projects is inconsistent with 
the established policy of AIIMS, past precedents and the recommendations of multiple 
Committees, as well as the directives of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court. 
The Committee takes into account that between 1992 and 2021, over 164 project staff 
were absorbed under this very framework, thereby setting a clear institutional and legal 
precedent. The Committee concurs with the representation submitted by the Project 
Research Staff and recognizes their invaluable contribution to the Institute’s research 
ecosystem. Having devoted over 15 years of continuous service in diverse projects, these 
staff members represent a highly trained and experienced human resource that has 
been instrumental in sustaining and advancing the research output of AIIMS. 
 
8.6.7 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that AIIMS urgently reconsider 
the case of absorption and regularization of all eligible Project Research Staff who have 
completed 15 years of service. Their integration into the regular workforce is not only a 
matter of justice and policy consistency but is also essential for strengthening the 
Institute’s research capacity and output by retaining skilled manpower already trained 
and specialized in the research ecosystem of the Institute. The Committee is of the 
considered view that a core research cadre be developed, in line with judicial directives, 
to ensure long-term continuity, stability and growth of the Institute’s research 
endeavours. 
 
8.7 ISSUES FACED BY NON-FACULTY EMPLOYEES 
 
8.7.1 The Committee received submissions highlighting concerns of discriminatory 
treatment faced by non-faculty employees at AIIMS. Despite their vital role in the 
functioning of the Institute, these employees have been denied benefits such as the option to 
shift from NPS to OPS, productivity-linked bonuses and parity in service conditions. Such 
disparities not only lower morale but also weaken team spirit and institutional harmony. The 
employees pointed out that this situation contradicts the AIIMS Act, and under AIIMS Rules 
16, 28 and 35, that permits the adoption of Central Government orders for welfare of staff. 
They further emphasized that repeated requests for parity in benefits, including NPS to OPS 
opt-in and productivity-linked bonuses already extended to other central institutions, continue 
to remain unaddressed. 

 
71 
 
 
8.7.2 The Committee took into consideration the submission of Non-faculty employees 
of AIIMS regarding alleged discriminatory treatment meted to non-faculty staff despite 
their vital role in the functioning of the Institute. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, in consultation with 
AIIMS, takes urgent response to address the concerns of non-faculty employees 
regarding parity in service conditions and welfare measures. Given their critical 
contribution to the functioning of the Institute, it is essential that non-faculty staffs are 
extended equal benefits that have been provided to their counterparts in other central 
institutions. The Committee is of the view that legitimate requests such as the option to 
shift from NPS to OPS, extension of productivity-linked bonuses and adoption of other 
welfare measures, which are in line with Central Government orders should be 
extended to non-faculty staff of AIIMS with due consideration. Ensuring equity in 
service conditions will not only enhance motivation and team spirit among employees 
but also strengthen institutional harmony and efficiency at AIIMS. 
 
8.8 WORKING HOURS OF RESIDENTS 
 
8.8.1 The Committee was informed that AIIMS, New Delhi follows the Government of 
India Residency Scheme in regulating the working hours of its resident doctors. For Junior 
Residents, the scheme stipulates that continuous active duty should not normally exceed 12 
hours a day, with a weekly holiday permitted and on-call duty limited to 12 hours at a time. In 
general, Junior Residents are expected to work around 48 hours a week, without exceeding 12 
hours at a stretch, though the Medical Superintendent may adjust working hours depending 
on workload and availability of doctors. Similarly, for Senior Residents, active duty is not to 
exceed 12 hours at a time, with one weekly holiday allowed by rotation and on-call duty 
capped at 12 hours. The overall quantum of workload, however, continues to vary from 
department to department based on specific clinical demands. 
 
8.8.2 The Resident Doctors Association submitted before the Committee their views on 
duty related matters. They submitted that they have to put in excessive duty hours, with 
residents reportedly working up to 36 hours at a stretch, well beyond the limits envisaged 
under the Residency Scheme. The working hours, while reflective of service exigencies, 
nevertheless to adversely affects the physical and mental health, diminish academic 
performance and potentially compromise the quality of patient care. Therefore, the 
Committee emphasizes the need for a balanced and humane duty structure. The Association 
proposed the formulation of an institutional policy to regulate and cap consecutive duty 
hours, along with the introduction of a mechanism for voluntary extra-duty shifts with 
appropriate compensation. It was further highlighted that during examination and thesis 
submission periods, residents face acute difficulties in reconciling clinical responsibilities 
with academic obligations. To mitigate this, the Association recommended granting six 
months of preparatory leave before final examinations and instituting temporary recruitment 
of resident doctors to manage the clinical workload during such intervals. 
 

 
72 
 
8.8.3 The Committee takes into account the submission of the Resident Doctors 
Association and expresses concern that Residents Doctors have to put in excessive duty 
hours, sometimes working upto 36 hours at a stretch well beyond the limits envisaged 
under the residency scheme. The Committee is of considered view that such extended 
working hours, while reflective of service exigencies, nevertheless to adversely affects 
the physical and mental health, diminish academic performance and potentially 
compromise the quality of patient care. Therefore, the Committee emphasizes the need 
for a balanced and humane duty structure. The Committee recommends that AIIMS 
management should strictly enforce the provisions of the Government of India 
Residency Scheme to ensure that the duty hour for Junior and Senior Residents do not 
exceed the prescribed limits. An institutional policy should be framed to regulate and 
cap consecutive duty hours, with provision for voluntary extra-duty shifts against 
appropriate compensation. The Committee further recommends that measures be put in 
place to balance clinical and academic responsibilities, particularly during examination 
and thesis submission periods. In this regard, the Committee recommends the Institute 
management, in consultation with resident doctors, to explore the feasibility and 
practicality of granting preparatory leave to final-year residents and arranging 
temporary recruitment of additional resident doctors to share the clinical workload.  
The Committee appreciates the role played by resident doctors in providing valuable 
fillip to the infrastructure constraints of regular doctors thus forming the backbone of 
healthcare. 
 
8.8.4 The Committee, in nutshell desires the AIIMS Management and the Department 
of Health and family welfare to take following steps for strengthening Human resources 
of AIIMS as a whole:- 
 
(i) Fast-track sanctioning and recruitment to fill vacancies and reduce workload 
imbalance; 
(ii) Expanding infrastructure and improving work life equilibrium by upgrading 
residential facilities and improving work conditions to construction of 
additional accommodation for faculty and staff ; 
(iii) Introduction of Structured career pathways linked incentives by providing 
choice in career pathways- clinical/research/academic/mixed with defined KPIs 
to ensure protect time and quality outcomes; 
(iv) Mentorship and career development by organising career development 
programmes and workshops and extending support to early career faculty and 
Scientists; 
(v) Incentivisation upon meeting for surpassing defined KPI targets that may be 
aligned with the NHA’s guidelines on utilization of ABPMJAY revenuel; 
(vi) Strategic collaborations with AIIMS for promoting interdisciplinary and 
international collaborations to expose young researchers to global standards;  
(vii) Enhance HR autonomy for responsive decision-making;  
(viii) Align HR metrics with strategic goals in education, research, and service 
delivery; and 
(ix) AIIMS, New Delhi should devise a standard protocol duty hours of junior and 
senior residents to be followed by all establishments across the country.

9.0 SWOT ANALYSIS AND STRATEGIC MANAGEMENT OF AIIMS NEW 
DELHI 
 
Strength 
9.1.1 AIIMS New Delhi continues to hold a distinguished position as India’s premier 
medical institution, supported by a strong global reputation and high patient trust. Its 
clinical excellence is reflected in its ability to manage more than 14,000 outpatient cases 
daily, while offering advanced super-specialty care across disciplines. The Institute 
maintains rigorous academic standards through its MBBS, MD/MS and DM/MCh 
programmes, attracting the nation’s most competitive candidates. With an annual 
research output exceeding 3,000 publications, AIIMS has established itself as a leading 
centre for clinical and biomedical research. Its autonomous governance structure, 
backed by a dedicated Act of Parliament, provides the flexibility needed to innovate in 
both academic and clinical domains. 
 
Weakness 
9.1.2 Despite these strengths, the Institute faces several internal challenges. Staff 
shortages, resulting largely from long lead times between post sanctioning and 
candidate joining; affect the balance between teaching, research and patient care. The 
absence of a structured referral system contributes to chronic overload of outpatient 
services, placing considerable strain on existing infrastructure. AIIMS also has very less 
formal collaboration with top global institutions, which limits opportunities for 
international exposure and joint research. Much of the campus infrastructure, including 
patient care and residential buildings, is over six decades old, requiring continuous 
maintenance with limited options for retrofitting. 
 
Opportunities 
9.1.3 At the same time, AIIMS is presented with significant opportunities. Digital 
transformation offers a pathway to modernize diagnostics, telemedicine and e-
governance. The Institute is well positioned to align itself with global benchmarks set by 
institutions such as Harvard, Oxford, Tokyo University Hospital and Peking Union 
Medical College, strengthening its role as a leader in medical education and research in 
the Global South. 
 
Threats 
9.1.4 Externally, the Institute faces threats such as talent attrition, with skilled 
professionals seeking better remuneration and work-life balance abroad or in the 
private sector. Technological adoption, particularly in AI, robotics and digital health, 
has progressed slowly compared to global peers. Moreover, public expectations for free, 
high-quality care continue to rise, without proportional expansion in resources or 
manpower. 
 
9.1.5 The Committee suggests the AIIMS, New Delhi management to take into account 
weaknesses and threat part of SWOT-Analysis so that AIIMS New Delhi must adopt a 

 
74 
 
series of strategic measures to address existing institutional weaknesses and mitigate 
emerging threats. The Committee, in this regard, recommends the Institute for fast-
track faculty recruitment by introducing streamlined hiring processes and offering 
competitive compensation packages, tenure-track positions, sabbaticals and research 
grants to attract and retain high-quality talent. The Committee feels that AIIMS should 
undertake reforms and operationalize a structured national referral framework to 
reduce OPD overload and ensure that the Institute primarily receives patients requiring 
advanced tertiary-level care. 
 
9.1.6 To enhance clinical efficiency and service delivery, the Committee recommends 
that AIIMS accelerate the integration of advanced technologies, including artificial 
intelligence, machine learning, data-science, robotic surgical systems and digital 
dashboards for patient flow and resource management. In order to capitalize on its 
strengths and emerging opportunities, the Committee desires that AIIMS strengthen its 
global collaborations by establishing Memoranda of Understanding with leading 
international universities for joint research, faculty exchanges and curriculum 
development.  
 
9.1.7 The Committee is of the firm opinion that adequacy of available fund at the nick 
of the time is indispensable for completion of undertaken construction and research 
projects without time and cost overruns. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
improving financial sustainability by budgetary allocation as per projected demand. 
Moreover, AIIMS should attract CSR contributions, philanthropic funding and other 
external resources to support infrastructure development and research innovation. The 
Committee desires that AIIMS establish interdisciplinary research hubs in key areas 
such as genomics, bioengineering and public health, and promote start-up incubation 
and translational innovation through the Centre for Medical Innovation and 
Entrepreneurship (CMIE). 
 
9.2 STRATEGIC MANAGEMENT 
 
9.2.1 Responding to the Committee’s query regarding the strategic management that can be 
adopted for having Always a Better Control (ABC) with requisite coordination for having 
overall professional working equilibrium and the organizational interventions required for 
achieving such cherished objectives, the Ministry responded as under:- 
(i) Implementation of a centralized dashboard for real-time tracking of patient flow, 
inventory, HR metrics, and financials. 
(ii) Use AI-driven analytics to forecast demand, optimize scheduling, and reduce 
bottlenecks. 
(iii) Linking of departmental performance to measureable outcomes : patient 
satisfaction, academic output, and operational efficiency. 
(iv) Use of digital triage tools to redirect non-tertiary cases to appropriate centres. 
(v) Training and skill development of mid-level managers and Department Heads in 
administration, strategic planning, and change management. 

 
75 
 
(vi) Regular monthly coordination meetings across departments to resolve operational 
conflicts and align priorities.  
9.2.2 The Committee is in agreement with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
in regard to the requisite steps to be taken for strategic management of AIIMS, New 
Delhi in order to have Always a Better Control (ABC). The Committee is of the 
considered view that the strategic management for a better managerial control requires 
digital command and control system, performance based accountability, referral system 
strengthening, therefore, AIIMS management must strive towards this direction. The 
Committee further recommends that certain organizational interventions viz. leadership 
development programme and professionally functioning Inter-departmental 
Coordination Committees must be evolved in order to achieve efficient working 
equilibrium.

10.1.2 The Committee observes that while AIIMS New Delhi is distinguished by its 
exceptionally high clinical load, strong public health role and growing research 
footprint, institutions such as Harvard Medical School, Oxford Medical School, Tokyo 
University Hospital and Peking Union Medical College represent diverse models of 
advanced biomedical research, technologically driven healthcare and structured 
academic training. Such comparative assessment highlights the unique strengths of each 
institution and provides insight into areas where AIIMS may further align with global 
best practices to enhance its academic and clinical impact. 
 
10.1.3 The Committee takes into account that AIIMS New Delhi demonstrates 
exceptional clinical service delivery and emerging research capabilities, but requires 
further strengthening in areas such as research infrastructure, faculty-to-student ratios, 
simulation-based training and adoption of advanced medical technologies. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that AIIMS New Delhi undertake targeted reforms 
to align more closely with global best practices, particularly by expanding its research 
ecosystem, enhancing interdisciplinary collaboration and increasing protected time and 
funding for investigator-led research. The Committee further recommends for 
establishment of advanced and global standard simulation and innovation centers, 
similar to those in institutions like Harvard and Oxford, to modernize clinical training 
and improve competency-based education. 
 
10.1.4 The Committee is of the considered view that AIIMS, New Delhi must explore 
international academic partnerships and faculty exchange programmes to enhance 
global exposure for students and researchers. The Committee opines that strengthening 
digital health systems, integrating AI-driven diagnostic tools and adopting structured 
referral mechanisms would go a long way in additionally improving efficiency and 
patient outcomes. 
 
10.2 Best Practices and Strategic Imperatives for Strengthening AIIMS New Delhi 
 
10.2.1 The Committee highlights that the leading global medical institutions reveals 
several best practices that AIIMS New Delhi must consider adopting to enhance its 
clinical efficiency, academic output and research excellence. One of the foremost areas is 
the development of a structured national referral system. Institutions such as the 

 
77 
 
Oxford Medical Sciences Division in the United Kingdom and Tokyo University 
Hospital in Japan function within tiered healthcare systems that regulate patient flow 
and ensure that tertiary centers receive referrals only for complex cases. For AIIMS, 
implementing a similar framework would help reduce overwhelming OPD congestion, 
streamline case load and preserve the academic and research bandwidth essential to a 
premier teaching hospital. The Committee observes that AIIMS New Delhi stands at a 
critical juncture where adopting global best practices and strengthening institutional 
mechanisms can significantly enhance its clinical efficiency, academic excellence and 
research impact. In view of the comparative assessment with leading international 
institutions, the Committee recommends that AIIMS should develop and implement a 
structured national referral framework to manage patient load effectively and preserve 
the Institute’s academic and research capacity. 
 
10.2.2 The Committee wills to pin-point another key area that relates to faculty 
development and retention. Global institutions such as Harvard Medical School and 
Peking Union Medical College offer tenure tracks, well-defined research pathways, 
competitive remuneration packages and extensive opportunities for international 
collaboration. Keeping in view, the faculty vacancies at AIIMS reportedly around 30 
percent, introducing measures such as competitive service conditions, sabbatical 
provisions and research-linked incentives would significantly strengthen faculty 
retention and professional growth. The Committee recommends that faculty 
development and retention be accorded high priority, with measures such as 
competitive compensation, sabbatical provisions, tenure-linked pathways and research 
incentives to address existing vacancies and attract high-quality talent. The Committee 
also recommends AIIMS to expand technology-driven patient care, including wider 
adoption of AI-enabled diagnostics, digital health platforms, robotics and telemedicine 
systems. 
 
10.2.3 The Committee understands that AIIMS, New Delhi would also get benefitted by 
expanding technology-driven patient care, drawing from models at Tokyo University 
Hospital and Harvard, where artificial intelligence, robotics and telemedicine are 
integral to precision healthcare. The Committee is of the considered view that scaling up 
digital health platforms such as e-Sanjeevani and integrating AI tools for diagnostics, 
triage and medical decision support would go a long way in enhancing efficiency, reduce 
waiting times and improve clinical outcomes. 
 
10.2.4 The Committee takes into account that in the domain of medical education, 
several global institutions have moved towards simulation-based learning, with Oxford 
and Harvard operating advanced simulation laboratories to train students in clinical 
skills without risk to patients. Therefore, the Committee is of the firm opinion that 
AIIMS could substantially enhance its skill-based training by investing in high-fidelity 
simulation centers and virtual reality–based learning environments. In the sphere of 
medical education, the Committee recommends that AIIMS establish advanced 
simulation and virtual reality–based training centers, similar to those in leading global 
institutions, to strengthen skill-based learning. 
 

 
78 
 
10.2.5 The Committee firmly believes that a stronger interdisciplinary research 
ecosystem is concomitant to forward looking advanced, modern and scientific pattern of 
delivering healthcare at affordable cost. Institutions like Stanford and Harvard have 
pioneered cross-disciplinary labs that integrate bioengineering, data science, and 
medicine to drive translational research. AIIMS can adopt a similar approach by 
fostering collaborations across departments and partnering with institutions such as 
IITs, IISc and other national research centers. To enable these advancements, 
administrative and financial support will be critical. The Committee advises for 
fostering interdisciplinary research ecosystems and strengthening collaborations with 
institutions such as IITs, IISc and global universities to promote innovation in-depth 
research and research collaboration. 
 
10.2.6 The Committee is of the opinion that the Governance reforms, including 
leadership development programmes for senior positions and the introduction of Key 
Performance Indicators (KPIs) for academic, clinical and research excellence, can 
promote greater accountability and strategic focus. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that the AIIMS Management should leave no stone unturned in making 
concerted efforts in this direction in order to achieve the cherished goal.  
 
10.2.7 The Committee is of the view that the infrastructure investment is required to 
expand residential accommodations, enhance simulation and research facilities and 
upgrade digital systems for telemedicine and e-governance. Sustainable funding 
mechanisms, such as establishing endowment funds, attracting CSR or private-sector 
investments and increasing budgetary allocations for research and international 
exchange programmes, will further strengthen the Institute’s capacity. The Committee 
also recommends comprehensive administrative and financial enhancements, including 
leadership development programmes, introduction of clear Key Performance Indicators 
(KPIs), expanded infrastructure for accommodation and research, upgraded digital 
systems, establishment of endowment funds and greater engagement with CSR and 
private-sector partners.

11.2 Fellowship Programme in Super Speciality Courses 
 
11.2.1 The Committee has come across the findings of studies on the impact of 
workload on the lifespan of a modern day doctor whereby due to mental stress the 
lifespan has come down by 8 to 10 years. Unless, the strength of faculty is enhanced the 
workload will remain too much. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry may commence fellowship programme in super-speciality courses so that 
AIIMS, New Delhi can be in a position to have some additional faculty in Cardiology, 
Neurology, Nephrology, and Neo-natology, etc. The Committee believes that once the 
fellowship courses are started some candidates who are already post DM will join the 
course that would ultimately increase the faculty and thereby reduce the workload to 
some extent.  
 
11.3 Implementation of National Rare Disease Policy 
 
11.3.1 The Committee has come across that AIIMS, New Delhi has been recognized as 
the Centre of Excellence for treatment of Rare Disease and, therefore, it is but natural

spirit. However, it is quite surprising that out of total number of patients suffering from 
Lysosomal Storage Disorder only 36 patients got the treatment, 42 patients are deprived

treatment. The Committee desires to know the number of patients who got approval for 
ERT treatment and the reasons for pending approval for the rest of the patients in

11.4 Mental Stress Management Session for Doctors and Allied Healthcare 
Practitioners 
 
11.4.1  The Committee is well aware that due to overcrowding of patients visiting 
from across the country for completely reliable and accurate treatment of various 
diseases, the doctors, allied healthcare practitioners and other staff of AIIMS, New 
Delhi remain constantly under severe mental stress, therefore, the Committee is of the 
considered view that there should be mental stress management session for the serving 
doctors and allied practitioners so that they found themselves fit to devote their mental 
focus towards treatment and palliative care of patient. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that Music Therapy for relieving their mental stress and opportunities for 
Yoga and Mediation may be arranged for doctors and allied professionals to keep them 
physically fit to take on the medical practices as per their assignment. The Committee 
believes so as nowadays mental stress is one of the reasons for most of the diseases, 
therefore, the mental strain and status of doctors and allied practitioners need to be 
taken care of and they should be given opportunity to participate in seminars, yoga-
sessions, meditation to get stress free and afresh.   
 
11.5 Exploring possibility for OPD in night 
 
11.5.1 The Committee came across a proposal from within for AIIMS, New Delhi 
management for exploring the possibility of opening OPD in the night in order to reduce 
the workload or overcrowding. An arrangement may be made for rotation of duties for 
deploying of doctors and allied practitioners on each day and night and the rest period 
for them be arranged on Monday if their turns comes on Sunday and the vice-versa. A 
plea has been taken into consideration that if aeroplane can fly day and night and train 
can run each day and night, there is no reason that OPD cannot be conducted likewise. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends D/o Health and Family Welfare and the AIIMS, 
New Delhi management to explore the possibility of conducting OPD round the clock for 
reducing overcrowding and enabling the patient to access healthcare without much 
hassles.

11.7 Exploring possibility of reallocating of control and management over Institute of 
Human Behaviour & Allied Sciences (IHBAS) under Central Government from 
Government of NCT, Delhi. 
 
11.7.1 The Committee is of the understanding that the Institute of Human Behaviour & 
Allied Sciences (IHBAS) was established in compliance with the directives of the Hon'ble 
Supreme Court in response to a public interest litigation in 1993. The Institute is an 
autonomous body registered under the Societies Act 1860, funded jointly by Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare, Government of India and Government of NCT of Delhi. As an 
autonomous body, the institute has its Memorandum of Association and Rules and 
Regulations duly approved under the Societies Act. 
 
11.7.2 The Committee appreciates the steps taken by Government of India towards 
improving the status of mental health in the country and lots of efforts have been made 
in the Budget (2026-27)  in this direction. However, the Committee is of the view that the 
control and management of IHBAS may be reallocated to Central Government from 
Government of NCT, Delhi to enhance the infrastructure and intake capacity for better 
mental health treatment and care. Hon’ble Supreme Court of India is of the view that 
IHBAS acts as a nodal agency for Central mental health programmes, the there is need 
to support the strengthening of such institutions. The Committee is of the considered 
view that concerted efforts must be made to enhance the infrastructure and facilities of 
IHBAS to the status of AIIMS like institutions to meet the challenges pertaining to 
mental healthcare.

12.1.1 AIIMS, New Delhi, over the years, has transformed into a global model of academic 
excellence, clinical service and public health leadership. Ranked as the number one medical 
college in the country for seven consecutive years (2018–2024) by the National Institutional 

 
83 
 
Ranking Framework (NIRF), conferred with the Best Extramural Research Institute at the 
DHR-ICMR Health Research Excellence Summit 2024 and recognized globally by

12.1.2 The Committee recognizes AIIMS, New Delhi a leader in quality assurance, 
having received NABH and NABL certifications for multiple facilities including the

12.2 AIIMS, New Delhi : A legacy of Laurels, a Future of Excellence 
 
12.2.1 The Committee takes into account the pivotal role of the institute serving as a 
model for newly established AIIMS across the country necessitates regular review and 
policy-level support. The Committee recommends that AIIMS, New Delhi to optimally 
utilize opportunity to recognize and reinforce best practices, scientific, modern, 
innovative models worth scaling and ensure that the institute continues to uphold its 
foundational mandate. Lessons from AIIMS, New Delhi can guide performance 
benchmarks, patient handling frameworks, infrastructure planning, digital health 
implementation and research ecosystems for the broader AIIMS network set up under 
PMSSY.

INTRODUCTION 
1. The Committee understands that in order to realize the vision set out for the 
Institute, AIIMS, New Delhi has been granted a high degree of academic, administrative 
and financial autonomy allowing it to chart its own path in pursuit of excellence. The 
Committee believes that strict adherence to level of autonomy granted to the Institute 
will certainly ensure that AIIMS, New Delhi will remain dynamic, responsive and 
forward-thinking in addressing the ever-evolving healthcare needs of the nation. The 
Committee recommends that the Government will remain committed to providing the 
necessary financial support to maintain and advance its operations, ensuring that 
AIIMS continues to serve as a world-class hub for patient care, medical education, 
cutting-edge research and Good Governance. 
(Para 1.4.4) 
2. The Committee believes that since the vision of AIIMS, New Delhi originates 
from its foundational mandate to function as a medical college or hospital as well as an 
institution of national importance empowered with the status and responsibility of 
university, therefore, all activities/efforts at each level of structural arrangement 
entrusted with specific functional behaviour must be made on the principle of 
Management By Objectives (MBO) rather than mere Management By Activities (MBA) 
so that the enshrined objectives/goals are achieved within the stipulated time-frame. In 
this regard, the Committee also recommends that the AIIMS, New Delhi must continue 
to serve as the apex referral center all over the country, a think-tank for national policy 
formation and a nerve center for healthcare innovation and reforms. 
(Para 1.4.5) 
 
3. The Committee further recommends AIIMS, New Delhi to be a global leader in 
equitable technology driven and patient Centric healthcare. The AIIMS, New Delhi 
must strengthen referral system nationwide, expand outreach by a tele-medicine and 
foster innovation to translational research. 
(Para 1.4.6)

funds by AIIMS, New Delhi, and acknowledges the gradual increase in the Budget 
Estimate (BE) to ₹5500.92 crore for FY 2026-27. However, the Committee observes that

AIIMS is executing a complex, 190-acre integrated Master Plan while simultaneously

that the Department proactively review and enhance the allocation at the Revised 
Estimate (RE) stage to bridge this ₹257 crore deficit. Ensuring adequate liquidity is

initiation of upcoming mega-projects, such as establishment of a CBRNE facility and

expansion of JPNATC and Centre of Excellence in Child Health at Jhajjar. The

thousands of patients look up to AIIMS for healthcare needs. The AIIMS management 
should overcome its lethargy and address the contradiction wherein on one hand 
patients are made to wait for long periods for surgical interventions whereas on the 
other hand the OTs are lying non-functional. Such non-functionality not only 
undermines patient care but also reflects gaps in maintenance, resource utilization and 
management failure to ensure timely operationalization of critical facilities. The

59. The Committee notes with concern the disproportionately high patient load at 
the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi leading to 
congestion/long waiting time for patients not just inside the hospital but wobbling 
queues outside too. The OPD data for the period January to December 2024 reveals that

62. The Committee took into consideration the action taken by AIIMS, New Delhi to 
reduce overcrowding and long waiting times through the new specialty centres, the 
Online Registration System (ORS) and token-based walk-ins. The Committee 
appreciates the introduction of online appointments through the Online Registration 
System (ORS) portal, along with a token system designed to regulate walk-in patients on 
a first-come, first-served basis. The distribution of OPD slots as 50 per cent allocated for 
online appointments, 30 per cent reserved for walk-ins and the remaining 20 per cent 
earmarked for cross-referrals is a rational approach. However, the Committee is of the 
view that despite these measures, the demand for services at AIIMS continues to exceed 
its capacity. The Committee therefore recommends that AIIMS, New Delhi further 
strengthen its digital appointment management system by making it mobile-friendly, 

 
101 
 
multilingual and integrated with centralized electronic medical records, real-time 
updates, automated reminders and referral linkages with other AIIMS and regional 
institutions. These measures, along with physical patient-support mechanisms, would 
streamline patient flow, reduce unnecessary congestion from routine follow-ups and 
ensure equitable access. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare replicate the ORS and token-based model across all AIIMS 
and major central hospitals for greater efficiency and transparency nationwide. 
(Para 7.4.2) 
 
63. The Committee also recommends that a structured two-way referral system be 
established between AIIMS institutions and other medical colleges in order to ensure 
effective distribution of patients across healthcare facilities. The Committee is of the 
considered view that the adoption of a hub-and-spoke model, linking Primary Health 
Centres (PHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs), district hospitals, medical colleges 
and AIIMS institutions, would facilitate seamless integration of services across different 
levels of care. The Committee also strongly recommends that the Government should 
seriously consider setting up the ‘Hub and Spoke’ model to address the problem of 
overcrowding in the hospitals in metropolitan cities. Such a system would enable 
patients to be directed to the most appropriate facility based on the nature and severity 
of their medical needs, thereby enhancing efficiency, reducing overcrowding at apex 
centres and improving outcomes. 
(Para 7.4.3)

Welfare, in consultation with AIIMS, explore the possibility of establishment of satellite

with estimated cost of Rs. 150 crore to Rs. 200 crore and search centres may be called as

with AIIMS, there would be a lot of public acceptability.  Since in Delhi, the travel
