The Committee strongly believes that tertiary level healthcare institutions can do more 
quality work, more research work and would be more contributory from the futuristic 
point of view once the salary of doctors in super-specialised centres is enhanced and 
made comparable to healthcare institutions in the private sector. 
(Para 8.1.4) 
 
93. The Committee is of the view that since AIIMS, Delhi envisage itself as a centre 
of excellence in Medical Education in Research and in Patient care. Its HR Policy must 
be aligned with its mission and vision i.e. in consonance with meritocratic recruitment 
supported academic integrity, training programme fostering clinical and Research 
Excellence and digital HR systems aiming at enhancing the governance and 
accountability. AIIMS management should chalk out specific course of action to fill up 
gaps in such alignment viz Low Faculty to Student ratio impacts the teaching and 
research mission, Limited career progression impacts motivation and innovation, 
Overburdened staff due to high patient load affects quality of care and academic output 
and More protected time needed for research or academics. 
(Para 8.1.5)  
 
VACANCIES IN NON-FACULTY POSITIONS 
 
94. The Committee is constrained to observe that the All India Institute of Medical 
Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, is presently functioning under severe shortage of both 
teaching and non-teaching staff. Out of a sanctioned strength of 1,306 faculty posts, as 
many as 508 remain vacant, while in the case of non-faculty staff, 3,056 out of 13,911 

 
110 
 
sanctioned posts are unfilled. The Committee notes with concern that such manpower 
deficit might adversely affect the Institute’s capacity to discharge its dual mandate of 
providing quality medical education and delivering world-class healthcare services. 
(Para 8.3.6) 
 
95. The Committee is alarmed to note that the highest number of vacancies exists at 
the level of Assistant Professor, which directly impacts the student–teacher ratio, 
academic mentorship and research productivity. The Committee further observes that 
vacancies in the cadre of Professors have been long pending due to protracted litigation 
and administrative delays, which might adversely impact leadership in several key 
departments.  
(Para 8.3.7) 
 
96. The Committee desires that AIIMS, New Delhi must have rationalized the 
pyramidal structure in appropriate ratio of Assistant Professors, Associate Professors 
and above as the future of Institution depends on the base of pyramid and the Assistant 
Professors are the future of the Institution, therefore, concerted efforts must be made to 
fill up the post of Assistant Professors, of course, keeping it to consideration the need to 
follow the roster system as per the constitution norms. 
(Para 8.3.8) 
 
97. In respect of non-faculty staff, the Committee is deeply concerned that shortages, 
particularly in the nursing cadre will not only increase the workload of the existing 
personnel but also pose a serious risk to patient safety, service delivery and the overall 
efficiency of healthcare operations. 
(Para 8.3.9) 
 
98. The Committee is of the firm view that such prolonged vacancies have the 
potential to dilute the academic standards of AIIMS Delhi and undermine its reputation 
as a centre of excellence in medical education, research and patient care. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that AIIMS Delhi should fast-track the ongoing 
recruitment processes and ensure that appointments to both faculty and non-faculty 
positions are completed within strict timelines. The Committee is of the opinion that 
while the reforms to introduce transparency, objective evaluation criteria and 
technology-driven recruitment are commendable, these measures, however, should not 
cause undue delay in filling up urgent vacancies. The Committee further recommends 
that contractual appointments be expanded as an interim measure to bridge immediate 
gaps, especially in the high-demand specialties and in the nursing cadre. 
(Para 8.3.10) 
 
99. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare extend all necessary support to AIIMS, New Delhi by way of expediting 
necessary approvals, removing administrative bottlenecks and providing adequate 
budgetary backing to conduct timely recruitment. The Committee further recommends 
that a system of biannual recruitment for nursing officers and an annual recruitment 
cycle for faculty and paramedical staff be institutionalised across all AIIMS institutions 

 
111 
 
so as to prevent the recurrence of such large-scale vacancies in the future. The 
Committee also recommends the Ministry to explore conducting NORCET more 
frequently than twice a year to increase the strength of nurse staff. 
(Para 8.3.11) 
 
100. The Committee strongly recommends that a joint monitoring mechanism 
between AIIMS Delhi and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare be established to 
periodically review recruitment progress, ensure accountability and project manpower 
requirements in consonance with the expansion plans of the Institute. The Committee 
emphasizes that addressing these shortages on an urgent basis is imperative to 
safeguard the academic excellence and healthcare standards of AIIMS Delhi. Any 
further delay in filling up these vacancies would, in the considered view of the 
Committee, severely compromise the ability of the Institute to retain its premier status 
and to meet the ever-growing demand for specialized medical services in the country. 
(Para 8.3.12) 
 
CADRE REVIEW & RESERVATION IN PROMOTIONS 
 
101. The Committee, after careful consideration of the submissions by representatives 
of various associations on pressing human resource challenges, is deeply concerned 
about the prolonged neglect of cadre review, last being conducted in 1992 leading to the 
acute shortage of promotion opportunities across different cadres in AIIMS. The 
Committee observes that the absence of cadre reviews at rational period of interval has 
led to stagnation, weakened staff morale and diminished efficiency, while the delay in 
filling up vacant posts, especially in Group D, continues to affect service delivery. 
Despite approval of fresh cadre review by the Standing Finance Committee and 
Governing Body, the proposal remain stalled at the Ministry level. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry take immediate steps to approve and 
implement the long-pending cadre review, ensuring the creation of adequate promotion 
posts for nurses, sanctioning of long-vacant positions and the establishment of clear and 
updated recruitment and promotion pathways for all categories of staff. 
(Para 8.4.4) 
 
102. The Committee further recommends the immediate implementation of provision 
of reservation in promotions in strict conformity with DoPT guidelines and National 
Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) directives, alongside the creation of a fully 
functional reservation cell with regular monitoring of rosters and active participation of 
SC/ST representatives in advisory and policy-making committees. By addressing these 
issues in a comprehensive and time-bound manner, the Ministry will not only enhance 
staff motivation and retention but also strengthen institutional efficiency and ensure 
that AIIMS continues to function with the highest standards of excellence. 
(Para 8.4.5) 
 
 
 

 
112 
 
IMPLEMENTATION OF ROTATORY HEADSHIP POLICY 
 
103. The Committee concurs with the submission of the Faculty Association of AIIMS 
(FAIMS) regarding the urgent need to implement the Rotatory Headship policy at 
AIIMS, New Delhi. Recognizing the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare’s earlier 
commitment to operationalize the said policy by June 2024, the Committee observes 
with a caution that further delay would undermine both faculty morale and institutional 
trust. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Institute take immediate steps to 
implement the Rotatory Headship policy and ensure democratic governance, equitable 
distribution of leadership roles and prevention of power centralization. The proposed 
reform, long overdue, is essential to foster departmental excellence, transparency and 
fairness and to uphold the reputation of the Institution as a model of academic and 
professional integrity. 
(Para 8.5.4) 
 
ABSORPTION/REGULARISATION OF PROJECT RESEARCH STAFF 
 
104. The Committee observes with concern that the Institute’s Order (Ref. No. 14/20-
Estt.(RCT) rejecting the absorption and regularisation of the eligible research staff 
despite 15 years of continuous service in various research projects is inconsistent with 
the established policy of AIIMS, past precedents and the recommendations of multiple 
Committees, as well as the directives of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court. 
The Committee takes into account that between 1992 and 2021, over 164 project staff 
were absorbed under this very framework, thereby setting a clear institutional and legal 
precedent. The Committee concurs with the representation submitted by the Project 
Research Staff and recognizes their invaluable contribution to the Institute’s research 
ecosystem. Having devoted over 15 years of continuous service in diverse projects, these 
staff members represent a highly trained and experienced human resource that has 
been instrumental in sustaining and advancing the research output of AIIMS. 
(Para 8.6.6) 
 
105. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that AIIMS urgently reconsider 
the case of absorption and regularization of all eligible Project Research Staff who have 
completed 15 years of service. Their integration into the regular workforce is not only a 
matter of justice and policy consistency but is also essential for strengthening the 
Institute’s research capacity and output by retaining skilled manpower already trained 
and specialized in the research ecosystem of the Institute. The Committee is of the 
considered view that a core research cadre be developed, in line with judicial directives, 
to ensure long-term continuity, stability and growth of the Institute’s research 
endeavours. 
(Para 8.6.7) 
 
ISSUES FACED BY NON-FACULTY EMPLOYEES 
106. The Committee took into consideration the submission of Non-faculty employees 
of AIIMS regarding alleged discriminatory treatment meted to non-faculty staff despite 

 
113 
 
their vital role in the functioning of the Institute. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, in consultation with 
AIIMS, takes urgent response to address the concerns of non-faculty employees 
regarding parity in service conditions and welfare measures. Given their critical 
contribution to the functioning of the Institute, it is essential that non-faculty staffs are 
extended equal benefits that have been provided to their counterparts in other central 
institutions. The Committee is of the view that legitimate requests such as the option to 
shift from NPS to OPS, extension of productivity-linked bonuses and adoption of other 
welfare measures, which are in line with Central Government orders should be 
extended to non-faculty staff of AIIMS with due consideration. Ensuring equity in 
service conditions will not only enhance motivation and team spirit among employees 
but also strengthen institutional harmony and efficiency at AIIMS. 
(Para 8.7.2) 
 
WORKING HOURS OF RESIDENTS 
 
107. The Committee takes into account the submission of the Resident Doctors 
Association and expresses concern that Residents Doctors have to put in excessive duty 
hours, sometimes working upto 36 hours at a stretch well beyond the limits envisaged 
under the residency scheme. The Committee is of considered view that such extended 
working hours, while reflective of service exigencies, nevertheless to adversely affects 
the physical and mental health, diminish academic performance and potentially 
compromise the quality of patient care. Therefore, the Committee emphasizes the need 
for a balanced and humane duty structure. The Committee recommends that AIIMS 
management should strictly enforce the provisions of the Government of India 
Residency Scheme to ensure that the duty hour for Junior and Senior Residents do not 
exceed the prescribed limits. An institutional policy should be framed to regulate and 
cap consecutive duty hours, with provision for voluntary extra-duty shifts against 
appropriate compensation. The Committee further recommends that measures be put in 
place to balance clinical and academic responsibilities, particularly during examination 
and thesis submission periods. In this regard, the Committee recommends the Institute 
management, in consultation with resident doctors, to explore the feasibility and 
practicality of granting preparatory leave to final-year residents and arranging 
temporary recruitment of additional resident doctors to share the clinical workload.  
The Committee appreciates the role played by resident doctors in providing valuable 
fillip to the infrastructure constraints of regular doctors thus forming the backbone of 
healthcare. 
(Para 8.8.3) 
 
108. The Committee, in nutshell desires the AIIMS Management and the Department 
of Health and family welfare to take following steps for strengthening Human resources 
of AIIMS as a whole:- 
(i) Fast-track sanctioning and recruitment to fill vacancies and reduce 
workload imbalance; 

 
114 
 
(ii) Expanding infrastructure and improving work life equilibrium by 
upgrading residential facilities and improving work conditions to 
construction of additional accommodation for faculty and staff ; 
(iii) Introduction of Structured career pathways linked incentives by providing 
choice in career pathways- clinical/research/academic/mixed with defined 
KPIs to ensure protect time and quality outcomes; 
(iv) Mentorship and career development by organising career development 
programmes and workshops and extending support to early career faculty 
and Scientists; 
(v) Incentivisation upon meeting for surpassing defined KPI targets that may 
be aligned with the NHA’s guidelines on utilization of ABPMJAY revenuel; 
(vi) Strategic collaborations with AIIMS for promoting interdisciplinary and 
international collaborations to expose young researchers to global 
standards;  
(vii) Enhance HR autonomy for responsive decision-making;  
(viii) Align HR metrics with strategic goals in education, research, and service 
delivery; and 
(ix) AIIMS, New Delhi should devise a standard protocol duty hours of junior 
and senior residents to be followed by all establishments across the country. 
(Para 8.8.4) 
 
SWOT ANALYSIS AND STRATEGIC MANAGEMENT OF AIIMS NEW DELHI 
 
Strength 
109. AIIMS New Delhi continues to hold a distinguished position as India’s premier 
medical institution, supported by a strong global reputation and high patient trust. Its 
clinical excellence is reflected in its ability to manage more than 14,000 outpatient cases 
daily, while offering advanced super-specialty care across disciplines. The Institute 
maintains rigorous academic standards through its MBBS, MD/MS and DM/MCh 
programmes, attracting the nation’s most competitive candidates. With an annual 
research output exceeding 3,000 publications, AIIMS has established itself as a leading 
centre for clinical and biomedical research. Its autonomous governance structure, 
backed by a dedicated Act of Parliament, provides the flexibility needed to innovate in 
both academic and clinical domains. 
(Para 9.1.1) 
Weakness 
110. Despite these strengths, the Institute faces several internal challenges. Staff 
shortages, resulting largely from long lead times between post sanctioning and 
candidate joining; affect the balance between teaching, research and patient care. The 
absence of a structured referral system contributes to chronic overload of outpatient 
services, placing considerable strain on existing infrastructure. AIIMS also has very less 
formal collaboration with top global institutions, which limits opportunities for 
international exposure and joint research. Much of the campus infrastructure, including 
patient care and residential buildings, is over six decades old, requiring continuous 
maintenance with limited options for retrofitting. 
(Para 9.1.2) 

 
115 
 
Opportunities 
111. At the same time, AIIMS is presented with significant opportunities. Digital 
transformation offers a pathway to modernize diagnostics, telemedicine and e-
governance. The Institute is well positioned to align itself with global benchmarks set by 
institutions such as Harvard, Oxford, Tokyo University Hospital and Peking Union 
Medical College, strengthening its role as a leader in medical education and research in 
the Global South. 
(Para 9.1.3) 
Threats 
112. Externally, the Institute faces threats such as talent attrition, with skilled 
professionals seeking better remuneration and work-life balance abroad or in the 
private sector. Technological adoption, particularly in AI, robotics and digital health, 
has progressed slowly compared to global peers. Moreover, public expectations for free, 
high-quality care continue to rise, without proportional expansion in resources or 
manpower. 
(Para 9.1.4) 
113. The Committee suggests the AIIMS, New Delhi management to take into account 
weaknesses and threat part of SWOT-Analysis so that AIIMS New Delhi must adopt a 
series of strategic measures to address existing institutional weaknesses and mitigate 
emerging threats. The Committee, in this regard, recommends the Institute for fast-
track faculty recruitment by introducing streamlined hiring processes and offering 
competitive compensation packages, tenure-track positions, sabbaticals and research 
grants to attract and retain high-quality talent. The Committee feels that AIIMS should 
undertake reforms and operationalize a structured national referral framework to 
reduce OPD overload and ensure that the Institute primarily receives patients requiring 
advanced tertiary-level care. 
(Para 9.1.5) 
 
114. To enhance clinical efficiency and service delivery, the Committee recommends 
that AIIMS accelerate the integration of advanced technologies, including artificial 
intelligence, machine learning, data-science, robotic surgical systems and digital 
dashboards for patient flow and resource management. In order to capitalize on its 
strengths and emerging opportunities, the Committee desires that AIIMS strengthen its 
global collaborations by establishing Memoranda of Understanding with leading 
international universities for joint research, faculty exchanges and curriculum 
development. 
(Para 9.1.6) 
 
115. The Committee is of the firm opinion that adequacy of available fund at the nick 
of the time is indispensable for completion of undertaken construction and research 
projects without time and cost overruns. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
improving financial sustainability by budgetary allocation as per projected demand. 
Moreover, AIIMS should attract CSR contributions, philanthropic funding and other 
external resources to support infrastructure development and research innovation. The 
Committee desires that AIIMS establish interdisciplinary research hubs in key areas 

 
116 
 
such as genomics, bioengineering and public health, and promote start-up incubation 
and translational innovation through the Centre for Medical Innovation and 
Entrepreneurship (CMIE). 
(Para 9.1.7) 
 
STRATEGIC MANAGEMENT 
 
116. The Committee is in agreement with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
in regard to the requisite steps to be taken for strategic management of AIIMS, New 
Delhi in order to have Always a Better Control (ABC). The Committee is of the 
considered view that the strategic management for a better managerial control requires 
digital command and control system, performance based accountability, referral system 
strengthening, therefore, AIIMS management must strive towards this direction. The 
Committee further recommends that certain organizational interventions viz. leadership 
development programme and professionally functioning Inter-departmental 
Coordination Committees must be evolved in order to achieve efficient working 
equilibrium. 
(Para 9.2.2) 
 
AIIMS VIS-À-VIS GLOBAL INSTITUTIONS 
117. The Committee observes that while AIIMS New Delhi is distinguished by its 
exceptionally high clinical load, strong public health role and growing research 
footprint, institutions such as Harvard Medical School, Oxford Medical School, Tokyo 
University Hospital and Peking Union Medical College represent diverse models of 
advanced biomedical research, technologically driven healthcare and structured 
academic training. Such comparative assessment highlights the unique strengths of each 
institution and provides insight into areas where AIIMS may further align with global 
best practices to enhance its academic and clinical impact. 
(Para 10.1.2) 
118. The Committee takes into account that AIIMS New Delhi demonstrates 
exceptional clinical service delivery and emerging research capabilities, but requires 
further strengthening in areas such as research infrastructure, faculty-to-student ratios, 
simulation-based training and adoption of advanced medical technologies. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that AIIMS New Delhi undertake targeted reforms 
to align more closely with global best practices, particularly by expanding its research 
ecosystem, enhancing interdisciplinary collaboration and increasing protected time and 
funding for investigator-led research. The Committee further recommends for 
establishment of advanced and global standard simulation and innovation centers, 
similar to those in institutions like Harvard and Oxford, to modernize clinical training 
and improve competency-based education. 
(Para 10.1.3) 
119. The Committee is of the considered view that AIIMS, New Delhi must explore 
international academic partnerships and faculty exchange programmes to enhance 
global exposure for students and researchers. The Committee opines that strengthening 

 
117 
 
digital health systems, integrating AI-driven diagnostic tools and adopting structured 
referral mechanisms would go a long way in additionally improving efficiency and 
patient outcomes. 
(Para 10.1.4) 
 
Best Practices and Strategic Imperatives for Strengthening AIIMS New Delhi 
 
120. The Committee highlights that the leading global medical institutions reveals 
several best practices that AIIMS New Delhi must consider adopting to enhance its 
clinical efficiency, academic output and research excellence. One of the foremost areas is 
the development of a structured national referral system. Institutions such as the 
Oxford Medical Sciences Division in the United Kingdom and Tokyo University 
Hospital in Japan function within tiered healthcare systems that regulate patient flow 
and ensure that tertiary centers receive referrals only for complex cases. For AIIMS, 
implementing a similar framework would help reduce overwhelming OPD congestion, 
streamline case load and preserve the academic and research bandwidth essential to a 
premier teaching hospital. The Committee observes that AIIMS New Delhi stands at a 
critical juncture where adopting global best practices and strengthening institutional 
mechanisms can significantly enhance its clinical efficiency, academic excellence and 
research impact. In view of the comparative assessment with leading international 
institutions, the Committee recommends that AIIMS should develop and implement a 
structured national referral framework to manage patient load effectively and preserve 
the Institute’s academic and research capacity. 
(Para 10.2.1) 
 
121. The Committee wills to pin-point another key area that relates to faculty 
development and retention. Global institutions such as Harvard Medical School and 
Peking Union Medical College offer tenure tracks, well-defined research pathways, 
competitive remuneration packages and extensive opportunities for international 
collaboration. Keeping in view, the faculty vacancies at AIIMS reportedly around 30 
percent, introducing measures such as competitive service conditions, sabbatical 
provisions and research-linked incentives would significantly strengthen faculty 
retention and professional growth. The Committee recommends that faculty 
development and retention be accorded high priority, with measures such as 
competitive compensation, sabbatical provisions, tenure-linked pathways and research 
incentives to address existing vacancies and attract high-quality talent. The Committee 
also recommends AIIMS to expand technology-driven patient care, including wider 
adoption of AI-enabled diagnostics, digital health platforms, robotics and telemedicine 
systems. 
(Para 10.2.2) 
 
122. The Committee understands that AIIMS, New Delhi would also get benefitted by 
expanding technology-driven patient care, drawing from models at Tokyo University 
Hospital and Harvard, where artificial intelligence, robotics and telemedicine are 
integral to precision healthcare. The Committee is of the considered view that scaling up 

 
118 
 
digital health platforms such as e-Sanjeevani and integrating AI tools for diagnostics, 
triage and medical decision support would go a long way in enhancing efficiency, reduce 
waiting times and improve clinical outcomes. 
(Para 10.2.3) 
 
123. The Committee takes into account that in the domain of medical education, 
several global institutions have moved towards simulation-based learning, with Oxford 
and Harvard operating advanced simulation laboratories to train students in clinical 
skills without risk to patients. Therefore, the Committee is of the firm opinion that 
AIIMS could substantially enhance its skill-based training by investing in high-fidelity 
simulation centers and virtual reality–based learning environments. In the sphere of 
medical education, the Committee recommends that AIIMS establish advanced 
simulation and virtual reality–based training centers, similar to those in leading global 
institutions, to strengthen skill-based learning. 
(Para 10.2.4) 
 
124. The Committee firmly believes that a stronger interdisciplinary research 
ecosystem is concomitant to forward looking advanced, modern and scientific pattern of 
delivering healthcare at affordable cost. Institutions like Stanford and Harvard have 
pioneered cross-disciplinary labs that integrate bioengineering, data science, and 
medicine to drive translational research. AIIMS can adopt a similar approach by 
fostering collaborations across departments and partnering with institutions such as 
IITs, IISc and other national research centers. To enable these advancements, 
administrative and financial support will be critical. The Committee advises for 
fostering interdisciplinary research ecosystems and strengthening collaborations with 
institutions such as IITs, IISc and global universities to promote innovation in-depth 
research and research collaboration. 
(Para 10.2.5) 
 
125. The Committee is of the opinion that the Governance reforms, including 
leadership development programmes for senior positions and the introduction of Key 
Performance Indicators (KPIs) for academic, clinical and research excellence, can 
promote greater accountability and strategic focus. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that the AIIMS Management should leave no stone unturned in making 
concerted efforts in this direction in order to achieve the cherished goal. 
(Para 10.2.6) 
 
126. The Committee is of the view that the infrastructure investment is required to 
expand residential accommodations, enhance simulation and research facilities and 
upgrade digital systems for telemedicine and e-governance. Sustainable funding 
mechanisms, such as establishing endowment funds, attracting CSR or private-sector 
investments and increasing budgetary allocations for research and international 
exchange programmes, will further strengthen the Institute’s capacity. The Committee 
also recommends comprehensive administrative and financial enhancements, including 
leadership development programmes, introduction of clear Key Performance Indicators 
(KPIs), expanded infrastructure for accommodation and research, upgraded digital 

 
119 
 
systems, establishment of endowment funds and greater engagement with CSR and 
private-sector partners. 
(Para 10.2.7) 
General Recommendations 
 
Mission Mode for filling up vacant posts as per sanctioned strength 
127. The Committee expresses deep anguish over the staggering 35% vacancy rate 
(452 vacancies) in faculty positions, along with Junior/Senior residents (700+ vacancies), 
and non-faculty posts (2,540 vacancies) which constrain service delivery and strain 
existing staff. Most alarmingly, the data reveals that while 32 faculty members resigned 
or superannuated in the years 2024-25 and 2025-26 (till January 2026), however, no new 
faculty members joined the institute during said period. The Committee disapproves 
such recruitment paralysis that infact severely jeopardizes the academic and clinical 
standards of AIIMS, New Delhi. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Department to calk out Strategic Action Plan with focused, time-bound recruitment 
drive with measurable targets and  milestones, viz. target filling (at least 85%) of 
sanctioned posts on fast track mission mode.  The Committee desires that the current 
328 advertised faculty positions may be finalised within the first two quarters of FY 
2026-27. 
(Para 11.1.5) 
128. Furthermore, the Committee does not approve the persistent reliance on 
contractual faculty i.e. currently 73 Assistant Professors must be phased out in favor of 
permanent appointments to ensure institutional commitment and belongingness and for 
ensuring a long-term accountability, therefore, contractual arrangements should serve 
only as temporary stop-gap management.  The Committee is of the considered view that 
long-standing contractual incumbents meeting eligibility criteria should be offered a 
regularisation/absorption pathway for better interest of both the professionals and the 
institutions.  The Committee also considers that the Department should introduce 
retention incentives tied to hard-to-fill specialties and underserved postings to improve 
the offer-to-joining ratio. 
(Para 11.1.6) 
Fellowship Programme in Super Speciality Courses 
 
129. The Committee has come across the findings of studies on the impact of 
workload on the lifespan of a modern day doctor whereby due to mental stress the 
lifespan has come down by 8 to 10 years. Unless, the strength of faculty is enhanced the 
workload will remain too much. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry may commence fellowship programme in super-speciality courses so that 
AIIMS, New Delhi can be in a position to have some additional faculty in Cardiology, 
Neurology, Nephrology, and Neo-natology, etc. The Committee believes that once the 
fellowship courses are started some candidates who are already post DM will join the 
course that would ultimately increase the faculty and thereby reduce the workload to 
some extent. 

 
120 
 
(Para 11.2.1) 
Implementation of National Rare Disease Policy 
 
130. The Committee has come across that AIIMS, New Delhi has been recognized as 
the Centre of Excellence for treatment of Rare Disease and, therefore, it is but natural 
that AIIMS, New Delhi should implement the National Rare Disease Policy in letter and 
spirit. However, it is quite surprising that out of total number of patients suffering from 
Lysosomal Storage Disorder only 36 patients got the treatment, 42 patients are deprived 
of Enzyme Replacement Therapy (ERT) and five patients died waiting for the 
treatment. The Committee desires to know the number of patients who got approval for 
ERT treatment and the reasons for pending approval for the rest of the patients in 
AIIMS, New Delhi. The Committee recommends that LSDs patients must get immediate 
treatment in AIIMS, New Delhi. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry 
of Health and Family Welfare must monitor that AIIMS, New Delhi implement the 
National Rare Disease Policy without fail and also display SOPs in this regard. 
(Para 11.3.1) 
 
 
Mental Stress Management Session for Doctors and Allied Healthcare Practitioners 
 
131. The Committee is well aware that due to overcrowding of patients visiting from 
across the country for completely reliable and accurate treatment of various diseases, 
the doctors, allied healthcare practitioners and other staff of AIIMS, New Delhi remain 
constantly under severe mental stress, therefore, the Committee is of the considered 
view that there should be mental stress management session for the serving doctors and 
allied practitioners so that they found themselves fit to devote their mental focus 
towards treatment and palliative care of patient. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that Music Therapy for relieving their mental stress and opportunities for 
Yoga and Mediation may be arranged for doctors and allied professionals to keep them 
physically fit to take on the medical practices as per their assignment. The Committee 
believes so as nowadays mental stress is one of the reasons for most of the diseases, 
therefore, the mental strain and status of doctors and allied practitioners need to be 
taken care of and they should be given opportunity to participate in seminars, yoga-
sessions, meditation to get stress free and afresh. 
(Para 11.4.1) 
 
Exploring possibility for OPD in night 
 
132. The Committee came across a proposal from within for AIIMS, New Delhi 
management for exploring the possibility of opening OPD in the night in order to reduce 
the workload or overcrowding. An arrangement may be made for rotation of duties for 
deploying of doctors and allied practitioners on each day and night and the rest period 
for them be arranged on Monday if their turns comes on Sunday and the vice-versa. A 
plea has been taken into consideration that if aeroplane can fly day and night and train 
can run each day and night, there is no reason that OPD cannot be conducted likewise. 

 
121 
 
The Committee, therefore, recommends D/o Health and Family Welfare and the AIIMS, 
New Delhi management to explore the possibility of conducting OPD round the clock for 
reducing overcrowding and enabling the patient to access healthcare without much 
hassles. 
(Para 11.5.1) 
Cleanliness in the waiting areas and washrooms  
 
133. The Committee takes into account with appreciation the submission of director 
AIIMS, New Delhi that AIIMS management have been put in a lot of efforts in regard to 
cleanliness in the waiting areas and washrooms and the institute is continuing to get the 
first prize for the cleanest hospital of the country under Kayakalpa. The Committee, 
however, came across that AIIMS management is facing challenges to maintain 
cleanliness in the older building especially the main hospital. The Committee, in this 
regard, recommends the AIIMS management to make all out efforts to ensure that the 
older buildings are kept clean up to the expected level and ensure safety, quality and the 
cleanliness. 
(Para 11.6)  
 
GLOBAL STANDING  
 
134. The Committee recognizes AIIMS, New Delhi a leader in quality assurance, 
having received NABH and NABL certifications for multiple facilities including the 
Trauma Centre, Burns & Plastic Surgery Block, Surgical Block, and NCI Jhajjar. The 
Committee desires that the Institute’s infection control, hygiene standards and surgical 
safety protocols must serve as model for replication in AIIMS like institutions and other 
leading hospitals across the country. 
(Para 12.1.2) 
AIIMS, New Delhi : A legacy of Laurels, a Future of Excellence 
 
135. The Committee takes into account the pivotal role of the institute serving as a 
model for newly established AIIMS across the country necessitates regular review and 
policy-level support. The Committee recommends that AIIMS, New Delhi to optimally 
utilize opportunity to recognize and reinforce best practices, scientific, modern, 
innovative models worth scaling and ensure that the institute continues to uphold its 
foundational mandate. Lessons from AIIMS, New Delhi can guide performance 
benchmarks, patient handling frameworks, infrastructure planning, digital health 
implementation and research ecosystems for the broader AIIMS network set up under 
PMSSY. 
(Para 12.2.1)

CHAPTER I 
INTRODUCTION 
1.1.1 India‘s healthcare system has undergone a profound transformation, evolving from its 
early foundations in community -oriented care to a modern, mul ti-tiered framework that 
integrates primary, secondary, and tertiary services. Rooted in the ancient ethos of Arogya 
(holistic well-being) and reinforced by successive national health policies, the system today 
reflects a balance between public responsibil ity and private sector innovation. Guided by the 
principles of Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Prayas , India envisions health as the 
cornerstone of national development and human capital growth. 
1.1.2 The government‘s vision, articulated through initiative s like the National Health 
Policy 2017 and Ayushman Bharat, is to achieve Universal Health Coverage (UHC) by 
ensuring equitable access, financial protection, and quality care across all socio -economic 
segments. Commitment for UHC is embedded in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), 
specifically target 3.8, which measures progress through two key indicators: service coverage 
and financial protection against out -of-pocket expenditure. India‘s policies and programmes 
are designed to accelerate progress toward these goals before the 2030 deadline.  
1.1.3 At the heart of this vision , India has launched ambitious national initiatives under 
Ayushman Bharat, which integrates primary care delivery through Ayushman Arogya 
Mandirs, financial protection via Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PMJAY), infrastructure 
strengthening under Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission ( PM-ABHIM), and 
digital integration through Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission ( ABDM). These pillars 
collectively advance UHC by expanding servi ce coverage and reducing financial hardship. 
India‘s healthcare objectives also emphasize mission -mode disease elimination and 
immunisation coverage, aligning with the UHC service coverage index. India is advancing 
both dimensions of UHC: expanding essenti al service coverage and reducing financial 
hardship. 
1.2 MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
1.2.1 The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is the nodal Ministry that is responsible 
for formulation and implementation of various schemes, programmes and n ational initiatives 
to provide universal access to quality healthcare. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
comprises of the following two Departments: 
(a) Department of Health and Family Welfare; and 
(b) Department of Health Research 
1.2.2 The Minist ry of Health and Family Welfare has also the following two attached 
Offices: 
(a) Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS):  It is an attached office of the 
Department of Health and Family Welfare and has subordinate offices spread all over 
the country. The  DGHS renders technical advice on all medical and public health 
matters and is involved in the implementation of various health services. 

2 
 
(b) National Health Authority  (NHA):  It has been set up as an attached Office to 
Ministry of Health & Family welfare vide extraordinary Gazette Notification no. 
3(4)12018- H&FW (Part.III) Vol.2 dated 01.02.2019 of NITI Aayog. NHA is the 
apex body responsible for implementing India's flagship public health 
insurance/assurance scheme called "Ayushman Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan  Arogya 
Yojana" & has been entrusted with the role of designing strategy, building 
technological infrastructure and implementation of "National Digital Health Mission" 
to create a National Digital Health Eco-system. 
1.3 VISION, MISSION AND OBJECTIVES 
1.3.1  The Vision, Mission and Objectives of the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare are indicated as under: 
Vision 
Attainment of highest possible level of health and well -being for all, 
through preventive and promotive health care and universal access to goo d 
quality health services without anyone having to face financial hardship as a 
consequence. 
Mission 
(i) To ensure availability of quality healthcare on equitable, accessible and 
affordable basis across regions and communities with special focus on under -
served population and marginalized groups. 
(ii) To establish comprehensive primary healthcare delivery system and well -
functioning linkages with secondary and tertiary care health delivery system. 
(iii)To develop the training capacity for providing human resources for he alth 
(medical, paramedical and managerial) with adequate skill mix at all levels. 
(iv) To regulate health service delivery and promote rational use of 
pharmaceuticals in the country. 
Objectives 
(i) To improve health status of the people through concerted action. 
(ii) To expand preventive, promotive, curative, palliative and rehabilitative 
services provided through public health sector with focus on quality. 
(iii)To progressively achieve Universal Health Coverage. 
1.3.2 The Committee takes note of the Vision, Mission, and Obje ctives of the Ministry 
of Health and Family Welfare, which collectively outline the strategic roadmap for the 
Ministry‘s activities. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of 
Health and Family Welfare should undertake all projects  and schemes in strict 
consonance with the vision of providing universal access to quality healthcare without 
causing fina ncial hardship to the citizens and execute these initiatives with the clear 
intention of achieving its cherished objectives, particularly the progressive realization of 
Universal Health Coverage and the establishment of robust linkages between primary, 

3 
 
secondary, and tertiary care. The Committee believes that the Department must move 
forward with 'Management by Objective' (MBO) rather than 'Mana gement by 
Activities' (MBA). This approach is essential to ensure equitable healthcare for 
marginalized communities, optimize human resources, and achieve the broader targets 
set out in the National Health Policy (NHP) 2017. 
1.4 DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
1.4.1 In this report, the Committee will undertake a comprehensive examination of the 
objectives, functioning, budgetary allocations, and utilization patterns of the Department of 
Health and Family Welfare, along with the institutions operatin g under its administrative 
control. The analysis will extend beyond financial oversight to assess the efficiency, 
transparency, and equity of resource deployment, ensuring that allocations translate into 
measurable improvements in healthcare delivery. 
1.4.2 The Committee will also evaluate the implementation of flagship healthcare policies 
and schemes with particular attention to their design, coverage, and impact. This will include 
a review of institutional performance, inter -sectoral coordination, critica l appraisal of 
achievements, and identifying the gaps and challenges, including disparities in access, quality 
of care, and sustainability of health financing. The overarching objective is to support the 
creation of a resilient, inclusive, and future -ready healthcare system that advances both 
national development and the well-being of all citizens. 
1.4.3 The Department of Health and Family Welfare , as stated in its Annual Report 2025 -
26, is committed to ensure the highest possible level of health and well -being of all through a 
preventive and promotive healthcare orientation in all developmental policies and universal 
access to good quality health care services while mitigating financial hardship.  The approach 
of the Department is to increase access to decen tralised public health systems by establishing 
new infrastructure in deficient areas and by upgrading the infrastructure in existing 
institutions with efforts being made for adequate staffing of these facilities by qualified health 
personnel. There is also  a need to strengthen the role of the public sector in social protection 
against the rising costs of healthcare services and the need to provide a comprehensive 
package of services with due prioritization to the health of women and children. The 
Department also acknowledges the importance of improved availability of quality drugs with 
robust logistical arrangement for procurement and storage of these drugs. 
1.4.4 In pursuance to this commitment  and approach  of the Department , several 
statutory/regulatory bodies and autonomous bodies/institutions work under the administrative 
control of the Department.

1.4.5 The Committee is of  the view that the statutory/ regulatory bodies  and 
autonomous institutions act as the vital organs and play a pivotal role in the successfu l 
functioning of the Department. T heir efficient and effective working is , therefore,  
indispensable for the result -oriented implementation of the core commitments  
undertaken by the Department , such as expanding decentralized public health 
infrastructure, ensuring adequate staffing, and providi ng a comprehensive package of 
services to achieve the objectives of universal access to healthcare , prioritizing women 
and children.  
1.4.6 The Committee , moreover,  feels that a streamlined monitoring mechanism 
utilizing Always Better Control (ABC) would f urther ensure the desirable Rate of 
Returns (RoR) on the heavy investments made in upgrading health infrastructure and 
mitigating financial hardship for ci tizens. The Committee, moreover , recommends that 
the Department should keep a constant Strength, Weak nesses, Opportunities and 
Threats (SWOT) Analysis of its organs/institutions for better results and efficient social 
protection. 
 
1.5 ESTABLISHMENT EXPENDITURE 
1.5.1 As indicated in the Notes on Demands for Grants 2026 –27, the establishment -related 
expenditure of the Department‘s Secretariat is met under the head ―Secretariat.‖ In addition, 
budgetary support is provided under the head ―Direction and Administration‖ to strengthen 
technical expertise in medical and public health and family welfare matters. Th is head also 
supports the implementation and monitoring of various health and family welfare 
programmes, and enables the Department to function as a focal point for the collection, 
processing and supply of biomedical and health -related information within t he country and 
abroad. 
1.5.2 The strengthening, capacity building and operational efficiency of the Secretariat and 
its administrative machinery are critical for achieving the vision, mission and objectives of the 
Department. The Secretariat plays a pivota l role in policy formulation, appraisal, supervision 
and performance monitoring of regulatory/autonomous bodies, research and teaching 
institutions, and hospitals under the Department‘s administrative control. Adequate 
augmentation of human resources, inst itutional capacity and infrastructure is therefore 
essential for effective implementation of healthcare policies and schemes across the country 
and for ensuring equitable, accessible, affordable and quality healthcare. A robust Secretariat 

6 
 
also enhances th e absorption capacity of various schemes, ensures optimal utilisation of 
allocated funds, and enables realistic assessment and projection of future budgetary 
requirements. 
 
 
 
1.5.3 It is observed that the allocation under the head ―Secretariat‖ was reduce d at the 
Revised Estimates (RE) stage during FYs 2023 –24 and 2024 –25. Further, the BE for FY 
2024–25 (Rs. 251.50 crore) was lower than the BE for FY 2023 –24 (Rs. 267.40 crore), which 
appears to be attributable to lower utilisation in FY 2023 –24, where the actual expenditure 
was Rs. 203.24 crore (about 76 per cent of BE). The BE for FY 2025–26 also remained below 
the BE level of FY 2023 –24. Although  in FY 2025 –26, the allocation at the RE stage 
enhanced to Rs. 299.25 crore, the actual expenditure up to 31 st January 2026 remained 72.73 
per cent of the revised allocation.

2.1.5 From the submissions made by the Department, the Committee observed that the 
projected demand has grown steadily, reaching ₹1.22 lakh crore in FY 2026 –27. The 
Budget Estimates have consistently been lower than the proposed/projected demands, 
reflecting partial acceptance of the Department‘s requ ests by the Ministry of Finance. 
The persistent gap between proposed demand and BE may constrain the expansion of 
health programmes. In FY 2026 –27, the gap between the proposed demand and BE 
exceeds 17%, which is substantial. 
 
2.1.6 The Department observes  that the BE for 2026 –27 has increased by 
approximately 6% over BE 2025 –26, however, considering the average inflation rate of 
around 5%, population growth, and the National Health Policy target of raising 
government health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP by 20 25, the Committee is of the view 
that the effective increase is marginal. In its 163 rd Report, the Committee had 
recommended higher allocations to significantly enhance healthcare infrastructure and 
services nationwide, particularly in light of the challen ges experienced during the 
COVID-19 pandemic, to ensure preparedness for future public health emergencies. 
 
2.1.7 Moreover, mid-year adjustments have resulted in reductions of approximately ₹6,600 
crore, ₹8,500 crore, and ₹3,000 crore in FYs 2022 –23, 2023–24, and 2025 –26, respectively. 
Frequent downward revisions may affect the continuity of long -term health ini tiatives. The 
concern is further reinforced by the fact that, except for FY 2023 –24, actual expenditure has 
remained below the Revised Estimates, which themselves are lower than the Budget 
Estimates. This raises concerns regarding the effective and timely utilization of allocated 
funds. 
 
2.1.8 It has also been noted that in FY 2025 –26, the Department utilized ₹70,345.61 crore 
as of 31st January 2026, which constitutes only 75.70% of the already reduced RE allocation. 
With only two months remaining in the financial year, there is a possibil ity of expenditure 
being rushed to enhance utilization. The Ministry of Finance has repeatedly issued guidelines 
to regulate expenditure within a financial year. In its 143 rd and 163rd Reports, the Committee 
recommended that the Department cap its expendit ure in the final month of the financial year 

12 
 
in accordance with existing guidelines and closely monitor fund utilization during the last 
quarter to ensure prudent and efficient use of public funds. 
 
2.1.9 The Committee expresses concern over the consistent  gap between the 
Department‘s projected demand and the Budget Estimates (BE), which has constricted 
the expansion of health programmes. In FY 2026–27, the gap exceeds 17%, a substantial 
shortfall that risks undermining the objectives of the National Health  Policy, 
particularly the target of raising government health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should engage more 
proactively with the Ministry of Finance during the pre -budget consultations to ensure 
that allocations are better aligned with projected needs, especially for critical schemes 
such as NACO, PMSSY, PM-ABHIM, and tertiary care services. 
 
2.1.10 While the BE for FY 2026 –27 shows a nominal 6% increase, this is effectively 
neutralized by inflation averaging around 5% and population growth, and is insufficient 
to meet the rising healthcare demands of the nation. Further, the Department submitted 
that the Annual GDP growth rate during the financial year 2025 -26 is 7.3% on constant 
price. In view there of, keeping in view the factors of inflation, population growth and 
alignment with the National Health Policy‘s mandate of increasing government health 
expenditure to 2.5% of GDP, the year -on-year budget allocation growth should be 
significantly more than the rate of 7.3%, must be around 14 -15%. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that future allocations be significantly enhanced to strengthen 
healthcare infrastructure, expand service delivery, and ensure preparedness for public 
health emergencies, in line with lessons learned from the COVID -19 pandemic. Further, 
the Committee also believes that by leveraging its IT platforms, third-party reviews, and 
stakeholder consultations, the Department should formulate realistic, evidence -based 
initial budget project ions that permit full funding and minimize the recurring cycle of 
mid-year downward revisions. 
 
2.1.11 The Committee further observes that frequent mid -year reductions at the 
Revised Estimate (RE) stage have disrupted the continuity and momentum of long -term 
health initiatives. The Department must take proactive measures to safeguard core, 
long-term health initiatives, such as NACO, PMSSY, PM -ABHIM, and Tertiary Care 
projects, from being disproportionately derailed by mid -year financial cuts. Reductions 
of ₹6,600 crore, ₹8,500 crore, and ₹3,000 crore in FYs 2022 –23, 2023–24, and 2025 –26 
respectively highlight the need for more stable and predictable funding for better result. 
Given the vulnerabilities exposed during the COVID -19 pandemic, consistent and 
uninterrupted funding is non -negotiable for building nationwide healthcare resilience. 
The Committee, in this regard, recommends that the Department should strengthen its 
expenditure planning and monitoring mechanisms to demonstrate consistent fund 
absorption capacity, thereby minimizing the likelihood of downward revisions. 
Enhanced transparency in reporting the reasons for underutilization will also improve 
accountability and strengthen the case for higher allocations in ensuing financial years.

2.1.12 The Committee expresses deep concern over the chronic issue of underutilization 
of funds, highlighted again in FY 2025 –26, where only 75.70% of the reduced RE

year, there is a  risk of skewed expenditure in a particular quarter of a financial year, 
which may compromise efficiency and value for money. The Department must 
implement stringent mechanisms for the even distribution of funds throughout the 
financial year. The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendations made in 143rd and 
163rd Reports that the Department cap its expenditure in the final month of the

substitute regular budgetary support.

ensure that health expenditure aligns with the National Health Policy target of 2.5% of 
GDP, with the Centre contributing at least 0.9% of GDP. The Committee, therefore,

a cl ear medium -term roadmap indicating year -wise targets for enhancing the Union 
Government‘s health outlay as a proportion of both GDP and the Total Union Budget. 
Such a roadmap should align with Finance Commission cycles and national health 
priorities, and b e placed before Parliament to ensure transparency and accountability. 
In parallel, the Department may strengthen coordination with States to encourage them 
to raise health allocations to at least 8% of their budgets, thereby ensuring balanced

centres, upgrading primary and secondary facilities, and equipping them with modern 
machinery alongside adequate human resources to ensure functionality. The Committee 
therefore recommends reorienting budgetary priorities to arrest the declining trend in 
capital allocation, improve fund utilization efficiency, and commit to sustained 
infrastructure and equipment investments, thereby strengthening healthcare capacity, 
accessibility, and long-term resilience.

2.4.7 The Committe e observes with deep concern that the allocation to the health 
sector, comprising the Department of Health & Family Welfare, Department of Health 
Research, and Ministry of Ayush, has remained stagnant at 0.28–0.33% of GDP over the 
last five years, which is  not in consonance with the National Health Policy (NHP), 2017 
target of raising Government Health Expenditure (GHE) to 2.5% of GDP by 2025. 
Although GHE has increased from 1.35% of GDP in 2017 –18 to 1.84% in 2021 –22, the 
pace of growth is insufficient to achieve the NHP target within the stipulated timeframe. 
The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendations made in the 126th and 163rd 
Reports, wherein it had urged the Government to increase health expenditure to 5% by 
2025, however, the FY 2025 -26 has now come to an end. The Committee, therefore, 
urges the Department to review the target under NHP to 5% in the next five years. The 
Committee is of considered view that Health Sector must be recognized as a priority 
sector for both economic and social deve lopment, requiring sustained investment in 
public health infrastructure, preventive care, and equitable service delivery. 
 
2.4.8 The Committee is not satisfied over delays in updating National Health Accounts 
(NHA) data, with information currently availabl e only up to FY 2021 –22. Despite the 
acknowledged two -year lag, data for FY 2023 –24 should already be available, yet it 
remains pending. In its 163rd Report, the Committee had highlighted that outdated data 
hampers effective monitoring and evaluation of go vernment schemes. The Committee, 
therefore, reiterates its recommendation that the Government leverage Information 
Technology and Artificial Intelligence for real -time data collection and processing, 
ensuring that expenditure data for a given financial yea r is made available by the last 
quarter of the following year. This will enable timely assessment of progress and 
alignment of schemes with intended objectives.

2.4.9 While the decline in Out -of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE) from 64.2% in 2013 –14 
to 39.4% in 2021–22 is encouraging, the Committee finds that OOPE still remains a 
significant barrier to healthcare access, particularly given India‘s large population 
living in poverty. As per the Global Multidimensional Poverty Index 2024, India is home 
to approxima tely 234 million poor people, the highest in the world, and is the only 
country among the five poorest nations with a medium Human Development Index 
(HDI). As highlighted in the 163rd Report, the Committee is optimistic that current 
figures may be lower, b ut underscores the urgent need to reduce OOPE further to 
ensure affordability and accessibility of healthcare. The Committee therefore 
recommends intensifying efforts to strengthen public health infrastructure, expand 
preventive and primary care services, leverage Public -Private Partnerships, and 
institute robust monitoring mechanisms to reduce OOPE and enhance accessibility. 
 
2.4.10 The Committee also emphasizes the need to strengthen preventive and primary 
healthcare services as a cornerstone of India‘s h ealth system. A strategic focus on 
preventive care and efficient resource utilization is crucial to achieving long -term 
improvements in accessibility and quality. Preventive interventions reduce the burden 
on tertiary care facilities, lower Out -of-Pocket E xpenditure (OOPE), and improve 
overall health outcomes. Given India‘s score of 67 on SDG -3 (ensuring healthy lives and 
wellbeing) in the Sustainable Development Report 2025, below the world average of 72 
and significantly lower than high -income countries a veraging 91, the Committee 
reiterates that stronger investments in preventive health, including immunization, 
maternal and child health, nutrition, and early detection of non -communicable diseases, 
are essential to bridge the gap. 
 
2.4.11 The Committee als o highlights the importance of leveraging Public -Private 
Partnerships (PPP) and innovative financing mechanisms to bridge the resource gap in 
the health sector. In its earlier reports, including the 163rd Report, the Committee 
emphasized that the current pace of increase in Government Health Expenditure (GHE) 
is inadequate to meet the National Health Policy target of 2.5% of GDP by 2025. Given 
the stagnant allocation of 0.28 –0.33% of GDP to the Ministry of Health & Family 
Welfare, Department of Health Resea rch, and Ministry of Ayush, it is imperative to 
explore supplementary avenues of investment. The Committee expects that PPPs can 
play a crucial role in expanding infrastructure, introducing advanced technologies, and 
improving service delivery, particularl y in underserved rural and tribal areas, 
therefore, the Ministry should strive in that direction.

2.5.5 The Committee observes that India‘s Current Health Expenditure (CHE ) as a 
percentage of GDP stands at 3.3 percent, which is considerably lower than that of other 
BRICS countries such as Brazil (9.6 percent), South Africa (8.7 percent), and Russia (7.0 
percent), as well as G20 nations where the average often exceeds 10 per cent. 
Furthermore, Government Health Expenditure (GHE) in India is only 1.84 percent of 
GDP, far below the 4 –10 percent range observed in most BRICS and G20 countries. 
This limited public investment translates into a high reliance on household spending, 
with Out -of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE) accounting for 45.1 percent of CHE. 
Comparative analysis shows that countries with higher government spending, such as 
Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom, not only achieve stronger health outcomes 
but also maintain O OPE levels below 15 percent, thereby ensuring greater financial 
protection for their populations. In light of this, the Committee recommends that India 
adopt a phased strategy to raise GHE to at least 5 percent of GDP by 2030, beyond the 
targets set under the National Health Policy (2017). This increase should be directed

OOPE is comparable to Mexico (41.4 percent) but remains f ar above countries such as 
South Africa (6.6 percent) and France (9.2 percent), where robust public financing and 
insurance systems provide strong financial protection. Evidence from both high -income 
countries like Canada and Japan, and medium -HDI countries such as Namibia (6.5% 
GHE and 7.3% OOPE) and lower -income countries like Rwanda (5% OOPE), 
demonstrates that effective risk pooling and community -based insurance models can 
substantially reduce household vulnerability to catastrophic health spending. In this 
context, the Committee recommends that India expand financial protection mechanisms 
by strengthening Ayushman Bharat and state -level insurance schemes, with particular 
emphasis on outpatient care, diagnostics, and medicines, which are major drivers of  
OOPE. Risk pooling should be incentivized through employer -based and cooperative 
insurance models, especially targeting informal sector workers who remain outside 
formal coverage.

2.5.9 The Committee notes that while the National Health Policy (2017) recommended that 
States/UTs increase their health spending to more than 8 percent of their total budget, the actual 
expenditure remains significantly below this benchmark, averaging only 5 .3 percent in 2023 –24 
and projected at 5.6 percent in 2024 –25. Although some states such as Delhi (11.4 percent), 
Odisha (8.0 percent), and Puducherry (8.7 percent) are approaching or surpassing the target, 
most others continue to allocate between 4–6 percent, reflecting a persistent gap in prioritization 
of health within state budgets. Given that health is a state subject, the Committee emphasizes 
that the Department encourage States/UTs to adopt a phased strategy to progressively raise 
health spending clo ser to the 8 percent benchmark. This should be supported by Union 
Government initiatives such as conditional Result -Based Financing under the National Health 
Mission, strengthening of the Public Health Management Cadre, and adoption of Indian Public 
Health Standards (IPHS) 2022. To ensure accountability and efficient utilization of funds, 
mechanisms such as CAG audits, PFMS tracking, and quarterly financial monitoring must be 
rigorously implemented, thereby ensuring equitable access to quality healthcare ac ross the 
country. 
 
2.5.10 In addition to urging States/UTs to progressively raise their health allocations closer to 
the 8 percent benchmark, the Committee recommends that greater emphasis be placed on 
strengthening state -level innovation and capacity buil ding in health service delivery. While 
Union initiatives such as Result -Based Financing under the National Health Mission, the Public 
Health Management Cadre, and adoption of IPHS and NQAS standards provide a strong 
framework, their impact will depend on h ow effectively states adapt these measures to local 
needs. States should be encouraged to pilot innovative models in areas such as digital health, 
telemedicine, and community -based outreach, particularly in underserved rural and tribal 
regions, and to inte grate these with centrally sponsored schemes for maximum efficiency. 
Moreover, capacity building of state health departments through specialized training, improved 
data systems, and performance-linked incentives will ensure that increased allocations trans late 
into measurable improvements in service delivery. By combining higher budgetary 
prioritization with innovation and institutional strengthening, States/UTs can accelerate 
progress towards equitable, quality healthcare and contribute meaningfully to nat ional health 
goals.

2.6.2 The Department also provided the key findings from the NHSRC –NIPFP study 
regarding systemic challenges in fund utilization as under: - 
 
a) The capital -intensive nature of the 15 th FC grants and their execution 
architecture has retarded the pace of progress of the grants. The tied nature of 
the grant with rigid budget provisions placed within a centralize d institutional 
arrangement for re-appropriation across components compounded the problem. 
 
b) Though provisions for human resources were made in at least 4 of the 6 
components, support for these was withdrawn after the first two years of the 
grant. Most stat es found it challenging to draw up a comprehensive plan on 
human resource deployment in the upgraded units poses uncertainty about the 
outcomes of these investments. 
 
c) The performance of the grant suffered significantly due to execution 
challenges arising f rom a de novo implementation architecture and 
unfamiliarity with the new fund-flow mechanism at the state level. 
 
d) Several states faced a mismatch of recommended allocation vis -à-vis the need 
in certain components calling for re -appropriation of funds. The procurement 
delays and financial bottlenecks were observed in the following States: 
 
(i) In Gujarat, although funds were released to procurement and other 
implementation agencies, progress in terms of actual outputs in the diagnostic 
component was impacted due to central procurement related delays. 
 
(ii) Besides cost escalations due to delays in procurement of land; Odisha 
being a coastal state has several water -logged districts where construction 
required further expenditure on appropriate strengthening of  building 
foundations. Procurement of raw materials were also stated to be costlier in 
remote and tribal regions which further puts upward pressure on costs. 
 
(iii) In states like Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh, penal interest was 
initially booked under the wrong budget head, impacting fund flow.

(iv) Delays attributable to issue of indents for HR recruitment & equipment 
procurement only after 75% of a building structure was complete. 
 
2.6.3 The Department further stated that National, State, and Distric t-level Committees 
(DLCs) were established to oversee and monitor grant works. The study recommends 
empowering DLCs to decide if a local body has the capacity for construction; if not, they 
should be authorized to assign the work to appropriate health depa rtment agencies. The 
Ministry currently uses the NHM -PMS portal for tracking expenditure and physical progress. 
However, the study brought out that the current data reporting has significant ―missing 
values‖ and ―divergence‖ between portal data and actual ground-level expenditure. 
 
2.6.4 The utilisation of XV -Finance Commission (XV -FC) Health Grants is monitored 
through a structured framework of input, output, and outcome indicators aligned with NHM 
and XV-FC guidelines, and tracked through national portals  and dashboards. Key indicators 
include the number of building -less SHCs/PHCs/CHCs constructed, functional SHC -AAMs 
and PHC -AAMs, availability of essential and desirable diagnostics at primary facilities, 
CHCs functioning as First Referral Units (FRUs), an d the percentage of funds utilised against 
funds released. The grants support strengthening of primary healthcare through construction 
of infrastructure, establishment of Urban AAMs/HWCs and BPHUs, upgradation of 
diagnostic facilities, and conversion of SH Cs/PHCs into AAMs for Comprehensive Primary 
Health Care (CPHC) services, thereby helping bridge primary healthcare gaps. States with 
higher fund utilisation have reported measurable improvements such as enhanced facility 
readiness, expanded service coverage—particularly for NCD screening and preventive care —
increased patient footfall at primary facilities, reduced burden on higher -level hospitals, and 
improved availability of diagnostics and essential medicines, with progress regularly tracked 
through routi ne programme reports, NP -NCD and AAM portals, and periodic state and 
national reviews. 
 
2.6.5 The Committee is displeased to note that although the 15th Finance Commission 
allocated ₹70,051 crore for health grants for FY 2021 –22 to FY 2025 –26, utilisation 
remains suboptimal. Against ₹44,495.12 crore (63.52% of the allocation) released to 
States, only ₹25,367.75 crore (57.01% of funds released) has been reported as 
expenditure. As observed in its 163rd Report, as of 30 January 2025, only 39.42% of the 
total approved funds had been released, with full disbursement limited to FY 2021 –22, 
and States had utilised just 59.31% of the released funds. The Committee reiterates that 
such low utilisation defeats the very objective of the financial support to orient heal th 
sector as patient -centric. It therefore strongly recommends that the Government 
undertake a comprehensive study to identify the causes of under -utilisation and 
implement corrective measures. The Union Government should also establish a 
dedicated institutional mechanism for regular coordination with States/UTs to address 
bottlenecks and ensure timely and optimal utilisation of these critical funds for 
strengthening primary healthcare. 
 
2.6.6 The NHSRC–NIPFP study highlights systemic challenges, including the capital-
intensive nature of the grants, rigid budget provisions, withdrawal of human resource 

30 
 
support after initial years, and execution difficulties arising from unfamiliar fund -flow 
mechanisms. States have also faced mismatches between allocations an d local needs, 
procurement delays, cost escalations in difficult terrains, and financial misclassifications 
disrupting fund flow. These constraints have slowed infrastructure development and 
service readiness despite the availability of funds. In view of t hese findings, the 
Committee recommends enhancing flexibility in fund re -appropriation to better align 
allocations with State -specific needs, restoring and sustaining human resource support 
to ensure service continuity, and empowering District-Level Committees to assign works 
to suitable agencies where local bodies lack capacity. Procurement processes should be 
streamlined, and data reporting systems strengthened to improve accuracy and 
transparency, minimising discrepancies between portal data and actual e xpenditure. 
Addressing these structural and operational bottlenecks will accelerate utilisation of 
Finance Commission health grants and facilitate timely infrastructure expansion, 
improved diagnostic capacity, and strengthened primary healthcare services a cross 
States.

3.1 CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME (CGHS):  
 
3.1.1 The Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) is a health scheme of the 
Government providing comprehensive medical facilities to Central Government employees, 
pensioners and members of their families in addition to other specified categories like 
Members of Parliament (MPs), ex -MPs, ex-Governors, ex-Vice-Presidents, Retired Judges of 
Supreme Court and High Court, Freedom Fighters an d members of their family etc. The 
facilities under this scheme include outpatient care through a network of allopathic, 
ayurvedic, homeopathic, unani/siddha dispensaries/units. The scheme was started in Delhi in 
1954. Over the time, it has spread to 81 ci ties. It serves nearly 15,93,741 primary cardholders 
and 42,30,229 beneficiaries through a network of 342 Allopathic Wellness Centres and 111 
AYUSH Units.

3.1.9 The Committee  notes that the reduction in capital outlay from ₹75.31 crore to 
₹38.86 crore at the RE stage in FY 2025 –26 was primarily due to the non -approval of

mechanisms to ensure that large-scale proposals such as the Koliwada centre are cleared 
in advance of budget finalisation, thereby avoiding mid -year surrender of funds. 
Further, capital allocations should be safeguarded with improved coordination between 
CGHS units and administrative authorities to ensure timely approvals and utilisation. 
This will enhance predictability in capital planning, prevent under -utilisation, and 
ensure that CGHS facilities are adequately modernised to meet the growing needs of 
beneficiaries.
