Action Taken
3.2 Against the BE provision of `750.00 crore and RE provision of `950.00 crore under Plan in
2016-17, the expenditure incurred upto 31st March, 2017 is `930.80 crore (97.98%)
Recommendation/Observation
3.3 The Committee notes that against the Twelfth Plan Outlay of 
`10029.00 crore only `3575.17 crore
was allocated to the Department at BE stage which was further reduced to `3266.50 crore in the Revised
Estimate (32% of the approved outlay). The actual expenditure was `3180.99 crore upto February, 2017.
The Committee observes that there is a huge mismatch to the tune of ` 6762.50 crore between the Twelfth
Plan Outlay and the RE allocation made for the Department. The Committee observes that though it
is always possible to generate more value for the funds allocated, it would be unrealistic to expect to
10

11
achieve key goals of Health Research or to make spectacular break-through in the newly-emerging
frontier areas of Health Research with only 32% of the approved outlays. India's rapidly growing
economy has thrown up huge health challenges and Department of Health Research has a crucial role
to play in ensuring health care to the population by way of generation of new knowledge and its
translation into health products.  The Government, therefore, owes an explanation to the Committee on
the reasons behind such a huge gap between the budgetary allocation made for the Department of Health
Research from 2012-13 to 2016-17 and the total approved outlays for the Twelfth Five Year Plan and
its impact on the Department's vision "to bring modern technology to the people through innovations".
(Para 2.2)
Action Taken
3.4 The Twelfth Plan Outlay was approved by the then Planning Commission based on the approved
cost of new schemes formulated by the Department of Health Research and the requirements of ICMR
for various activities. However, year to year budgetary allocations were decided by the Ministry of
Finance (Department of Expenditure) despite projected demand by the Department during budgetary
discussions.
3.5 The shortfall in allocations have affected implementation of the five newly launched schemes of
Department of Health Research in 2013-14 as well as funding of intra mural and extra mural research
projects and strengthening of health research infrastructure.
Further Recommendation
3.6 The Committee notes from the Department's reply that year to year budgetary allocations
were decided by Ministry of Finance despite projected demand by the Department during budgetary
discussions and shortfall in allocations have affected implementation of the five newly launched
schemes in 2013-14. However, on perusal of the expenditure figures, the Committee notes that
the same are below the RE allocations made from 2012-13 to 2016-17, thereby leading to cuts
in allocations in subsequent RE allocations as a result of which the functioning of the five
schemes got adversely affected. The Committee therefore strongly recommends that in order to
ensure adequate allocations from Ministry of Finance in the future, a robust monitoring
mechanism should be put in place for proper utilization of allocated funds through effective
financial management to ensure that the schemes do not get sidetracked due to lack of funds.
Recommendation/Observation
3.7 The Committee observes that the health challenges in India are huge and complex due to its large
population, rapid industrialization, demographic transition, huge maternal and infant mortality and high
burden of diseases like communicable diseases (TB, Malaria, HIV, emerging and re-merging infections),
non-communicable diseases (Cardio-vascular diseases, diabetes, cancer etc). To address the high disease
burden, our national health research agenda needs to be updated constantly and indigenous health
products would need to be developed to combat these challenges.
This is all the more important in view of the fact that the global trade and intellectual property
rights regimes have made it difficult to use health products and processes developed outside due to their
high costs and restrictions placed on producing cost effect generics. (Para 2.10)

12
Action Taken
3.8 Department appreciates the observations of the Hon'ble Committee.
Recommendation/Observation
3.9 A paradigm shift in pursuing the national research agenda will therefore need to be made to address
these challenges but this is not possible with the current low budget allocation to the Department of
Health Research. The Committee takes note of the Secretary's submission that the budget of the National
Institute of Health in the U.S. whose functions are as that of ICMR in India, is 32 billion dollars a year
and a large amount of that budget goes into basic research. The Committee also takes note of the
Secretary's submission that it takes two-and-a-half billion dollars to develop a new drug from scratch
and it needs thousands of scientists working on it at different stages. (Para 2.11)
Action Taken
3.10 Department appreciates the observations of the Hon'ble Committee.
Recommendation/Observation
3.11 Taking all the above facts into account, the Committee observes that if the objective of providing
affordable quality healthcare for the people and translating research outputs into measurable social and
national outcome is to be realized, investments in health research will have to be increased substantially.
The Committee therefore lends its support to the Department's demand for additional funds to the tune
of 
`835.00 crore for 2017-18 and recommends that the Ministry of Finance should increase the budgetary
allocation to the Department of Health Research so that the Department is able to ensure continuity in
critical healthcare research. (Para 2.12)
Action Taken
3.12 Need for allocation of additional funds would be emphasized with justification at the time of pre-
budget discussions in the Ministry of Finance for deciding the RE 2017-18 and BE 2018-19.
Further Recommendation
3.13 The Committee would like to know the quantum of additional funds allocated to the
Department of Health Research at RE 2017-18 stage in pursuance to the recommendation of the
Committee. The Committee also desires to be apprised whether the Department through ICMR
generates any funds internally.
Recommendation/Observation
3.14 The Committee is constrained to note the under-utilisation of funds w.r.t. to three schemes of the
Department. The Committee feels that on one hand the Department is reporting under-utilisation of funds
with respect to its three schemes and on the other hand, the Department had given an enhanced amount
as its projected requirement for the next financial year. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department should strongly monitor the funds allocated at BE stage so as to ensure that the projected
funds sought are allocated at RE stage in 2017-18. (Para 2.15)

13
Action Taken
3.15 Necessary action will be taken to project the requirements on rational/realistic basis at RE stage.
Further Recommendation
3.16 The Committee is not satisfied with the routine reply of the Department that "necessary
action will be taken to project the requirements on rational/realistic basis at RE stage". As this
is not a comprehensive reply, the Committee would like the Department to indicate the specific
action taken or proposed to be taken by it for realistic and effective budgetary formulation and
proper utilization of allocated funds through prudent management of funds and timely
implementation of the schemes.
III. INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation
3.17 Currently, health research in the country is primarily carried out by 31 Institutes of ICMR which
was established in 1911 and is one of the oldest medical research bodies in the world. The Committee
observes from the information furnished that in two years i.e. 2015 and 2016, only 1685 research papers
(965 in 2015 and 720 in 2016) have been published by ICMR scientists and 3 patents have been granted
against 45 patents filed. This clearly indicates that the health research output is not up to the mark and
not commensurate with the magnitude and disease burden in India. Given the fact that the country
contributes to a fifth of the world's share of diseases (12th Plan Report) and one of the vital elements
in improving this situation is the need for a relevant research base that would equip policy makers to
take informed health policy decisions, the health research output needs to be augmented substantially to
cater to the health challenges faced. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the ICMR should evolve
mechanisms to boost quality health research output by way of building alliances and partnerships and
create a vibrant ecosystem for the purpose. The Committee is of the view that evolving such frameworks
would lead to granting of more patents which, in turn, would generate the much needed funds for ICMR
and health research. (Para 3.6)
Action Taken
3.18 ICMR has noted the observations of the Hon'ble Committee and as suggested will strive hard in
developing new partnerships for enhancing research output. ICMR has recently signed a MoU with
Project ECHO (Extension for Community Healthcare outcome) at the University of New Mexico Health
Science Centre (UNMHSC) with a mission to de-monopolize knowledge and augment the capacity to
provide best healthcare for the remote and underserved people. MoU has also been signed with IIT to
use best technology for innovation and translational research. MoU with AYUSH will help in better
understanding of the Traditional Medicines. More such partnerships will be developed.
Further Recommendation
3.19 The Committee appreciates that ICMR has recently signed MoUs with (i) Project ECHO
(Extension of Community Healthcare Outcome), at the University of New Mexico Health Science
Centre (UNMHSC); (ii) IIT for best technology innovation; and (iii) AYUSH for traditional medicines.

14
The Committee is of the view that ICMR needs to vigorously pursue its research collaborations
and also ensure an increased emphasis on translating discoveries into health/medical products
and disseminating such discoveries in a way that is optimally beneficial to the public. The
Committee would like to be apprised of health outcomes stemming from these collaborations.
Recommendation/Observation
3.20 As per submission of the Secretary (HR), ICMR has about 800 scientists working across the 32
institutes. The Committee is of the view that for a country of the size and scale of India, the human
resource within ICMR is very small and needs to be augmented substantially. The Committee simultaneously
believes that India faces unique health challenges due to its large population and high disease burden
and augmentation of human resources of ICMR alone will not serve the purpose unless we develop a
critical mass of scientists who are dedicated to carry out basic, applied and clinical research and
innovation. It is thus obvious that enhancing the health research output will require tapping of all
available avenues of research. One of the many such avenues is the research being carried out in our
medical colleges where research is a mandate of postgraduate training in both MCI and NBE programmes.
The country produces around 30,000 Postgraduate students every year who are required to complete a
research thesis for a degree. But due to multiple reasons, like inconsequential research topics, inappropriate
research metholodies, poor guidance etc., potential scientific talent of PG students is wasted. If post-
graduate students could be guided to conduct research relevant to the national health system, critical
human resource gaps can be filled. The Committee would therefore, like the ICMR to guide post graduate
students in their dissertations by linking with them and faculty guides across India. (Para 3.7)
Action Taken
3.21 ICMR has a robust HRD Program and having many schemes which are meant for guidance to post
graduates students in their dissertation, MD/MS/DM/MCh/MDS thesis support. This scheme is primarily
aimed at promoting good quality research in medical colleges through students pursuing post-graduation
courses as well as to improve visibility and accessibility of their research work to larger research
audience. ICMR provides financial assistance of `50,000/- to selected candidates pursuing postgraduate
courses. Number of Awards are limited to 100 per year MDS being not more than 20%. The candidate
should be medical graduates who are admitted to these courses in any of the MCI/DCI recognized
Institutes/Colleges and who wish to avail ICMR award/financial assistance for pursuing their post
graduate thesis. The financial assistance of `50000/- would be provided in two instalments:
` 35,000/- at the time of selection when the award letter is issued and `15,000/- at the end of the course
on production of required documents, including one publication in an indexed journal.
ICMR also has a short term studentship program for under-graduate medical students to develop
interest in health research in initial years of life. Around 1000 fellowships are given per year and sum
of `10,000 are sanctioned for this. More such efforts will be made in future.
Further Recommendation
3.22 While making the above recommendation the Committee had expected the Department to
chalk out an action plan for linking research thesis for postgraduate degree across several

15
medical institutions in the country so as to generate nationally relevant data periodically on
antibiotic resistance, air pollution related health effects, adverse effects of new drugs in Indian
patients, diabetes etc. However, the reply of the Department is silent on this issue. The Committee
would, therefore, like this issue to be addressed by the Department.
ICMR Intervention with Multiple Nutrition to Fight Malnutrition
Recommendation/Observation
3.23 The Committee believes that with the intervention of multiple micro-nutrients amongst children for
eliminating malnutrition, a major problem of the country could be solved. The World Bank estimates that
India is one of the highest ranking countries in the world in respect of the number of children suffering
from malnutrition. The 2015 Global Hunger Index Report ranked India 20th amongst leading countries
with a serious hunger situation. India's National Family Health Survey (NFHS) and State Government's
School Health Programme (SHP) have also indicated that the number of anaemic and malnourished
children is rising. As per the latest SHP report for the year 2015-16, the number of anaemic children
are 6.06 lakh that increased from 5.13 lakh in 2014-15. In view of the above, the Committee recommends
that the efficacy of this intervention with multiple micro nutriments should be tested in different regions
of the country on a priority basis. If the results are successful, the intervention programme could be
implemented as a national programme to tackle malnutrition. The Committee would also like to emphasize
upon the need for co-ordination between the concerned Ministries/Departments to make the programme
successful. (Para 3.15)
Action Taken
3.24 ICMR do agree with the observations of the Committee for the problem of malnutrition in the
country and has made attempts in this direction through its National Institute of Nutrition at Hyderabad.
The Institute has come up with a micronutrient mix that is likely to be opted by Government for its
flagship programmes. The product has been tested on 400 children in Nalgonda district of Andhra
Pradesh in 2014. During initial research, scientists found that anaemia among pre-school going children
came down from 48 per cent to 10 per cent. There was an impact of micronutrient on cognitive activities
too. The micronutrient tested by the National Institute of Nutrition has seven micronutrients, including
two minerals and five vitamins. These include Vitamin A, Vitamin B12, Folic Acid and Vitamin C. An
extended multisite study is required.
Further Recommendation
3.25 The Committee is happy to note that the National Institute of Nutrition of ICMR has come
up with an effective micronutrient mix for children in management of anemia among children
during initial research in Nalgonda district of Andhra Pradesh but more multi site research
studies need to be carried out to evaluate its potential benefits. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department should conceptualize and implement the multi site research
study regarding the micronutrient within a time-frame. The Committee is, however, constrained
to note that the reply of the Department is silent on the issue of inter-Ministerial coordination
on combating anemia among children as emphasized by the Committee. The Committee, therefore,
desires to be updated in this regard.

16
IV INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT FOR HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation
3.26 The Committee also notes that the number of VRDLs in the country are not evenly distributed in
all States, which results in loss of time and resources in transporting samples from States having no
VRDLs to States having presence of VRDLs. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends setting up
of at least one VRDL in each State to ensure that 'samples' collected are analysed in shortest possible
time, in order to stem any outbreak of epidemic. (Para 4.7)
Action Taken
3.27 Efforts will be made to have an equitable geographical distribution of VRDLs in the country.
Further Recommendation
3.28 The Committee treats the Ministry's reply as an 'open ended' one. This approach simply
generalise the issue instead create doubts whether the Department is serious about setting up
more VRDLs in the country. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department
should come out with a blueprint to set up VRDLs in each State and approach the Ministry of
Finance with a tangible plan for require to funds for setting up VRDLs in every State, as any
further delay would only exacerbate the veritable time bomb of diseases engulfing this country
year after year.

ESTABLISHMENT OF MULTIDISCIPLINARY RESEARCH UNITS (MRUs) IN GOVERNMENT
MEDICAL COLLEGES
Recommendation/Observation
3.29 The Committee observes that 12 medical colleges have not been released funds due to pending UCs.
The Committee does not understand why there is a persistent delay in furnishing of UCs and apprehends
that the delay in submission of UCs may lead to time overrun and cost escalation of MRUs. The
Committee is of the firm view that if the Department streamlines its monitoring mechanism and pursues
liquidation of UCs in a sustained manner, all pending UCs can be liquidated within a short span of time.
The Department should therefore take up the issue of pendency of UCs at the highest level to expedite
their liquidation. (Para 5.3)
Action Taken
3.30 Out of 12 medical colleges, 6 medical colleges have already cleared the pending UCs in respect of
other schemes of MoH&FW. Funds have already been released to 3 medical colleges and releases in
respect of the other 3 medical colleges are in the pipeline. Letters have been addressed to the Principal
Secretaries of Health and Family Welfare of the remaining States for expeditious settlement of UCs so
that the process of release of grant under the scheme of Multi-Disciplinary Research Units (MRUs) could
be initiated.
Further Recommendation
3.31 The Committee notes that though out of 12 medical colleges, 6 medical colleges have cleared
the pending UCs, the Department has not mentioned the reasons as to why the remaining six

17
medical colleges have not been able to liquidate their pending UCs. The Committee would,
therefore, expect the Department to accomplish the liquidation of pending UCs of the remaining
medical colleges within a stipulated time period and apprise the Committee about the results
achieved in actual liquidation of pending UCs.

STATES
Recommendation/Observation
3.32 The Committee notes that setting up of MRHRUs in States is dependent upon the receipt of
proposals from States. Keeping in view the fact that there exists wide disparities between States, the
Committee is of the view that it becomes the responsibility of Centre to ensure that benefits of this scheme
be reaped by all the States and hence it should facilitate and guide them in sending their proposals. The
Centre should also proactively initiate activity in all States to set up MRHRUs. (Para 6.6)
Action Taken
3.33 The recommendation is noted for compliance.
Further Recommendation
3.34 The Committee finds the reply as too routine one. The Committee expected some details
of the measures which are being taken to guide the States in sending their proposals for setting
up of MRHRUs. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should in clear
terms spell out the steps being taken by it to ensure setting up of MRHRUs in every State.

Recommendation/Observation
3.35 The Committee notes that the Department has persistently not utilized the funds in the years
2015-16 and 2016-17. The Committee is of the view that the North-Eastern region being hilly and under
developed, requires special focus and the Department should take special efforts and ensure that funds
allocated are utilised in proper manner. (Para 8.3)
Action Taken
3.36 The observation of the Committee is noted for compliance.
Further Recommendation
3.37 The Committee notes that the Department has not utilized the funds properly under this
head, though north-eastern part of the country lags behind from the rest of India in healthcare

PENDING UCS
Recommendation/Observations
1.4 The Committee time and again has been impressing upon the Ministry the imperative need for
speedy liquidation of pending UCs. Though some progress has been made, there is still a large number
of pending UCs and it seems that the efforts made by the Ministry to liquidate them are not enough.
The Committee, therefore, believes that a pro-active and aggressive approach is required on the part of
the Ministry for liquidation of pending UCs. The Committee is of the firm view that in this era of
e-governance and with IT resources currently available, submission of UCs should be possible almost on
"Push of a button". The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should chalk out an action
plan for online submission of UCs and also take up the matter of pendency of UCs with States which
have a large number of pending UCs like Andhra Pradesh, Bihar , Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh,
Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Uttarakhand etc. so that all pending UCs are settled within a period of six months.
(Para 2.17)
Action Taken
1.5 Presently, following remedial Action taken have been taken by the Ministry of AYUSH to reduce the
pendency of Utilization of Certificates (UCs) in respect of erstwhile Centrally Sponsored Scheme for
Development of AYUSH Hospitals & Dispensaries and National AYUSH Mission (NAM) :
(a) Various review meeting had been conducted under the Chairmanship of Secretary (AYUSH)
regarding pendency of Utilization Certificates. During the meeting of State AYUSH / Health
Ministers the issue was flagged at the level of Hon'ble MoS.

(AYUSH) & Joint Secretary regarding liquidation of Utilization Certificates.

regarding various issues including liquidation of pending Utilization Certificates.

has been noted. Further, the States having large pending UCs are being specifically addressed for early

or through email.

X. RESEARCH COUNCILS
Central Council for Research in Homoeopathy (CCRH)
Recommendation/Observations
1.17 The Committee observes that Homoeopathy is more popular in India than anywhere else in the
world. The Committee is, however, of the view that in order to improve the efficacy of Homoeopathy,
there is an imperative need for interdisciplinary research that focuses on correlating Homoeopathic
concepts of health and treatment with bio-medical concepts. The Committee would therefore like the
CCRH to start interdisciplinary research for exploring the scientific basis of homoeopathy concepts of
health and treatment. (Para 10.8)
Action Taken
1.18 The observations of the committee that Homoeopathy is very popular in India and many other parts
of world is very true and there is a need to undertake interdisciplinary research to enrich the scientific
base of Homoeopathy. Considering this, Council has initiated collaborative research programme to
systematically undertake interdisciplinary research projects since 2005. In this program, proposals are
invited from interested Scientists/ Institutes of repute and provided with all the technical and financial
support in a transparent manner. In fact a special committee for interdisciplinary research having eminent

7
scientists from IIT Mumbai, IIEST Kolkata, Bose institute, ICMR, AIIMS, New Delhi and many other
institutions has been constituted to give an adequate push to this research.
1.19 Studies are undertaken keeping in view the two objectives: to enrich the scientific base of homoeopathy
and to improve its application in clinical practice, development of new drugs for emerging health
challenges. Studies are aimed to understand the biological effect of homoeopathic medicines; animal
experimentation to assess anti-viral properties; physiochemical studies; standardization and optimization
of the process of drug manufacturing and to know the presence of nanoparticles in these medicines. The
focus is to elucidate the the nature of Homoeopathic medicines in physiochemical dimensions so that
standardization can be done and the theories/ concepts of homoeopathy can remain intact while applying
the modern approach to the studies. Till date Council has collaborated with various reputed institutes like
Bose Institute (Kolkata), Central Drug Research Institute (Lucknow), Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate
Medical Education and Research (JIPMER, Pondicherry), All India Institute of Medical Sciences (New
Delhi), University of Madras (Chennai), Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (Hyderabad), Panjab
University, Indian Institute of Technology (Delhi)etc. and has had 30 National and 03 International
collaborations. 33 projects have been concluded in this field and 15 are ongoing.
1.20 So far th rough these collaborations we are able to understand preventive effect of Belladonna on
Japanese Encephalitis, molecular level understanding of anti-diabetic effect of few homoeopathic
preparations, inhibitory effect of potentised medicines in kidney stone formation, mechanism of apoptotic
effect of medicines in Cancer cells by certain drugs, Lycopodium in improving the memory function,
presence of nanoparticles in Homoeopathic potencies, understanding the physicochemical nature of
Homoeopathic medicines etc.
1.21 Presently, studies for development of medicines for prevention/ treatment of Dengue, Chickungunya,
Rota virus, Acute encephalitis syndrome, Malaria, etc. are being undertaken. Studies to understand the
immune modulation in human by the homoeopathic medicines is also in progress. More studies on other
priority areas are under consideration beside this state of art of laboratories are being established at
Kolkata, and Mumbai for nurturing scientists to undertake studies in this nascent field. Ph.D. program
and fellowship scheme has been introduced this year to give impetus to interdisciplinary research.

3.4 The Committee is not convinced by the achievements listed out by the Ministry with respect
to physical targets of the 12th Plan. The problem in guidelines regarding publication of Research
project paper, re-advertisement of posts, changing the nomenclature of All India Institute of

activities in a systematic manner. It is quite intriguing that a vertical AYUSH structure under

up. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to put in place a robust monitoring
mechanism with respect to the procedural issues for a better monitoring of the progress of
projects/schemes. The Committee would also like the Ministry to timely implement the scheme

quality control of AYUSH drugs and proper coordination among various AYUSH centres.

Accounts 2013-14), it would be befitting to allocate a substantially higher proportion of the Health
Budget for the Ministry of AYUSH. AYUSH has huge potential for effective prevention and therapy that
is also safe and cost effective. Inadequate allocation for AYUSH is, in the opinion of the Committee,
the main reason for not achieving the objectives of AYUSH. The Committee simultaneously observes that
it is imperative that in order to obtain the best possible health outcomes, allocation of resources is
prioritized across competing ends and the available resources deployed in a more efficient manner. The
Committee would, therefore, like the Ministry to prioritize the schemes and utilize funds accordingly and
move the Ministry of Finance for more funds at RE 2017-18 stage based on the efficient and productive
utilization of BE 2017-18 allocation. (Para 2.8)

III. REGULA TION AND QUALITY CONTROL OF AYURVEDIC, SIDDHA, UNANI AND
HOMOEOPATHIC (ASU&H) DRUGS
Recommendation/Observations
3.12 The Committee finds that a large number of samples of ASU&H drugs have failed the testing
procedure in 2013-14, 2014-15 and 2015-16. Even in the year 2016-17, out of 330 samples which were
tested, 36 samples have failed. Interestingly 35 samples were Homoeopathic drugs and only 1 ASU drug.
The Committee would like to point out that the Ministry has not informed about the action taken with
respect to the defaulters as done in previous years. The Committee feels that testing of samples and
consequent action thereupon is one of the most important components of quality control of ASU&H
drugs. The Committee is of the firm view that in case of samples failing the testing process, strict action
needs to be taken. However, merely issuing show cause notices, suspending/cancelling licenses would not
help as the defaulters may start with a new and different license. The Committee believes that in order
to ensure proper and effective regulation of ASU&H drugs, the defaulters must be prosecuted for trying
to play with the lives of people. The Committee, therefore, recommends that stringent measures should
be in place against the erring manufacturers so as to dissuade them from trying to pass just any
formulation as ASU&H drugs. (Para 3.7)
Action taken
3.13 The Committee is informed that as per Section 33 E, 33 EE, 33 EEA in Chapter-IV A of the Drugs
and Cosmetics Act, 1940 respectively are already in place to deal with misbranded, adulterated and
spurious ASU drugs. The State Licensing Authorities are empowered to prohibit the manufacture and sale
of ASU drugs under section 33EEC of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. Ministry of AYUSH has

27
written letters to State Government from time to time to check the quality of ASU drugs in accordance
to the provisions under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules, 1945. Nevertheless, the observations
and recommendations of Hon'ble PSC have been noted and appropriate directions tangible with the legal
provisions may be issued to the State Authorities to take effective actions against erring manufacturers.
Further Recommendation
3.14 The Committee is aware of the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules
made thereunder regarding dealing with misbranded, adulterated and spurious ASU drugs and
also about powers of State Licensing Authorities in this regard. Despite these provisions,
misbranded, adulterated and spurious ASU&H drugs have remained a festering problem and the
safety, efficacy and quality of AYUSH drugs have not been assured. The Committee would like
the Ministry to amend the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 in an appropriate manner so that
defaulters are brought to book and strict action taken against them. The Committee is of the
firm view that suitable amendments alone can help in controlling/monitoring the sale of
misbranded, adulterated and spurious ASU drugs.
Recommendation/Observations
3.15 The Committee is dismayed to note that even after two years since the decision of the creation of
a vertical structure in CDSCO was taken, no real progress has been made so far. Only 12 regulatory posts
have been notified. Recruitment rules for these posts were still in the process of finalization. The
Committee would like to point out that even through CDSCO is under the Department of Health and
Family Welfare of which the Ministry of AYUSH was once a part of, things are not moving at a swift
pace towards finalization of the vertical structure. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry
may take up this issue with the Department of Health and Family Welfare on a priority basis and also
fix a timeline for creation of this vertical structure. The Committee would like to emphasize the fact that
regulation and quality control of ASU&H drugs is one of the most important areas in the Ministry and
if the ASU&H drugs market is regulated efficiently, it will go a long way in building credibility of these
drugs and strengthen the process of mainstreaming of AYUSH. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its
recommendation made in its 95th Report that all inter-ministerial issues may be ironed out within a
designated timeline and the vertical structure created at the earliest. (Para 3.11)
Action Taken
3.16 In order to ensure that the inter-ministerial issues are sorted out amicably, a meeting was held on
8th February, 2017 under the chairmanship of Secretary (AYUSH) with the Addl. Secretary (Health and
FW) and DCG (I) to discuss and review inter alia issues of AYUSH vertical establishment in CDSCO.
Minutes of the meeting have been circulated and a specific letter written to Department of Health and
Family Welfare on 29th March, 2017 with the approval of MoS (AYUSH) for taking necessary action
in respect of issuing a formal communication/notification about the AYUSH vertical structure, work
allocation of the designated Technical officers of the Ministry of AYUSH for discharge of their duties
and for sending statutory issues/documents of AYUSH drugs to the DCG (I) and registration of AYUSH
Ethical Committees. Ministry of AYUSH has already taken up the task of framing recruitment rules in

28
consultation with DoPT, UPSC and Law Ministry before the recruitment process is initiated for the
twelve (12) regulatory posts including seven (07) posts of Inspectors and five (05) posts of Assistant
Drug Controllers and Deputy Drug Controllers.
Further Recommendation
3.17 The Committee has already recommended with respect to this issue in para 3.11.
Recommendation/Observation
3.18 The Committee also takes into cognizance the fact that the Central Sector Scheme for developing
Pharmacovigilance system for ASU&H drugs was still being conceptualized. The Committee urges upon
the Ministry to immediately iron out all pending issues concerning pharmacovigilance system for AYUSH
so that the scheme is implemented as early as possible and all necessary approvals sought and other
procedural formalities completed. (Para 3.12)
Action Taken
3.19 It is envisaged to seek the approval for implementing the Central Sector Scheme of Pharmacovigilance
of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy Medicines in 2017-18, for which necessary allocation has

Further Recommendation
3.20 The Central Sector Scheme for developing Pharmacovigilance system for ASU&H drugs was
envisaged in the 12th Plan but the scheme could not be implemented even after conclusion of
the 12th Plan period. The Committee is of the view that this inordinate delay in implementation

Recommendation/Observation
3.21 The Committee observes that in the past the oft-repeated contention of the Ministry has been that
due to the ineffectiveness of the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954,
it has not been possible to take stringent action against the misleading and exaggerated claims of
efficacy of the AYUSH remedies and that certain amendments were needed to be carried out in the said
Act. The Department of Health and Family Welfare which had constituted a Task Force for suggesting
amendments to the aforesaid Act, has been requested to expedite consolidation of the amendment provisions
recommended by the Task Force. But the latest submissions of the Ministry indicate that the amendment
to the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act is far from being materialized. The Committee would like the
Ministry to indicate the time-frame within which the amendment of the Magic Remedies Act would be
enacted. (Para 3.15)

29
Action Taken
3.22 The Department of Health and Family Welfare is responsible to take up the revision or amendment
of the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954. However, it is understood
that a view has been taken on the recommendations of the Group of Ministers to include the regulatory
provisions for advertisements of drugs in the new legislation being framed for Drugs and Cosmetics.
Ministry of AYUSH separately took up the amendment of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 to insert
regulatory provisions for Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs related advertisements, on which final view
is to be taken on the basis of comments/suggestions/objections received from the stakeholders and to
consider whether or not or in what manner the intended rules be notified.
Further Recommendation
3.23 The Committee is constrained to note the snail's pace of progress made in amending the
Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954. Taking into account the
fact that the lack of stringent regulatory provisions has allowed unscrupulous elements to dupe
innocent people by making tall claims about providing cure to cancer, liver cirrhosis, kidney
failure and other chronic diseases without scientific evidence, the Committee in its 75th Report
concerning Ministry of AYUSH (the then Department of AYUSH) presented to Parliament on 9th
December , 2013 had recommended that urgent measures be taken to amend the said Act. Almost
four years have passed since then, but the amendment could not be finalized. The Committee,
therefore, deprecates the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in whose legislative domain the
amendment to the said Act falls, for its inertia and indifference in the matter and would like
the Ministry of AYUSH to convey this Committee's displeasure to the former. The Committee
would also recommend that the necessary amendments be carried out expeditiously within a
specified time-frame and the outcome intimated to the Committee.
IV . NATIONAL AYUSH MISSION (NAM)
3.24 The Committee is aware that the overall standard of AYUSH education in the country continues to
be extremely poor. The Committee feels that the mandatory requirement of accreditation of teaching
hospitals and surprise inspection teams are efforts in the right direction. Further, in order to promote
AYUSH education, effective curricula reforms will also need to be carried out. The Committee also
recommends that practitioners of Allopathy should be sensitized to the strengths of AYUSH system and
to the cross system referrals between healthcare providers of all systems of medicine so that ignorance
about AYUSH is dispelled and AYUSH is integrated in the health delivery system. The Committee also
recommends that the Ministry should prepare a framework for fostering collaborative and interdisciplinary
AYUSH research of contemporary relevance. Further, NEET and NPGET test for UG and PG students
to regulate the entry of qualified students into these institutions is a much awaited step. The Committee,
therefore, recommends the Ministry that these measures may be implemented at the earliest for visible
improvement in the quality of AYUSH education. (Para 4.6)

30
Action Taken
National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) for admission in Under-Graduate course of ASU&H
colleges:
3.25 In order to bring meritorious students to the ASU&H systems of medicine in the country, a decision
was taken that the entrance exam being conducted by the private association may be stopped and all
admissions in Under-Graduate course of ASU&H colleges shall be made only through National Eligibility
cum Entrance Test (NEET) to be conducted by the CBSE from the Academic Year 2017-18. This matter
was taken up with CBSE and Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
3.26 Meanwhile, the Ministry has received representations from certain State Governments expressing
their inability to admit students into AYUSH-UG courses for the Academic Year 2017-18 as CBSE has
not included the AYUSH-UG courses in its notification. In this regard, the Ministry has also received
representations about allowing the management/NRI quota as it is being permitted for MBBS/BDS seats.
The matter was examined by the Ministry and after considering the representations made by the State
Governments, following has been decided and conveyed to the State Governments on 26.04.2017:
(i) Since, it is important to ensure that meritorious students/candidates come to AYUSH streams
of medicine, it would be advisable to the State/UT Government to adopt the merit list of NEET
for admission in AYUSH-UG courses for the Academic Year 2017-18 as per the existing
reservation policies of the concerned State Government in tune with CBSE notification of

Entrance Test (CET) of the concerned State Government as per the existing Rules and Policies

(iii) Admission in AYUSH-UG Courses shall be compulsorily through NEET merit list from the A.Y .
2018-19.

Recommendation/Observation

regarding place, time and phytochemical properties of medicinal plants, which are the three basic

projects in the healthcare delivery system. From a perusal of Annexure III, it is not clear as to
how many outcomes of research projects of CCRS have led to development/introduction of new
health products or technologies into the healthcare system. The Committee, therefore, desires
to be apprised of the measurable health products/processes and innovative technologies introduced
into health programmes of the country as a result of the research projects undertaken by CCRS
during the last five years. The Committee also recommends that a time-frame for completion
of research projects need to be finalised and preparatory exercises like procurement of equipment
and recruitment of staff need to be completed expeditiously so that the real work is set in motion
without any delay.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A GLANCE
II. BUDGET ALLOCATION
The Committee is not convinced by the achievements listed out by the Ministry with respect
to physical targets of the 12th Plan. The problem in guidelines regarding publication of Research
project paper, re-advertisement of posts, changing the nomenclature of All India Institute of
Unani Medicine, All India Institute of Homeopathy, delay in finalization of draft curriculum, non-
availability of teaching faculties, non-availability of separate psychiatry unit in NIH, Kolkata etc.
are routine issues. They could have been resolved with a streamlined monitoring mechanism for
early and timely intervention of the Ministry and necessary remedial measures taken. The
Committee also takes serious note of the fact that the Central Sector Scheme of Pharmacovigilance
of Ayurveda Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy medicines could not be implemented for want of
regulatory structure and centralized coordination system for carrying out pharmacovigilance
activities in a systematic manner. It is quite intriguing that a vertical AYUSH structure under
the aegis of the CDSCO with no specific time-frame as such is still in the process of being set
up. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to put in place a robust monitoring
mechanism with respect to the procedural issues for a better monitoring of the progress of
projects/schemes. The Committee would also like the Ministry to timely implement the scheme
of pharmacoviligance of AYUSH medicines and setting up of a vertical AYUSH structure for
quality control of AYUSH drugs and proper coordination among various AYUSH centres.
(Para 3.4)
The Committee points out that two of the fundamental issues that hamper allocation of
more funds to the Ministry are pending UCs and lack of absorption capacity. It would like to be
updated about the corrective measures taken by the Ministry to address these concerns. The
Committee also desires to be apprised of the quantum of additional funds, if any, allocated at
RE stage and utilization figures thereof. (Para 3.7)
The Committee in its previous Reports on Demands for Grants have been exhorting the
Ministry to quickly sort out the lingering issues concerning the regulatory framework of AYUSH
drugs. The Ministry has not been able to set up a central vertical structure of AYUSH drugs
regulation under CDSCO uptill now, despite the fact that the National Health Policy 2017 recognizes
the need to establish a robust and effective quality assurance mechanism for AYUSH drugs. The
feedback that Secretary (AYUSH) had taken review meeting is hardly convincing. The fact
remains that the current arrangement is not producing the intended results. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that an empowered committee may be set up to monitor the progress of
the new regulatory structure of AYUSH drugs which may submit periodical progress reports to
the Ministry. (Para 3.11)
III. REGULA TION AND QUALITY CONTROL OF AYURVEDIC, SIDDHA, UNANI AND
HOMOEOPATHIC (ASU&H) DRUGS
The Committee is aware of the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules
made thereunder regarding dealing with misbranded, adulterated and spurious ASU drugs and
37

38
also about powers of State Licensing Authorities in this regard. Despite these provisions,
misbranded, adulterated and spurious ASU&H drugs have remained a festering problem and the
safety, efficacy and quality of AYUSH drugs have not been assured. The Committee would like
the Ministry to amend the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 in an appropriate manner so that
defaulters are brought to book and strict action taken against them. The Committee is of the
firm view that suitable amendments alone can help in controlling/monitoring the sale of
misbranded, adulterated and spurious ASU drugs. (Para 3.14)
The Committee has already recommended with respect to this issue in para 3.11.
(para 3.17)
The Central Sector Scheme for developing Pharmacovigilance system for ASU&H drugs was
envisaged in the 12th Plan but the scheme could not be implemented even after conclusion of
the 12th Plan period. The Committee is of the view that this inordinate delay in implementation
of the project reflects lack of efficiency and inadequate follow-up by the administrative machinery
in the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends to the Ministry to constantly
monitor and follow up on the implementation of this important project concerning pharmacovigilance
of AYUSH drugs so that the issue of time-lag in utilization of allocated funds and implementation
of this Project is promptly addressed. (Para 3.20)
The Committee is constrained to note the snail's pace of progress made in amending the
Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954. Taking into account the
fact that the lack of stringent regulatory provisions has allowed unscrupulous elements to dupe
innocent people by making tall claims about providing cure to cancer, liver cirrhosis, kidney
failure and other chronic diseases without scientific evidence, the Committee in its 75th Report
concerning Ministry of AYUSH (the then Department of AYUSH) presented to Parliament on 9th
December, 2013 had recommended that urgent measures be taken to amend the said Act. Almost
four years have passed since then, but the amendment could not be finalized. The Committee,
therefore, deprecates the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in whose legislative domain the
amendment to the said Act falls, for its inertia and indifference in the matter and would like
the Ministry of AYUSH to convey this Committee's displeasure to the former. The Committee
would also recommend that the necessary amendments be carried out expeditiously within a
specified time-frame and the outcome intimated to the Committee. (Para 3.23)
IV. NATIONAL AYUSH MISSION (NAM)
The Committee appreciates the Ministry for introducing National Eligibility cum Entrance
Test (NEET) for bringing meritorious students to the AYUSH systems of medicine in the country.
The Committee would, however, like to reiterate that the Ministry must make efforts to integrate
traditional as well as modern system of medicine and education so that an integrated approach
can be taken in health delivery system. The Committee would also like to highlight the need for
curricula reforms in order to promote quality AYUSH education and recommends to the Ministry
to take necessary action in this regard. (Para 3.27)

39
V . NATIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS BOARD
The Committee is of the view that merely advising the State Missions to take the initiative
to maintain passport database of medicinal plants is not enough. The Committee would, therefore,
recommend to the Ministry to play a pro-active role in this regard and incentivize the State
Governments to start maintaining a database of medicinal plants. (Para 3.30)
VI. STATUS OF PROGRESS OF SCHEMES IN NORTH EASTERN STATES
The Committee is disdained to note that work on various research projects were hampered
at RARI, Gangtok and RARI, Itanagar due to infrastructural constraints which should have been
taken care of in the first instance before the starting of these Institutes. The Committee also
notes that the reply of the Ministry is bereft of the specific information asked for by the
Committee as to whether the knowledge generated through the research carried out at these
Research Institutes have facilitated solutions to the health issues specific to the North Eastern
region. The Committee further desires to know the time-lag in translating research outcomes
at these Institutes into tangible health products. (Para 3.33)
North Eastern Institute of Ayurveda and Homoeopathy (NEIAH), Shillong
The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the final outcome in filling up vacant posts

North Eastern of Folk Medicine (NEIFM), Passighat
The Committee desires to know as to by when NEIFM is targeted to be made functional and
whether there is any time and cost overruns involved in making the Institute operational. The
Committee would also like to highlight the fact that without adequate manpower, the very
purpose of setting up of this Institute would be defeated and it would take a very long time for
the NEIFM, Passighat to become operational. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a pro-
active approach needs to be adopted by the Ministry to fill up the vacant posts so that NEIFM
becomes operational as early as possible. (Para 3.40)
VIII. NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF HOMOEOPATHY, KOLKATA
The Committee finds the reply of the Ministry with respect to expansion of the existing 100
bedded to 250 bedded hospital very vague and evasive as the present status of the work done in

completion of work of internal electrical connections by CPWD would not take much time and
hopes that all other expansion related works are complete in all respects so that 250 bedded
hospital become operational at the earliest. The Committee would also like to be apprised if there
has been any cost escalation due to delay in the expansion work. (Para 3.43)
